  (*on aurait pu*), *il aurait fallu* + infinitive, polite past (*j'aurais voulu savoir*), and
  next lesson's *si j'avais su, …*
- *J'aurais dû* + infinitive = I should have; *j'aurais pu* + infinitive = I could have.
- In the news, *aurait fait, serait entré* = reportedly (recognition only; honors 12h2).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: If I had known: si + plus-que-parfait and the conditionnel passé
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 imagined the present (*Si j'avais le temps, je viendrais*). Lesson 10 built the
conditionnel passé (*je serais venu*). This lesson puts the plus-que-parfait (lesson 02) after
*si* and completes the system: *Si j'avais su, je serais venu.* — If I had known, I would have
come. You'll also mix the types (a past cause with a present result), use *si seulement* for
wishes and regrets, and set a condition without *si* at all.

The theme is turning points: chance meetings, career changes, luck and bad luck, the day
everything changed. It stays personal: honors lesson 12h1 does the same thing with history.

## The past unreal condition

To imagine a past that didn't happen, French uses the **[[past unreal condition]]** (type 3): *si* +
plus-que-parfait, then the conditionnel passé.

| si + plus-que-parfait | conditionnel passé |
|---|---|
| *Si j'avais su,* | *je serais venu(e).* — If I'd known, I'd have come. |
| *Si tu m'avais appelé,* | *je t'aurais aidé.* — If you'd called me, I'd have helped you. |
| *S'il n'avait pas plu,* | *on aurait mangé dehors.* — If it hadn't rained, we'd have eaten outside. |
| *Si nous étions partis plus tôt,* | *nous n'aurions pas raté le train.* |
| *Si vous aviez parié sur ce cheval,* | *vous auriez gagné.* |
| *Si elles s'étaient reconverties plus tôt,* | *elles auraient été plus heureuses.* |

Both halves are compound tenses, and both follow the passé composé's rules: *être* or *avoir*,
agreement with *être* (*étions partis, s'étaient reconverties*), *ne … pas* around the
auxiliary. As always, either half can come first: *Je serais venu si j'avais su.*

What it's for:

- imagining another past: *Si je n'avais pas croisé Lucie ce jour-là, je ne serais jamais parti au
  Chili.*
- regret: *Si j'avais travaillé un peu plus, j'aurais eu mon bac.*
- relief: *Si tu n'avais pas freiné, on aurait eu un accident.*
- reproach: *Si tu m'avais écouté, on ne se serait pas perdus !*

### Example 1: from the facts to the past unreal condition

*Facts.* Malik missed his bus. He walked to work and met Léa, his future wife, in a café.

*Task.* Say what would have happened if he hadn't missed the bus.

1. Turn each fact around: he missed the bus → he didn't miss it; he met Léa → he wouldn't have
   met her.
2. Put the condition in the plus-que-parfait: *rater* takes *avoir* → *s'il n'avait pas raté son
   bus*.
3. Put the result in the conditionnel passé: *rencontrer* takes *avoir* → *il n'aurait pas
   rencontré Léa*.
4. Result: *S'il n'avait pas raté son bus, il n'aurait pas rencontré Léa.* — If he hadn't missed
   his bus, he wouldn't have met Léa.

Notice the reversal: a true positive fact becomes negative in the sentence, and the other way
round. That's what "unreal" means.

## Mixed conditionals

Sometimes the condition and the result belong to different times. French then mixes the types,
just as English does. These are **[[mixed conditionals]]**.

### Mixed 1: a past cause, a present result

*Si* + plus-que-parfait, then the conditionnel présent.

- *Si j'avais pris le train, je serais déjà là.* — If I'd taken the train, I'd be there by now.
- *Si elle n'avait pas fait ce stage, elle ne serait pas architecte aujourd'hui.* — If she hadn't
  done that internship, she wouldn't be an architect today.
- *Si on s'était couchés plus tôt, on serait moins fatigués.* — If we'd gone to bed earlier, we'd
  be less tired.

Words like *aujourd'hui, maintenant, déjà, encore* often signal a present result.

### Mixed 2: a lasting situation, a past result

*Si* + imparfait, then the conditionnel passé.

- *Si j'étais plus courageux, je l'aurais fait.* — If I were braver (I'm not, in general), I'd
  have done it.
- *Si Marc parlait allemand, il aurait accepté ce poste à Berlin.* — If Marc spoke German (he
  doesn't), he'd have taken that job in Berlin.

Here the imparfait describes something that is still true, a permanent trait or skill; the
result was a single past event.

![A diagram in two rows titled Mixed conditionals: each half has its own time. Top row: a box marked past, Si j'avais pris le train, labelled plus-que-parfait, with an arrow to a box marked now, je serais déjà là, labelled conditionnel présent; the timeline under it has a dot in the past and a circle at maintenant. Bottom row: a box marked always, Si j'étais plus courageux, labelled imparfait, with an arrow to a box marked past, je l'aurais fait, labelled conditionnel passé; the timeline under it has a long band labelled a lasting trait and a dot in the past, before maintenant.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: which tenses?

*Task.* Complete each sentence. Ask two questions: when is the condition? When is the result?

| sentence | condition | result | answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Si tu ___ (venir) hier, tu aurais vu Paul.* | past (*hier*) | past | *étais venu(e)* (type 3) |
| *Si tu ___ (venir) hier, tu connaîtrais Paul maintenant.* | past | present (*maintenant*) | *étais venu(e)* (mixed 1) |
| *Si j'___ (être) moins timide, je lui aurais parlé à la fête.* | always | past (*à la fête*) | *étais* (mixed 2) |
| *Si j'___ (être) moins timide, je lui parlerais.* | now | now | *étais* (type 2) |

The *si* clause and the main clause each get the tense that fits their own time. The only rule
that never moves: no conditionnel after *si*.

## Si seulement: if only

*Si seulement* + imparfait or plus-que-parfait, usually with no main clause, expresses a wish or
a regret:

- *Si seulement j'avais plus de temps !* — If only I had more time! (a wish about now: imparfait)
- *Si seulement je l'avais écouté !* — If only I'd listened to him! (a regret about the past:
  plus-que-parfait)

You can add a main clause, with the usual tenses: *Si seulement il avait parié sur moi, on aurait
gagné.*

## A condition without si

- *Sans* + noun, then the conditionnel: *Sans ton aide, j'aurais abandonné.* — Without your help,
  I'd have given up. (= *Si tu ne m'avais pas aidé, …*) *Sans cette rencontre, je ne serais pas
  là aujourd'hui.* (mixed: past meeting, present result)
- *À ta place* (A2), which you met with the conditionnel présent, works with the conditionnel
  passé too: *À ta place, j'aurais refusé.* — If I'd been you, I'd have said no.

## The rule, one last time

In every type, after *si* meaning "if": no futur and no conditionnel.

- ~~Si j'aurais su~~ → *Si j'avais su*.
- ~~Si tu serais venu~~ → *Si tu étais venu*.

The conditionnel always goes in the other half of the sentence.

## All the si-clauses together

| type | *si* + … | main clause | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 real | present | present / futur / imperative | *Si tu viens, on ira au cinéma.* |
| 2 unreal now | imparfait | conditionnel présent | *Si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais.* |
| 3 unreal past | plus-que-parfait | conditionnel passé | *Si j'avais su, je serais venu.* |
| mixed 1 | plus-que-parfait | conditionnel présent | *Si j'avais pris le train, je serais déjà là.* |
| mixed 2 | imparfait | conditionnel passé | *Si j'étais plus courageux, je l'aurais fait.* |

![A path that forks at a signpost labelled 8 h 15, le bus. The solid upper path, labelled ce qui s'est passé (what happened), passes a bus driving away, a man walking, and a café with two people in it. The dotted lower path, labelled ce qui se serait passé (what would have happened), passes a bus with the man inside, and an office (bureau) with the man standing alone. Captions: Il a raté son bus. Il a rencontré Léa. / S'il n'avait pas raté son bus, il n'aurait pas rencontré Léa.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Turning points: the words

- *Le tournant* (turning point): *un tournant dans ma vie*. A moment that decides things is
  *décisif* (*décisive*): *une rencontre décisive*.
- *La rencontre* is a meeting, often by chance. *Croiser quelqu'un* is to come across or pass
  someone (*J'ai croisé ton frère au marché*); *croiser les bras* is to fold your arms. (To cross
  a street is *traverser*, A1.)
- *Le coup de foudre* is love at first sight, literally a lightning strike (*J'ai eu le coup de
  foudre pour elle*, and also *pour cette ville*). *Un coup de chance* is a stroke of luck; *la
  malchance* is bad luck.
- *Bouleverser* is to turn upside down, or to move deeply (*Ce film m'a bouleversé*), and *le
  bouleversement* is an upheaval.
- Careers: *l'orientation* (choosing your studies: *le conseiller d'orientation*, the careers
  adviser), *la vocation* (a calling: *Elle a trouvé sa vocation*), *la reconversion* and *se
  reconvertir* (to retrain, change careers: *Il s'est reconverti dans la menuiserie*; conjugated
  like *finir*: *nous nous reconvertissons*).
- Character: *courageux* (*courageuse*), *le courage*, and its opposite *lâche* (cowardly; *un
  lâche* is a coward).
- Taking a chance: *le pari* (bet), *parier* (*Je parie qu'il va pleuvoir*). *Le succès* is
  success with the public, a hit (*Le film a eu un grand succès*); personal success is more often
  *la réussite* (A2).
- Getting through: *la difficulté* (*avoir des difficultés à* + infinitive), *s'en sortir* (to
  pull through, to cope: *Je m'en sors*; passé composé *je m'en suis sorti*), *se débrouiller* (to
  manage, get by: *Je me débrouille en espagnol*; *Débrouille-toi !* — Sort it out yourself!).
- *Prévisible* (predictable) and *imprévisible* (unpredictable): *La vie est imprévisible.*

## Dialogue: Une rencontre dans le train

Sophie and Antoine were at university together. Fifteen years later, they meet on a train.

> **Antoine :** Sophie ? Ça alors ! Quel coup de chance !
>
> **Sophie :** Antoine ! Tu n'as pas changé ! Tu es toujours prof de maths ?
>
> **Antoine :** Non, je me suis reconverti il y a cinq ans. Je suis boulanger maintenant.
>
> **Sophie :** Boulanger ? Si tu me l'avais dit à vingt ans, je ne t'aurais pas cru !
>
> **Antoine :** Moi non plus ! Mais j'étais épuisé. Si j'avais continué, je serais malade
> aujourd'hui. Et toi ?
>
> **Sophie :** Moi, je suis restée dans la même entreprise. Si j'étais plus courageuse, j'aurais
> changé de métier aussi. Si seulement j'avais eu ton courage !
>
> **Antoine :** Ce n'est pas du courage, c'est un pari. Ça aurait pu mal finir.
>
> **Sophie :** Mais tu t'en es sorti ! Bon, je descends à Dijon… Si on ne s'était pas croisés
> aujourd'hui, on ne se serait jamais revus !

Antoine: Sophie? Well I never! What a stroke of luck! Sophie: Antoine! You haven't changed! Are
you still a maths teacher? Antoine: No, I retrained five years ago. I'm a baker now. Sophie: A
baker? If you'd told me that at twenty, I wouldn't have believed you! Antoine: Nor would I! But I
was exhausted. If I'd carried on, I'd be ill today. And you? Sophie: I stayed in the same company.
If I were braver, I'd have changed jobs too. If only I'd had your courage! Antoine: It isn't
courage, it's a bet. It could have ended badly. Sophie: But you pulled through! Right, I get off
at Dijon … If we hadn't bumped into each other today, we'd never have seen each other again!

*Si tu me l'avais dit* has two pronouns (*me* + *l'*); lesson 16 explains the order. Find the
mixed conditionals: *Si j'avais continué, je serais malade aujourd'hui* (past → now) and *Si
j'étais plus courageuse, j'aurais changé de métier* (always → past).

## Reading: Le jour où tout a basculé

A magazine asked readers about the turning point in their lives.

> *« Le tournant de ma vie, c'est une panne de voiture. En 2014, je travaillais dans une banque à
> Nantes et je m'ennuyais. Un soir d'hiver, ma voiture est tombée en panne sur une petite route.
> Un agriculteur s'est arrêté pour m'aider et, pendant qu'on attendait la dépanneuse, il m'a parlé
> de son métier pendant une heure. C'était imprévisible : je suis rentrée chez moi bouleversée.*
>
> *Six mois plus tard, j'avais démissionné et je commençais une formation agricole. Ma reconversion
> n'a pas été facile. J'ai eu des difficultés, j'ai connu la malchance (deux étés de sécheresse !),
> et parfois je me suis demandé si j'avais fait le bon choix. Mais je me suis débrouillée et je
> m'en suis sortie.*
>
> *Aujourd'hui, j'ai une petite ferme et je vends mes légumes au marché. Si ma voiture n'était
> pas tombée en panne ce soir-là, je serais encore à la banque. Et si cet homme ne s'était pas
> arrêté, je n'aurais jamais pensé à ce métier. Je ne crois pas au destin, mais je crois aux
> rencontres décisives. Si seulement j'avais pu le remercier ! Je ne connais même pas son nom. »*
>
> *Camille, 43 ans*

Translation:

> "The turning point of my life was a car breakdown. In 2014 I worked in a bank in Nantes and I
> was bored. One winter evening my car broke down on a small road. A farmer stopped to help me,
> and while we were waiting for the breakdown truck, he talked to me about his work for an hour.
> It was unpredictable: I went home deeply moved.
>
> Six months later, I had resigned and I was starting an agricultural training course. My career
> change wasn't easy. I had difficulties, I had bad luck (two summers of drought!), and sometimes
> I wondered whether I'd made the right choice. But I managed and I got through it.
>
> Today I have a small farm and I sell my vegetables at the market. If my car hadn't broken down
> that evening, I'd still be at the bank. And if that man hadn't stopped, I'd never have thought of
> this job. I don't believe in fate, but I believe in decisive encounters. If only I'd been able to
> thank him! I don't even know his name."
>
> Camille, 43

(*basculer* = to tip over, to change completely; *tomber en panne* = to break down; *la dépanneuse*
= the breakdown truck; *la formation* = training; *la sécheresse* = drought, lesson 19.)
Notice *je me suis demandé si j'avais fait le bon choix*: *si* = whether, so the tense is free.

## Pronunciation

- *Si j'avais su* [si ʒavɛ sy]: the first thing many learners hear and remember. Say it as one
  group.
- *Le coup de foudre* [ku d(ə) fudʁ]: the *p* of *coup* is silent.
- *Le pari* and *Paris* sound the same [paʁi]. *Parier* has two syllables: [pa-ʁje].
- *Lâche* [lɑʃ] or [laʃ]: both are heard, and most speakers say it like *la* + *ch*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~Si j'aurais su~~ → *Si j'avais su*.
- A past result needs the conditionnel passé: *Si tu m'avais invité, je serais venu.* With *je
  viendrais* the result moves to now or later (I'd come now): keep the conditionnel présent for a
  present result, as in *je serais là maintenant*.
- ~~Si je n'aurais pas raté le bus~~ → *Si je n'avais pas raté le bus*.
- Agreement: *Si elle était partie plus tôt, elle serait arrivée à l'heure* (*être* verbs agree in both
  halves).
- *Croiser* is not "to cross the road" (*traverser*).
- *Le succès* is masculine and ends in *-ès* in the singular too: *un grand succès, des
  succès*.

## Key points

- Past unreal condition: *si* + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé: *Si j'avais su, je serais
  venu.*
- Mixed: past cause → present result (*si j'avais pris le train, je serais déjà là*); lasting
  situation → past result (*si j'étais plus courageux, je l'aurais fait*). Give each half the
  tense of its own time.
- *Si seulement* + imparfait (a wish now) or + plus-que-parfait (a regret).
- Without *si*: *sans* + noun (*Sans ton aide, j'aurais abandonné*), *à ta place* + conditionnel.
- Never the conditionnel after *si* = if, in any type.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: By then I will have …: future time clauses and the futur antérieur
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last three lessons imagined things that aren't, or weren't, true. This one looks ahead at
things that will be true, in order: first one thing, then another. You'll learn two habits that
English speakers find odd at first:

- after *quand, dès que* and similar words, French uses the **[[futur simple]]** where English uses
  the present: *Quand tu arriveras, on mangera.* — When you arrive, we'll eat.
- for an action that will be finished before another future one, French uses the futur
  antérieur: *Quand tu auras fini, tu m'appelleras.* — When you've finished, call me.

The futur antérieur is the last compound tense of the family you met in lesson 10. The theme is
the city of tomorrow: building sites, cycle lanes, renovation, and the plans a town makes for
2030 and beyond.

## Quand + futur: the future in time clauses

In lesson 03 you used time clauses about the past (*Dès qu'il avait fini, il sortait*). For the
future, the time clause goes in the future too:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *Quand tu arriveras, on mangera.* | When you arrive, we'll eat. |
| *Lorsque le tram sera là, tout le monde le prendra.* | When the tram is here, everyone will take it. |
| *Dès qu'il fera beau, on ira à la plage.* | As soon as the weather is nice, we'll go to the beach. |
| *Aussitôt que je saurai la date, je te le dirai.* | As soon as I know the date, I'll tell you. |
| *Une fois que tu seras installé, tu m'inviteras ?* | Once you're settled in, will you invite me? |
| *Tant que la rue sera fermée, les bus passeront par le pont.* | As long as the street is closed, the buses will go over the bridge. |

*Lorsque* means the same as *quand* and is a little more formal. *Aussitôt que* is a more formal
*dès que*. The main clause can also be an imperative: *Quand tu arriveras, appelle-moi.*

Three things to keep apart:

- A habit takes the present, as in English: *Quand il pleut, je prends le bus.* — When(ever)
  it rains, I take the bus.
- In relaxed speech you'll often hear the present in both halves for a future plan: *Quand tu
  arrives, tu m'appelles.* That's fine informally. What careful French avoids is a mixture, a
  present after *quand* with a futur in the main clause: write *Quand tu arriveras, tu
  m'appelleras*, or say the informal version.
- *Si* is different. *Si* + present (type 1) says "maybe": *Si tu viens, on ira au cinéma.*
  *Quand* + futur says "it will happen": *Quand tu viendras, on ira au cinéma.* Never a futur after
  *si* meaning "if" (lesson 09).

## The futur antérieur

The **[[futur antérieur]]** is the futur simple of *avoir* or *être* + the past participle. Same
auxiliaries, same agreement as the passé composé:

| | finir (avoir) | partir (être) | s'installer (être) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je / j' | aurai fini | serai parti(e) | me serai installé(e) |
| tu | auras fini | seras parti(e) | te seras installé(e) |
| il / elle / on | aura fini | sera parti(e) | se sera installé(e) |
| nous | aurons fini | serons parti(e)s | nous serons installé(e)s |
| vous | aurez fini | serez parti(e)(s) | vous serez installé(e)(s) |
| ils / elles | auront fini | seront parti(e)s | se seront installé(e)s |

The auxiliary has the futur's endings: *-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont*. Compare the conditionnel
passé (*j'aurais fini*): one letter apart in writing, and a different meaning.

### 1. Finished before another future action

The futur antérieur marks the action that comes first; the futur simple, the one that
follows:

- *Quand tu auras fini, tu m'appelleras.* — When you've finished, (you'll) call me. (First you
  finish, then you call.)
- *Dès que j'aurai reçu la réponse, je vous écrirai.* — As soon as I've had the answer, I'll write
  to you.
- *Une fois que la ville aura terminé le chantier, la rue sera beaucoup plus calme.* — Once the
  town has finished the building work, the street will be much quieter.
- *On partira quand tout le monde sera arrivé.* — We'll leave when everyone has arrived.

Where English says "when you have finished", French nearly always says *quand tu auras fini*.

### 2. Finished by a point in the future

With *d'ici* + a date, *avant* + a date, or *dans* + a length of time, the futur antérieur says
what will be done by then:

- *D'ici 2030, la ville aura construit trois lignes de tram.* — By 2030, the city will have built
  three tram lines.
- *D'ici demain, j'aurai terminé le rapport.* — I'll have finished the report by tomorrow.
- *Dans deux ans, nous aurons rénové toutes les écoles du quartier.* — In two years' time, we'll
  have renovated all the neighbourhood's schools.

*D'ici* means "between now and" a future time; it also means "from here" (*D'ici, on voit la
mer*), and *d'ici là* is "by then, between now and then".

### 3. A guess about the past (recognition)

The futur antérieur can also guess why something has happened: *Paul n'est pas là ? Il aura
oublié.* — Paul isn't here? He must have forgotten. *Elle se sera trompée de route.* — She must
have taken the wrong road. You only need to recognise this; for your own sentences, *il a dû
oublier* says the same thing.

![A horizontal timeline with an arrow pointing right. A marker labelled maintenant is at the left. Just after it, a short bracket labelled futur proche: je vais partir. Further on, a longer bracket labelled futur simple: je partirai. Further right, a vertical flag labelled d'ici 2030, with a filled dot just before it labelled futur antérieur: j'aurai fini (finished before the flag). Under the timeline, a second example row: Quand tu auras fini (dot first), tu m'appelleras (arrow after).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: building the futur antérieur

*Task.* Put each verb in the futur antérieur.

| verb, subject | auxiliary? | futur of the auxiliary | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| *construire*, nous | avoir | *aurons* | *nous aurons construit* |
| *arriver*, elles | être | *seront* | *elles seront arrivées* |
| *se décider*, tu (a woman) | être (pronominal) | *seras* | *tu te seras décidée* |
| *inaugurer*, la mairie | avoir | *aura* | *la mairie aura inauguré* |
| *prendre*, je | avoir | *aurai* | *j'aurai pris* |

Same method as every compound tense: choose the auxiliary, conjugate it, add the participle,
check the agreement.

### Example 2: futur simple or futur antérieur in the time clause?

*Task.* Read each sentence and say why the tense was chosen.

1. *Quand le tram passera devant chez moi, je vendrai ma voiture.* Futur simple: the two things
   happen together, or nearly. "When the tram runs past my house."
2. *Quand la mairie aura fini les travaux, je vendrai ma voiture.* Futur antérieur: the work will
   be over first, then I'll sell. "When the town hall has finished the work."
3. *Dès que je recevrai ta lettre, je te répondrai* and *Dès que j'aurai reçu ta lettre, je te
   répondrai* are both correct. The second stresses that the letter must have arrived first.
4. *Quand tu arrives, tu m'appelles* is relaxed spoken French; in writing, use *Quand tu
   arriveras, tu m'appelleras*.

## Three future tenses on one line

| tense | form | use | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| futur proche | *aller* + infinitive | near, decided, everyday speech | *Je vais partir.* |
| futur simple | stem + *-ai, -as, -a* … | predictions, promises, plans further ahead; after *quand* | *Je partirai en juin.* |
| futur antérieur | *aurai / serai* + participle | finished before another future moment | *J'aurai fini d'ici juin.* |

## The city of tomorrow: the words

- *L'urbanisme* (town planning) is the job of the town hall and of *l'architecte* (*un architecte,
  une architecte*). Before building, architects show *une maquette*, a scale model.
- *Le chantier* is the building site (*la rue est en chantier* = there's building work in the
  street). *Construire* (*je construis, nous construisons, j'ai construit*: like *conduire*) gives
  *la construction*; *rénover* gives *la rénovation*.
- *Aménager* is to develop or lay out an area (*aménager les berges du fleuve*), or to fit out a
  space (*aménager une cuisine*); *nous aménageons*, with *e* before *o*. Not to be confused with
  *déménager* (to move house, A1).
- *La zone* (area, zone): *une zone industrielle, une zone rurale*. *La zone piétonne* is for
  pedestrians only; *la piste cyclable* is the cycle lane.
- Money: *l'investissement*, *investir* (like *finir*: *nous investissons*), *financer* (*nous
  finançons*, with *ç* before *o*), *le financement*.
- Time: *à court terme* (in the short term), *à long terme* (in the long term), *progressivement*
  (gradually), *terminer* (to finish, to end: a little more formal than *finir*).
- *Inaugurer* is to open officially (*Le maire inaugurera le pont en mai*), *l'inauguration* the
  opening ceremony.
- *La prévision* is a forecast (*les prévisions météo*); *prédire* is to predict (like *dire*,
  except *vous prédisez*).

![A town plan in two halves. The left half, titled Aujourd'hui, shows a block of flats, a road full of cars, and a fenced building site with a crane, labelled le chantier. The right half, titled En 2030, shows a paved square with people walking and a no-cars sign, labelled la zone piétonne; a row of trees; a green lane with a bicycle symbol, labelled la piste cyclable; and a tram on rails, labelled le tramway.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: La réunion publique

At a public meeting in the town hall, an architect presents a model of the new square.

> **L'architecte :** Voici la maquette de la future place. Quand nous aurons terminé les travaux,
> les voitures ne passeront plus ici : ce sera une zone piétonne.
>
> **Un habitant :** Et le chantier va durer combien de temps ?
>
> **L'architecte :** Dix-huit mois. D'ici l'été prochain, nous aurons fini la première partie.
>
> **Une habitante :** Et pour les vélos ? Il n'y a pas de piste cyclable dans la rue principale.
>
> **L'architecte :** Elle est prévue. Une fois que la ville aura prolongé le tram, on aménagera
> une piste cyclable des deux côtés.
>
> **Un habitant :** Et qui va payer tout ça ?
>
> **L'architecte :** La ville et la région financent le projet. C'est un gros investissement, mais
> à long terme, la ville sera plus agréable.
>
> **Une habitante :** C'est beau, sur la maquette. Je le croirai quand je l'aurai vu !

The architect: Here's the model of the future square. When we've finished the work, cars won't
come through here any more: it'll be a pedestrian zone. A resident: And how long will the building work
last? The architect: Eighteen months. By next summer, we'll have finished the first part. A
resident: And for bikes? There's no cycle lane on the main street. The architect: It's planned.
Once the town has extended the tram, we'll put in a cycle lane on both sides. A resident: And who's going to pay for all that? The architect: The town and the
region are funding the project. It's a big investment, but in the long term, the town will be more
pleasant. A resident: It looks lovely on the model. I'll believe it when I've seen it!

Count the futur antérieurs: *nous aurons terminé*, *nous aurons fini*, *la ville aura prolongé*,
*je l'aurai vu*. Each one is finished before the other future action, or before a date (*d'ici
l'été prochain*).

## Reading: Valmont en 2032

From the magazine of an imaginary town.

> *À quoi ressemblera notre centre-ville dans six ans ? Le conseil municipal a présenté hier son
> grand projet d'urbanisme, « Valmont 2032 ».*
>
> *La première étape commencera cet été. Dès que l'école Jean-Moulin aura fermé pour les
> vacances, les ouvriers commenceront sa rénovation. À court terme, la circulation sera difficile
> rue de la Gare, mais la mairie promet que le chantier ne durera pas plus de deux ans.*
>
> *Ensuite, la ville construira progressivement quatre kilomètres de pistes cyclables. Quand elles
> seront toutes ouvertes, on pourra traverser Valmont à vélo en vingt minutes. D'ici 2030, la
> mairie aura aussi aménagé les bords de la rivière : à la place du parking, il y aura un parc.*
>
> *Le projet coûtera 48 millions d'euros. La ville en financera la moitié ; la région et l'État
> paieront le reste. Pour le maire, cet investissement est indispensable : « À long terme, une
> ville sans voitures dans son centre attirera des familles. » L'opposition, elle, prédit des
> problèmes pour les commerçants tant que les travaux dureront.*
>
> *Si tout se passe comme prévu, le maire inaugurera la nouvelle zone piétonne au printemps 2032.
> Les habitants pourront voir la maquette du projet à la mairie jusqu'au 30 novembre.*

Translation:

> What will our town centre look like in six years? Yesterday the town council presented its big
> town-planning project, "Valmont 2032".
>
> The first stage will begin this summer. As soon as the Jean-Moulin school has closed for the
> holidays, workers will start its renovation. In the short term, traffic will be difficult on rue
> de la Gare, but the town hall promises that the building work won't last more than two years.
>
> Then the town will gradually build four kilometres of cycle lanes. When they are all open, you'll
> be able to cross Valmont by bike in twenty minutes. By 2030, the town hall will also have laid
> out the riverbanks: instead of the car park, there will be a park.
>
> The project will cost 48 million euros. The town will fund half of it; the region and the state
> will pay the rest. For the mayor, this investment is essential: "In the long term, a town with no
> cars in its centre will attract families." The opposition, for its part, predicts problems for
> shopkeepers as long as the building work lasts.
>
> If all goes as planned, the mayor will open the new pedestrian zone in spring 2032. Residents can
> see the model of the project at the town hall until 30 November.

(*le conseil municipal* = town council, lesson 22; *l'ouvrier* = worker; *la circulation* =
traffic, lesson 04; *le commerçant* = shopkeeper.) The article is dated 2026, so "in six years"
is 2032. Notice the mix: *si tout se passe comme prévu* is a real condition (type 1), while
*dès que, quand, tant que* all take the future.

## Pronunciation

- *J'aurai* (futur antérieur) and *j'aurais* (conditionnel passé): in careful speech [ʒɔʁe] /
  [ʒɔʁɛ]; many speakers say them the same, so listen for the context. In writing, check the *s*.
- *Lorsque* traditionally elides only before *il, elle, on, en, un, une*: *lorsqu'il, lorsqu'elle*, but *lorsque
  Paul*.
- *Construire* [kɔ̃stʁɥiʁ]: the *ui* is one quick syllable, as in *huit*.
- *Le chantier* [ʃɑ̃tje] has two syllables.

## Common mistakes

- *Quand j'arrive à Paris, je t'appellerai* mixes a present and a futur. You may hear it, but
  write *Quand j'arriverai à Paris, je t'appellerai*.
- ~~Quand j'aurais fini, je t'appellerai~~ → *Quand j'aurai fini, je t'appellerai* (futur
  antérieur, no *s*). For your own future plans, no conditionnel after *quand*. (In reported
  speech you will meet it: *Il a dit qu'il m'appellerait quand il aurait fini*, lesson 17.)
- ~~J'aurai parti~~ → *Je serai parti(e)*.
- *Si* ≠ *quand*: ~~Si tu viendras~~ → *Si tu viens*, but *Quand tu viendras*.
- *Aménager* ≠ *emménager* (to move in) ≠ *déménager* (to move out).

## Key points

- After *quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, une fois que, tant que*, a future action takes the
  futur simple (English uses the present).
- Futur antérieur = *aurai / serai* … + participle: *j'aurai fini, elle sera partie, nous nous
  serons levés*.
- It marks what will be finished first (*Quand tu auras fini, tu m'appelleras*) or by a date
  (*D'ici 2030, on aura construit …*).
- *Il aura oublié* = he must have forgotten (recognition).
- Three futures: *je vais partir, je partirai, j'aurai fini*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Et si … ? L'uchronie (alternate history)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 11 you rewrote personal pasts: *Si je n'avais pas raté mon bus, je n'aurais pas
rencontré Léa.* Historians, novelists and readers love to do the same with history: what if a
battle had gone the other way? French has a word for this kind of story, *l'uchronie*, and a
favourite subject for it: Napoléon at Waterloo.

This honors lesson shows you the genre, tells the real events of 1815 first (with every date
checked), and then gives you an original "what if" text built from the grammar of this module:
the **[[si-clause]]** of type 3, mixed conditionals, the conditionnel passé and the plus-que-parfait.
Everything in the fiction section is labelled as fiction.

## A genre with a French name

*L'uchronie* (alternate history) is made like *l'utopie*: *u-* means "no" in Greek, *topos* is a
place and *chronos* is time. A utopia is a place that doesn't exist; an *uchronie* is a time that
never existed. The word was coined by the French philosopher Charles Renouvier: it appeared in
1857, and in 1876 he published a whole book called *Uchronie (l'utopie dans l'histoire)*, an
"apocryphal" history of Europe "as it was not, as it might have been".

Renouvier wasn't the first to imagine history differently. In 1836, Louis Geoffroy published
*Napoléon et la conquête du monde (1812–1832)*, in which Napoléon wins in Russia in 1812, then
conquers England and the whole world. It is often described as the first book built on a
point of divergence (*le point de divergence*): one moment where invented history leaves real
history. Since then, French and English writers have produced hundreds of uchronies, many of them
about Napoléon.

Every uchronie answers the same question: *Que se serait-il passé si … ?* — What would have
happened if …? That is a type-3 si-clause.

## What really happened in 1815 (facts)

Read this first. Everything in it is history.

> *En 1814, après sa défaite, Napoléon Ier avait perdu son empire : il avait abdiqué et il était
> parti en exil sur l'île d'Elbe, en Méditerranée. Mais il s'est échappé et, le 20 mars 1815, il
> était de retour à Paris, aux Tuileries. C'est le début des « Cent-Jours ».*
>
> *Les grandes puissances d'Europe ont aussitôt réuni leurs armées contre lui. Le 15 juin, Napoléon est entré
> en Belgique pour battre séparément les Prussiens et l'armée de Wellington. Le 16 juin, à Ligny, il a vaincu les
> Prussiens du maréchal Blücher, mais ils se sont retirés en bon ordre. Napoléon a envoyé le
> maréchal Grouchy les poursuivre avec environ 33 000 hommes.*
>
> *La veille de la grande bataille, il a plu très fort. Le 18 juin 1815, près de Waterloo, à une
> vingtaine de kilomètres au sud de Bruxelles, le sol était trempé et l'attaque française n'a
> commencé que vers la fin de la matinée. L'armée de Wellington a résisté toute la journée. Dans
> l'après-midi, les Prussiens de Blücher, que Grouchy n'avait pas arrêtés, sont arrivés sur le
> côté de l'armée française. Napoléon attendait Grouchy : c'est Blücher qui est venu. Le soir, la
> défaite était complète.*
>
> *Le 22 juin, Napoléon a abdiqué une seconde fois, en faveur de son fils. Le roi Louis XVIII est
> revenu à Paris le 8 juillet. Les Anglais ont envoyé Napoléon sur l'île de Sainte-Hélène, au
> milieu de l'Atlantique sud, où il est arrivé le 15 octobre 1815. Il y est mort le 5 mai 1821.*

Translation:

> In 1814, after his defeat, Napoléon I had lost his empire: he had abdicated and gone into exile
> on the island of Elba, in the Mediterranean. But he escaped and, on 20 March 1815, he was back in
> Paris, at the Tuileries palace. This is the start of the "Hundred Days".
>
> The great powers of Europe immediately brought their armies together against him. On 15 June, Napoléon
> entered Belgium to beat the Prussians and Wellington's army separately. On 16 June, at Ligny, he defeated Marshal
> Blücher's Prussians, but they withdrew in good order. Napoléon sent Marshal Grouchy to pursue them
> with about 33,000 men.
>
> The day before the great battle, it rained very hard. On 18 June 1815, near Waterloo, about twenty
> kilometres south of Brussels, the ground was soaked and the French attack only began towards the
> end of the morning. Wellington's army held out all day. In the afternoon, Blücher's Prussians,
> whom Grouchy hadn't stopped, arrived on the side of the French army. Napoléon was waiting for
> Grouchy: it was Blücher who came. By the evening, the defeat was complete.
>
> On 22 June, Napoléon abdicated for the second time, in favour of his son. King Louis XVIII came
> back to Paris on 8 July. The British sent Napoléon to the island of Saint Helena, in the middle
> of the South Atlantic, where he arrived on 15 October 1815. He died there on 5 May 1821.

(*abdiquer* = to give up the throne; *s'échapper* = to escape; *poursuivre* = to pursue;
*trempé* = soaked; *résister* = to hold out.) The text mixes tenses as lesson 02 taught: the
plus-que-parfait for what was over before the story (*avait perdu, avait abdiqué*), the passé
composé for events, the imparfait for the background (*le sol était trempé, Napoléon
attendait*). *C'est le début* is a present: history books often slip into the present for
vividness.

![A timeline of 1815 with five dated points on a solid line: 20 mars, retour à Paris; 16 juin, Ligny; 18 juin, Waterloo; 22 juin, abdication; 15 octobre, Sainte-Hélène. At 18 juin a dotted branch leaves the line upwards, labelled fiction: et si Grouchy était arrivé ?, and ends in a cloud with a question mark. The solid line is labelled histoire (fact).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The grammar of "what if"

An uchronie needs three tools from this module:

| tool | form | example |
|---|---|---|
| type 3 si-clause | *si* + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé | *Si Grouchy était arrivé, Napoléon aurait gagné.* |
| mixed conditional | *si* + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel présent | *Si Napoléon avait gagné, l'Europe serait différente aujourd'hui.* |
| conditionnel passé alone | *aurait* / *serait* + participle | *Son fils aurait régné après lui.* |

Two more habits make the text sound like real history writing:

- Hedge. Nobody knows what would have happened, so careful writers add *peut-être*, *sans
  doute* (probably, lesson 07), *probablement*, or use *pouvoir*: *Napoléon aurait peut-être
  gagné. Il aurait pu gagner.*
- Keep the facts in the indicative. What really happened stays in the passé composé or the
  plus-que-parfait (*Grouchy n'est pas arrivé*); only the invented part goes in the conditionnel.

### Example 1: from a fact to a counterfactual

*Fact.* Grouchy didn't come; Blücher's Prussians reached the battlefield; Napoléon lost.

1. Choose the point of divergence: Grouchy's arrival.
2. Reverse it in the plus-que-parfait: *Grouchy n'est pas arrivé* → *si Grouchy était arrivé*.
   (*Arriver* takes *être*; *Grouchy* is a man, so no extra *-e*.)
3. Imagine the result in the conditionnel passé, and hedge: *Napoléon aurait peut-être gagné la
   bataille.*
4. Result: *Si Grouchy était arrivé à temps, Napoléon aurait peut-être gagné la bataille.* — If
   Grouchy had arrived in time, Napoléon might have won the battle.

### Example 2: a chain of consequences

Uchronies rarely stop at one sentence. Each result becomes the next condition:

1. *S'il n'avait pas plu la veille, Napoléon aurait attaqué dès le matin.*
2. *S'il avait attaqué dès le matin, les Prussiens ne seraient pas arrivés à temps.*
3. *Si les Prussiens n'étaient pas arrivés à temps, Wellington se serait sans doute retiré.*

Notice how each result clause in the conditionnel passé (*aurait attaqué*) becomes a
plus-que-parfait in the next *si* clause (*s'il avait attaqué*). The conditionnel never moves to
the *si* side.

## Fiction: Le soleil du 18 juin

What follows is an original "what if" text. It is fiction: everything in the conditionnel was
invented, and only the last paragraph goes back to the facts.

> *Fiction. Et si, le 17 juin 1815, il n'avait pas plu ?*
>
> *Imaginons. Le sol aurait été sec, et l'artillerie française aurait pu se déplacer sans peine.
> Napoléon aurait attaqué dès six heures du matin. À deux heures de l'après-midi, l'armée de
> Wellington, fatiguée, aurait sans doute reculé vers Bruxelles, et les Prussiens seraient arrivés
> trop tard.*
>
> *Après cette victoire, l'empereur serait entré dans Bruxelles en triomphe. Les rois d'Europe
> auraient-ils accepté la paix ? Peut-être pas : presque toute l'Europe était unie contre lui.
> Napoléon aurait peut-être gagné une bataille, mais pas la guerre.*
>
> *Supposons pourtant qu'il ait gagné la guerre. Son fils aurait régné après lui sous le nom de
> Napoléon II, et le Premier Empire aurait duré plus longtemps. Louis XVIII ne serait pas revenu
> sur le trône. Et aujourd'hui, l'expression anglaise « to meet one's Waterloo » (subir sa
> défaite finale) n'existerait sans doute pas : si Napoléon avait gagné, Waterloo serait le nom
> d'une victoire.*
>
> *Mais tout cela ne s'est pas passé. Il a plu, la bataille a commencé tard, Blücher est arrivé.
> Le reste appartient à l'histoire.*

Translation:

> Fiction. What if it hadn't rained on 17 June 1815?
>
> Let's imagine. The ground would have been dry, and the French artillery could have moved easily.
> Napoléon would have attacked from six in the morning. By two in the afternoon, Wellington's tired
> army would no doubt have fallen back towards Brussels, and the Prussians would have arrived too
> late.
>
> After this victory, the emperor would have entered Brussels in triumph. Would the kings of Europe
> have accepted peace? Perhaps not: nearly all of Europe was united against him. Napoléon might
> have won a battle, but not the war.
>
> Let's suppose, though, that he had won the war. His son would have reigned after him as Napoléon
> II, and the First Empire would have lasted longer. Louis XVIII wouldn't have returned to the
> throne. And today the English expression "to meet one's Waterloo" (to suffer your final
> defeat) probably wouldn't exist: if Napoléon had won, Waterloo would be the name of a victory.
>
> But none of this happened. It rained, the battle began late, Blücher arrived. The rest is
> history.

(*l'artillerie* = artillery, the big guns; *se déplacer sans peine* = to move easily; *reculer* =
to fall back; *en triomphe* = in triumph; *unie* = united; *le trône* = the throne; *subir* = to
suffer; *appartenir à* = to belong to.)

Read it as a grammar map:

- Fact in the past: *Il a plu, la bataille a commencé tard* (passé composé).
- The invented past, in the conditionnel passé: *aurait attaqué, aurait reculé, seraient
  arrivés, serait entré*; *aurait pu se déplacer* uses *pouvoir* to hedge.
- A mixed conditional at the end: *si Napoléon avait gagné, Waterloo serait le nom d'une victoire*
  (past cause, present result), and *n'existerait pas* for today.
- *Supposons qu'il ait gagné*: *supposons que* + subjunctive (lesson 09); *ait gagné* is a
  past subjunctive, which you only need to recognise here (honors lesson 08h1).

### Example 3: writing your own point of divergence

*Task.* Write three sentences on the model, about the abdication of 22 June.

1. The fact, in the passé composé: *Le 22 juin 1815, Napoléon a abdiqué.*
2. The divergence, in a type-3 si-clause: *S'il n'avait pas abdiqué, il aurait peut-être essayé
   de défendre Paris.*
3. A present consequence, in a mixed conditional: *S'il avait défendu Paris, l'histoire de France
   serait peut-être très différente aujourd'hui.*

Check: plus-que-parfait after every *si*; conditionnel passé for a past result, conditionnel
présent for today; a hedge (*peut-être*) in each invented result.

## Words for empires and battles

- *L'empire* (masculine) and *l'empereur* (*l'impératrice* for a woman, or the emperor's wife):
  *Napoléon Ier a été empereur des Français de 1804 à 1814, puis en 1815.* *Le règne* is the reign;
  *régner* is to reign (*il règne, nous régnons*, with *è* before a silent ending).
- *Le roi* and *la reine*: *le roi Louis XVIII*.
- *L'armée* (feminine), *la bataille*, *la conquête* (*la conquête de l'Europe*), *la défaite*
  (the opposite of *la victoire*, A2).
- *Vaincre* (to defeat) is irregular; in everyday French you mostly meet it in the infinitive
  (*vaincre la peur*), the passé composé or as *vaincu* (*les vaincus* = the defeated): *il vainc, ils vainquent, il a vaincu*. It isn't drilled; in speech,
  *battre* (to beat) is more common: *Ils ont battu Napoléon*.
- *L'uchronie* itself: *J'ai lu une uchronie où Napoléon gagne à Waterloo.*

## Common mistakes

- ~~Si Grouchy serait arrivé~~ → *Si Grouchy était arrivé*. History doesn't change the rule.
- Putting a fact in the conditionnel: *Napoléon aurait perdu à Waterloo* means "Napoléon
  apparently lost" (the news use, honors 12h2) or "would have lost". For the fact, write
  *Napoléon a perdu à Waterloo*.
- Forgetting to hedge: *Napoléon aurait gagné la guerre* sounds like a certainty; *aurait peut-être
  gagné* is how careful writers put it.
- *Il vainc* (no *t*), *ils vainquent* (*c* → *qu* before a vowel).
- Mixing up *la défaite* (defeat) and *le défaut* (flaw, fault).

## Key points

- *L'uchronie*: a story of history as it didn't happen, a word from Renouvier (1857; book 1876);
  Geoffroy's *Napoléon et la conquête du monde* (1836) is often called the first.
- Real 1815 dates: 20 March back in Paris; 16 June Ligny; 18 June Waterloo; 22 June abdication;
  15 October Saint Helena; died 5 May 1821.
- Grammar of "what if": *si* + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé (type 3) or conditionnel
  présent (a result today); the result of one sentence becomes the *si* of the next.
- Keep facts in the indicative, the invented part in the conditionnel, and hedge with *peut-être,
  sans doute, aurait pu*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Selon nos informations …: the conditionnel in the news
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 10 you met a sentence that didn't mean "would": *L'incendie aurait fait deux blessés.* —
The fire is reported to have injured two people. French news uses the conditionnel all the time
in this way, to pass on information that hasn't been confirmed. This honors lesson is about that
use, the **[[reportive conditional]]** (*le conditionnel journalistique*): how it works in the
present and the past, how it shows that a fact is not yet certain, and how to read a news story
with that in mind.

You already know every form you need: the conditionnel présent (*il serait*) and the
conditionnel passé (*il aurait quitté*). Only the meaning is new.

## Same forms, a different meaning

In a news report, the conditionnel says: "this is what we have been told; we can't confirm it
yet". It is a way of reporting a claim without taking responsibility for it. Linguists give this
use several names (*conditionnel journalistique, conditionnel de la rumeur, conditionnel
reportatif*); they all mean the same thing.

| confirmed (indicative) | unconfirmed (conditionnel) | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Le suspect est en fuite.* | *Le suspect serait en fuite.* | The suspect is reportedly on the run. |
| *Le suspect a quitté le pays.* | *Le suspect aurait quitté le pays.* | The suspect is said to have left the country. |
| *L'accident a fait trois blessés.* | *L'accident aurait fait trois blessés.* | The accident reportedly injured three people. |
| *La ministre annoncera sa démission demain.* | *La ministre annoncerait sa démission demain.* | The minister is expected to announce her resignation tomorrow (unconfirmed). |

The time is the same as in the indicative sentence next to it:

- **[[conditionnel présent]]** for something true now, or planned for later: *serait en fuite,
  annoncerait demain*;
- **[[conditionnel passé]]** for something that has already happened: *aurait quitté, aurait fait*.

English has no single tense for this. It uses "reportedly", "allegedly", "is said to", "is
thought to", "according to unconfirmed reports". When you translate, pick one of those, never
"would".

## Why the news uses it

A journalist who writes *Le suspect a quitté le pays* states a fact. If it turns out to be wrong,
the paper has published something false. With *Le suspect aurait quitté le pays*, the paper says
only that someone claims it. French grammars, such as the Office québécois de la langue
française's, describe this use as common in the press: it gives information *sous toutes
réserves* (with every reservation, without vouching for it).

This is also a question of ethics. The *Charter of Munich*, a declaration of journalists' duties
and rights adopted in Munich in 1971, asks journalists to publish only facts whose
origin is known, or else to accompany them with the necessary reservations. The reportive
conditional is one of the ordinary ways of showing that reservation in French.

## Naming the source

A careful report usually says who the information comes from, with *selon* or *d'après* (A2) +
the source, and keeps the conditionnel as well:

- *Selon la police, le voleur serait entré par une fenêtre.* — According to the police, the thief
  got in through a window.
- *D'après une dépêche de l'AFP, le président aurait annulé son voyage.* — According to an AFP
  report, the president has cancelled his trip.
- *Selon nos informations, l'usine fermerait en juin.* — According to our information, the factory
  is to close in June. (*Selon nos informations* means the paper's own sources: nobody official
  has said it yet.)

The vocabulary of sources:

- *Une agence de presse* sells news to newspapers, radio and television. France's best-known
  agency is the *Agence France-Presse* (AFP), founded under that name in 1944; it continued the
  *Agence Havas*, which dates from 1835. *Une dépêche* is a short news report sent by an agency.
- *Le correspondant* (*la correspondante*) is a journalist based in another city or country:
  *notre correspondante à Bruxelles*.
- *De source sûre* means "from a reliable source": *J'ai appris de source sûre que …*. It sounds
  stronger, but the source is still unnamed.
- *Officiel* (*officielle*) is the opposite of rumour: *une annonce officielle, le bilan
  officiel*. *Provisoire* means provisional, not final: *un bilan provisoire* (a provisional toll)
  will often change.

## Other signals of uncertainty

The conditionnel is not alone. Watch for:

- *présumé* (alleged, presumed): *l'auteur présumé du vol* (the alleged thief). French law presumes
  a person innocent until a court decides, so the press calls people *présumés* or *suspects*
  until then. *Le suspect* (*la suspecte*) is a person the police suspect.
- *vraisemblablement* (in all likelihood) and *apparemment* (apparently, lesson 17): *Le feu
  serait vraisemblablement d'origine électrique.*
- *Il semblerait que* + subjunctive, sometimes the indicative (it would seem that): *Il semblerait que
  l'incendie soit accidentel.*
- Verbs that report without confirming: *affirmer, prétendre* (lesson 17): *Il affirme qu'il était
  chez lui.*

And one verb that does the opposite: *démentir* (to deny officially, to refute a report). *La
mairie a démenti l'information.* — The town hall denied the report. *Démentir* is conjugated like
*mentir* (lesson 02): *je démens, il dément, nous démentons*; *un démenti* is an official denial.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: From rumour to fact
  accDescr: A flow chart. A piece of information starts as a rumour or a claim. A first report uses the conditionnel with a source, for example selon la police, le suspect aurait quitté le pays. Then there are two possible outcomes. If it is confirmed by an official source, the report switches to the indicative: le suspect a quitté le pays. If the authorities deny it, the report says: la police a démenti l'information. A note says that a provisional toll, un bilan provisoire, can still change.
  A["A rumour or a claim"] --> B["First report, conditionnel + source: Selon la police, le suspect aurait quitté le pays."]
  B --> C{"What happens next?"}
  C -- "confirmed officially" --> D["Indicative: Le suspect a quitté le pays."]
  C -- "denied" --> E["Un démenti: La police a démenti l'information."]
  B --> F["Numbers stay provisoires until the final count"]
```

### Example 1: confirmed or not?

*Task.* Rewrite each confirmed sentence as an unconfirmed report, then rewrite the last one as
confirmed.

1. *Le musée a fermé ses portes.* (past, *avoir*) → *Le musée aurait fermé ses portes.*
2. *Les deux suspects sont partis en voiture.* (past, *être*, agreement kept) → *Les deux suspects
   seraient partis en voiture.*
3. *Le maire veut se présenter à nouveau.* (now) → *Le maire voudrait se présenter à nouveau.*
4. *Le chantier finira en mars.* (later) → *Le chantier finirait en mars.*
5. Unconfirmed → confirmed: *La grève aurait commencé à six heures* → *La grève a commencé à six
   heures.*

Careful with sentence 3: *Le maire voudrait* can also be the ordinary polite or wishful
conditionnel ("the mayor would like"). Only the context tells you. In a news story with *selon*
and a source, it is usually reportive.

### Example 2: reading a dispatch critically

*Text.*

> *Valmont, 7 h 30. Un incendie s'est déclaré cette nuit dans un entrepôt de la zone industrielle
> de Valmont. Selon les pompiers, il n'y a pas de victimes. D'après plusieurs témoins, le feu
> aurait commencé vers deux heures du matin dans un camion garé près du bâtiment. L'entrepôt
> appartiendrait à une entreprise de transport. Les causes de l'incendie restent inconnues.*

*Task.* Sort the information.

| confirmed (indicative) | unconfirmed (conditionnel) | source |
|---|---|---|
| a fire broke out in a warehouse (*s'est déclaré*) | — | the reporter |
| no victims (*il n'y a pas*) | — | the fire brigade |
| — | started around 2 a.m. in a lorry (*aurait commencé*) | witnesses |
| — | the warehouse belongs to a transport company (*appartiendrait*) | not given |
| the causes are unknown (*restent*) | — | the reporter |

Two points to notice: the reporter states as fact only what the fire brigade confirmed; and one
claim (*appartiendrait*) has no named source at all, so treat it with the most caution.

## Reading: one story, three moments

Three updates on the same imaginary story, as they might appear on a news site during one day.

> *9 h 05. Disparition d'un tableau au musée de Saint-Aubin.* *Un tableau du XVIIIe siècle
> aurait disparu cette nuit du petit musée de Saint-Aubin. Selon nos informations, le voleur
> serait entré par une fenêtre du premier étage. La mairie n'a pas encore confirmé.*
>
> *13 h 40. Le vol confirmé.* *La mairie a confirmé ce midi le vol d'un tableau de 1754. Le
> conservateur du musée a découvert la disparition à 8 heures. D'après les gendarmes, le voleur
> présumé aurait agi seul. Le musée n'a pas communiqué la valeur du tableau. Notre correspondante
> sur place précise que le musée restera fermé jusqu'à lundi.*
>
> *19 h 15. Un suspect interpellé.* *Les gendarmes ont interpellé un homme de 34 ans en fin
> d'après-midi. Il aurait reconnu les faits, selon une source proche de l'enquête, mais son avocat
> dément cette information. Les gendarmes auraient vraisemblablement retrouvé le tableau dans sa
> voiture : ils doivent le confirmer demain.*

Translation:

> 9.05 a.m. Painting missing at the Saint-Aubin museum. An 18th-century painting has reportedly
> disappeared overnight from the small museum in Saint-Aubin. According to our information, the
> thief got in through a first-floor window. The town hall has not yet confirmed.
>
> 1.40 p.m. Theft confirmed. The town hall confirmed at noon the theft of a painting from 1754.
> The museum's curator discovered the disappearance at 8 o'clock. According to the gendarmes, the
> alleged thief acted alone. The museum has not released the value of the painting. Our
> correspondent on the spot adds that the museum will stay closed until Monday.
>
> 7.15 p.m. Suspect detained. Gendarmes detained a 34-year-old man late in the afternoon. He has
> reportedly admitted the facts, according to a source close to the investigation, but his lawyer
> denies this. The gendarmes have in all likelihood found the painting in his car: they are
> to confirm it tomorrow.

(*le conservateur* = curator; *agir* = to act; *communiquer* = to release (information);
*les gendarmes* = a police force under military status, common outside big towns; *interpeller* =
to detain for questioning; *reconnaître les faits* = to admit the facts, lesson
17; *l'avocat* = lawyer; *proche de* = close to.)

Watch the verbs change mood through the day: *aurait disparu* (9 h 05, unconfirmed) becomes *la
mairie a confirmé le vol* (13 h 40, confirmed). The suspect's confession stays in the
conditionnel (*aurait reconnu*) because it is unconfirmed and denied, and so does the find in the
car (*aurait retrouvé*), even with *vraisemblablement*: likely is not confirmed.

## A short checklist for reading the news

1. Find the verbs: indicative (stated as fact) or conditionnel (reported)?
2. Find the source: *selon / d'après* whom? Official, a witness, "our information", or nobody?
3. Look for the words of caution: *présumé, provisoire, vraisemblablement, apparemment*.
4. Look for a *démenti*: who denies what?
5. Check the time: a first report at 9 a.m. is often corrected by the evening.

## Common mistakes

- Translating every reportive conditional with "would": *Le suspect serait en fuite* is not "the
  suspect would be on the run", but "the suspect is reportedly on the run".
- Using it for your own opinion. If you think something is true, say *je pense que* (lesson 07);
  the reportive conditional passes on what others say.
- Mixing up *démentir* (to deny a report officially) and *mentir* (to lie), or *nier* (to deny
  doing something, lesson 17): *Le ministre dément la rumeur. Le suspect nie les faits.*
- Thinking *de source sûre* means confirmed: the source is still unnamed.
- Forgetting the agreement: *l'auteure présumée, les suspects présumés*.

## Key points

- The reportive conditional reports unconfirmed information: *Le suspect serait en fuite* (now),
  *aurait quitté le pays* (past), *La ministre annoncerait sa démission demain* (later).
- Translate it with "reportedly, allegedly, is said to", never "would".
- A careful report names its source: *selon, d'après, selon nos informations, une dépêche de
  l'AFP, notre correspondant*.
- Other signals: *présumé, provisoire, vraisemblablement, de source sûre* (unnamed); confirmation
  switches to the indicative; *démentir* = to deny a report officially.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The painting I told you about: dont, ce qui, ce que, ce dont
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A2 you joined sentences with *qui, que* and *où*, and you may have met *dont, ce qui* and
*ce que* in a preview. This lesson makes them active: "the painting I told you about", "the artist
whose work is in the Louvre", "what I need", and the spotlight frame *Ce que j'aime, c'est la
lumière.* The theme is art: painting, drawing, sculpture and museums.

A word on *le tableau*: at A1 it was the board in a classroom. In a museum it means a painting:
*un tableau de Monet* — a painting by Monet. (*La peinture* is both the art of painting and the
paint itself; it can also mean one painting.)

## Quick review: qui, que, où

A **[[relative pronoun]]** joins a second clause to a noun and stands for that noun. The noun is its
**[[antecedent]]**, and the clause it starts is a **[[relative clause]]**. The pronoun depends on the job
the antecedent does in the relative clause:

| job in the relative clause | pronoun | example |
|---|---|---|
| subject | *qui* | *le peintre qui a fait ce portrait* — the painter who did this portrait |
| direct object | *que / qu'* | *le tableau que j'ai acheté* — the painting (that) I bought |
| place or time | *où* | *la galerie où elle expose* — the gallery where she exhibits; *le jour où …* |

Remember that after *que*, a participle with *avoir* agrees with the antecedent, because *que* is a
direct object that comes first: *la sculpture que j'ai vue, les dessins qu'il a faits.*

## dont: replacing de + a noun

Many French verbs, adjectives and nouns are followed by *de*. When the antecedent belongs after
that *de*, neither *qui* nor *que* fits. French uses *dont*.

| construction with *de* | simple sentence | with *dont* |
|---|---|---|
| *parler de* — to talk about | *Je t'ai parlé de ce tableau.* | *C'est le tableau dont je t'ai parlé.* — the painting I told you about |
| *avoir besoin de* — to need | *J'ai besoin de ce livre.* | *le livre dont j'ai besoin* — the book I need |
| *se souvenir de* — to remember | *Je me souviens de cette expo.* | *une expo dont je me souviens* — an exhibition I remember |
| *s'inspirer de* — to draw on | *Elle s'inspire de ce style.* | *le style dont elle s'inspire* — the style she draws on |
| *avoir envie de* — to want | *J'ai envie de ce dessin.* | *le dessin dont j'ai envie* — the drawing I want |
| *être fier de* — to be proud of | *Il est fier de cette œuvre.* | *l'œuvre dont il est fier* — the work he's proud of |

English hangs the preposition at the end ("the painting I told you about"). French can't do
that: the *de* moves to the front, inside *dont*. If you're not sure, rebuild the simple sentence
first and look for *de* + the noun.

### dont + a noun: whose, of which

*Dont* also replaces *de* in front of a noun, where English says "whose":

- *Le fils de cet artiste est sculpteur.* → *C'est l'artiste dont le fils est sculpteur.* — the
  artist whose son is a sculptor.
- *Les toiles de cette peintre sont au musée d'Orsay.* → *une peintre dont les toiles sont au
  musée d'Orsay* — a painter whose canvases are in the Musée d'Orsay. (*La toile*: canvas.)

### Word order after dont

After "whose", English moves the noun to the front ("the painter whose works I know"). After
*dont*, French keeps the ordinary order: subject, verb, then the rest.

- *le peintre dont je connais les œuvres* — the painter whose works I know (*je connais les
  œuvres*, in the usual order)
- not ~~le peintre dont les œuvres je connais~~

When the noun after *dont* is the subject of its clause, it comes first anyway, so nothing
changes: *l'artiste dont le tableau est au Louvre.*

The article stays, too: *dont les œuvres*, *dont le fils*. English "whose" has no article, but the
French noun keeps its *le, la, les*.

### Two traps

- No agreement with *dont*. It is never a direct object, so a participle doesn't agree with
  it: *les tableaux dont j'ai parlé* (not *parlés*), *l'exposition dont nous avons parlé*. Compare
  *les tableaux que j'ai vus*, where *que* is a direct object.
- *Dont* is not "from where". For coming from a place, say *d'où*: *la ville d'où vient le
  peintre* — the town the painter comes from. (*La ville dont il vient* is old-fashioned
  literary French; don't copy it.)

### Example 1: building a dont sentence

Join *Voici la sculptrice. Je t'ai montré les sculptures de cette sculptrice.*

1. The shared noun, *la sculptrice*, comes after *de* in the second sentence (*les sculptures
   de cette sculptrice*), so the pronoun is *dont*.
2. Put *dont* after the antecedent, then the clause in its normal order, article kept: *dont je
   t'ai montré les sculptures*.
3. Result: *Voici la sculptrice dont je t'ai montré les sculptures.* — Here is the sculptor whose
   sculptures I showed you. (No agreement on *montré*: the direct object, *les sculptures*, comes
   after the verb.)

## What: ce qui, ce que, ce dont, ce à quoi

When there is no noun to describe, French puts *ce* ("the thing") in front of the relative
pronoun. *Ce qui, ce que, ce dont* and *ce à quoi* all translate as "what" (the thing that). The
choice follows the same logic as before:

| form | when | example |
|---|---|---|
| *ce qui* | the gap is the subject | *Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est l'art contemporain.* — What interests me is contemporary art. |
| *ce que / ce qu'* | the gap is the direct object | *Je ne comprends pas ce que ce tableau représente.* — I don't understand what this painting shows. |
| *ce dont* | the verb takes *de* | *Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est de calme.* — What I need is peace and quiet. |
| *ce à quoi* | the verb takes *à* | *Ce à quoi je pense, c'est à nos vacances.* — What I'm thinking about is our holiday. |

*Ce à quoi* goes with verbs that take *à*: *penser à, s'intéresser à, s'attendre à* (to expect),
*réfléchir à* (to think about). After a preposition with no noun, the relative is *quoi*; you'll
see more of it in lesson 14.

*Tout ce qui* and *tout ce que* mean "everything that" / "all (that)": *Tout ce que tu vois ici
est à vendre.* — Everything you see here is for sale. *Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or.* — All
that glitters is not gold.

English often says just "what" or "that". French always needs *ce*: *Dis-moi ce que tu penses*
(not ~~Dis-moi que tu penses~~, which would mean "Tell me that you think"). Before an
infinitive, *quoi* is fine and very common: *Je ne sais pas quoi dire.* — I don't know what to say.

## Putting something in the spotlight: mise en relief

French word order is fairly fixed, so to stress one part of a sentence French moves it into a
frame. This is called **[[mise en relief]]** (emphasis). There are two frames.

### Ce qui / ce que / ce dont …, c'est …

Start with *ce qui, ce que, ce dont* or *ce à quoi*, then give the answer after *c'est*:

- *J'aime la lumière.* → *Ce que j'aime, c'est la lumière.* — What I love is the light.
- *Les couleurs me plaisent.* → *Ce qui me plaît, ce sont les couleurs.* — What I like is the
  colours.
- *J'ai peur du vide.* → *Ce dont j'ai peur, c'est du vide.* — What I'm afraid of is heights.

In careful French the preposition is repeated after *c'est*: *Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est de
calme. Ce à quoi je pense, c'est à nos vacances.* In relaxed speech you'll also hear it
dropped (*c'est le calme*). Write the careful version. With a plural noun, careful French uses
*ce sont*; everyday speech often keeps *c'est*.

### C'est … qui / c'est … que

Put the stressed part between *c'est* and *qui* (if it's the subject) or *que* (anything else):

- *Ce tableau m'a le plus touché.* → *C'est ce tableau qui m'a le plus touché.* — It's this
  painting that moved me most.
- *Je préfère Monet.* → *C'est Monet que je préfère.* — It's Monet I prefer.
- *Monet a peint ses nymphéas à Giverny.* → *C'est à Giverny que Monet a peint ses nymphéas.*
  — It was at Giverny that Monet painted his water lilies.

Two agreement points:

- After *c'est moi qui, c'est toi qui …*, the verb agrees with the pronoun: *C'est moi qui ai
  choisi. C'est nous qui avons payé. C'est vous qui êtes l'artiste ?*
- After *c'est … que*, the usual *que* rule applies: *C'est cette sculpture que j'ai achetée*
  (*que* = *cette sculpture*, a direct object before *avoir*).

## Which pronoun? A chooser

Ask what job the noun would do in the simple sentence:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Choosing a relative pronoun
  accDescr: Start from the question "what is the gap in the relative clause?". If it is the subject of the verb, use qui. If it is the direct object, use que or qu'. If it is a place or a time, use où. If it is de plus a noun, use dont. If it is another preposition, ask whether the noun is a person: for a person use qui (lequel is also possible); for a thing use lequel, auquel or duquel, taught in lesson 14. With no noun, put ce in front: ce qui, ce que, ce dont, ce à quoi.
  A["What is the gap in the relative clause?"] --> B["the subject"]
  A --> C["the direct object"]
  A --> D["a place or a time"]
  A --> E["de + noun"]
  A --> F["another preposition"]
  B --> B1["qui"]
  C --> C1["que / qu'"]
  D --> D1["où"]
  E --> E1["dont"]
  F --> G{"a person?"}
  G -- yes --> G1["qui (or lequel)"]
  G -- no --> G2["lequel, auquel, duquel (lesson 14)"]
```

No noun before it? Add *ce*: *ce qui, ce que, ce dont, ce à quoi*.

### Example 2: choosing in context

Complete *Le musée ___ je te parle a une salle ___ on peut dessiner, et un guide ___ explique
tout.*

1. *Je te parle du musée*: *de* + noun → *dont*.
2. *On peut dessiner dans cette salle*: a place → *où*.
3. *Le guide explique tout*: the guide is the subject → *qui*.

*Le musée dont je te parle a une salle où on peut dessiner, et un guide qui explique tout.* — The
museum I'm telling you about has a room where you can draw, and a guide who explains everything.

## ce que in a relative or in a question?

At A2 you met the **[[indirect question]]**: *Qu'est-ce que tu veux ?* → *Je sais ce que tu veux.*
Its *ce que* looks exactly like the relative one, and both mean "what": *Je me demande ce que ce
dessin représente* (a question after *se demander*) and *Ce que ce dessin représente n'est pas
clair* (a relative). You don't need to tell them apart to use them; just remember that "what" is
*ce qui / ce que* in both, never *qui*, which is "who": *Je ne sais pas qui est venu.*

## Reading: an exhibition

> Le week-end dernier, je suis enfin allée voir l'exposition dont tout le monde parle : les
> portraits de Lucie Berthier, une peintre contemporaine qui vit et travaille à Marseille. La
> galerie où elle expose est petite, mais ce que j'y ai vu m'a beaucoup touchée.
>
> Berthier peint surtout des gens ordinaires : un boulanger, une infirmière, deux enfants dans un
> parc. Ce qui rend ses tableaux si particuliers, c'est la lumière. Elle dit qu'elle s'inspire des
> peintres classiques, en particulier de Vermeer, dont elle admire la douceur. Pourtant, son style
> n'a rien d'ancien : les fonds sont presque abstraits, avec de grandes taches de couleur.
>
> Le portrait dont je me souviens le mieux représente une vieille dame assise près d'une fenêtre.
> Ce à quoi on pense devant ce tableau, c'est au temps qui passe. Je suis restée longtemps devant,
> sans rien dire.
>
> Avant de partir, j'ai acheté un petit dessin dont j'avais envie depuis le début de la visite. Ce
> n'est pas un chef-d'œuvre, mais c'est exactement ce dont j'avais besoin pour mon salon. Comme dit
> mon père, la beauté est une question de goût : chacun apprécie ce qui lui parle.

Last weekend I finally went to see the exhibition everyone is talking about: the portraits of
Lucie Berthier, a contemporary painter who lives and works in Marseille. The gallery where she is
showing is small, but what I saw there moved me a lot.

Berthier mainly paints ordinary people: a baker, a nurse, two children in a park. What makes her
paintings so special is the light. She says she draws on the classical painters, especially
Vermeer, whose softness she admires. Yet her style is not at all old-fashioned: the backgrounds
are almost abstract, with large patches of colour.

The portrait I remember best shows an old lady sitting near a window. What you think of in front of
this painting is time passing. I stayed in front of it for a long time without saying anything.

Before leaving, I bought a small drawing I had wanted since the beginning of the visit. It isn't a
masterpiece, but it's exactly what I needed for my living room. As my father says, beauty is a
matter of taste: everyone appreciates what speaks to them.

(*Le fond*: background. *La tache*: patch, stain. Lucie Berthier and her gallery are invented;
Vermeer is the 17th-century Dutch painter famous for his light.)

Notice *m'a beaucoup touchée*: the narrator is a woman, *m'* is the direct object of *toucher* and
comes before *avoir*, so the participle agrees. *Toucher* means "to touch", and also "to move"
(emotionally).

## Dialogue: in the gallery

> Inès : Alors, lequel tu préfères ?
>
> Marc : C'est le portrait qui me plaît le plus, celui de la vieille dame.
>
> Inès : Moi, ce que je trouve beau, c'est le petit dessin au fond.
>
> Marc : Celui dont tu m'as parlé hier ?
>
> Inès : Oui. C'est exactement ce dont j'ai besoin pour mon entrée.
>
> Marc : Tu penses à tout, sauf au prix !
>
> Inès : Mais si, j'y ai pensé ! Tout ce que j'ai sur moi, c'est cinquante euros, et il coûte quarante.
>
> Marc : Alors achète-le !

Inès: So, which one do you prefer? — Marc: It's the portrait I like best, the one of the old lady. —
Inès: What I find beautiful is the little drawing at the back. — Marc: The one you told me about
yesterday? — Inès: Yes. It's exactly what I need for my hall. — Marc: You think of everything
except the price! — Inès: But I did think of it! All I've got on me is fifty euros, and it costs
forty. — Marc: Then buy it!

## A few words for art

![A museum wall. From left to right: a portrait of a person in a wooden frame, labelled "le portrait"; a pencil drawing of a cat on white paper, labelled "le dessin"; a large landscape painting in a gold frame, with a small plaque and a red rope barrier in front of it, labelled "le chef-d'œuvre"; and a grey statue on a plinth, labelled "la sculpture".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *l'œuvre* is feminine (*une œuvre de Rodin*); *le chef-d'œuvre*, plural *les chefs-d'œuvre*.
- *le peintre*, and *la peintre* for a woman; *le sculpteur, la sculptrice*.
- *l'inspiration* (feminine) and *s'inspirer de*: *Où trouvez-vous votre inspiration ?*
- *le goût*: taste, in food and in art (*avoir bon goût*). *Des goûts et des couleurs, on ne
  discute pas.* — There's no accounting for taste.

## Pronunciation

- *Chef-d'œuvre* is said "shay-DUH-vr": the *f* is silent. The plural *chefs-d'œuvre* sounds the
  same.
- In *sculpture, sculpteur, sculptrice* the *p* is silent: "skool-TOOR", "skool-TUR".
- *Dont* rhymes with *bon*: the *t* is usually silent (*dont il parle* = "don eel"), though careful
  speakers sometimes link it before a vowel.
- *L'œuvre*: the *œu* is the vowel of *peur*.

## Common mistakes

- *que* instead of *dont* with a *de* verb: ~~le livre que j'ai besoin~~ → *le livre dont j'ai
  besoin*.
- English word order after *dont*: ~~dont les œuvres je connais~~ → *dont je connais les œuvres*.
- Dropping the article after *dont*: ~~dont fils est peintre~~ → *dont le fils est peintre*.
- Agreeing the participle with *dont*: ~~les expos dont j'ai parlées~~ → *dont j'ai parlé*.
- "What" as *que* or *quoi* before a subject and verb: ~~Je sais que tu veux~~ (= I know that you
  want) → *Je sais ce que tu veux*.
- *Ce qui* and *ce que* mixed up: *ce qui* is the subject of the next verb (*ce qui me plaît*), *ce
  que* is followed by its own subject (*ce que je veux*).
- *c'est moi qui a* → *c'est moi qui ai*: the verb agrees with *moi*.

## Key points

- *dont* = *de* + the antecedent, after verbs, adjectives and nouns with *de*: *le tableau dont je
  parle, l'artiste dont le fils est sculpteur*.
- After *dont*, normal word order and the article stay: *dont je connais les œuvres*.
- No participle agreement with *dont*; *d'où* (not *dont*) for "from where".
- "What" = *ce qui* (subject), *ce que* (object), *ce dont* (*de* verbs), *ce à quoi* (*à* verbs);
  *tout ce qui / que* = everything that.
- Mise en relief: *Ce que j'aime, c'est …; C'est ce tableau qui …; C'est à Giverny que …*; careful
  French repeats the preposition (*Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est de calme*).
- After *c'est moi qui*, the verb agrees with *moi*: *C'est moi qui ai choisi.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The project I'm working on: lequel, auquel, duquel
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 covered the gaps that *qui, que, où* and *dont* fill. One kind is left: the antecedent
comes after a preposition other than *de*. "The project I'm working on", "the reason for
which", "the meeting during which", "the trade fair we're taking part in". French puts the
preposition in front and adds a relative pronoun after it: *le projet sur lequel je travaille*.
These pronouns are everywhere in the world of work, which is this lesson's theme: companies,
departments, projects and partners.

At A1 you met *lequel* as a question word (*Lequel tu veux ?* — Which one do you want?). Here it
works as a relative pronoun, with the same forms.

## Preposition + qui for people

For a person, the simplest choice is the preposition + *qui*:

- *la collègue avec qui je travaille* — the colleague I work with
- *le client pour qui nous préparons ce rapport* — the client we're preparing this report for
- *la responsable à qui j'ai écrit* — the manager I wrote to

*Qui* after a preposition normally means a person. For things you need *lequel*.

## Preposition + lequel for things

*Lequel* agrees with the antecedent, like an adjective, and comes straight after the preposition:

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| singular | *lequel* | *laquelle* |
| plural | *lesquels* | *lesquelles* |

- *le projet sur lequel je travaille* — the project I'm working on
- *la raison pour laquelle il est parti* — the reason (why) he left
- *les outils avec lesquels nous travaillons* — the tools we work with
- *les conditions dans lesquelles les salariés travaillent* — the conditions employees work in
- *la société pour laquelle elle travaille* — the company she works for

*Lequel* can refer to people too, especially in writing (*la personne avec laquelle j'ai parlé*).
After *parmi* (among) and *entre* (between) it is the only choice, even for people: *les candidats
parmi lesquels nous avons choisi* — the candidates we chose from (never *parmi qui*).

## à + lequel = auquel

*À* contracts with *le* and *les*, just as in *au* and *aux*:

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| singular | *auquel* | *à laquelle* |
| plural | *auxquels* | *auxquelles* |

You need these after verbs and expressions with *à*: *participer à, penser à, s'intéresser à,
répondre à, s'adresser à* (to speak to, contact), *assister à* (to attend), *grâce à*.

- *le salon auquel nous participons* — the trade fair we're taking part in
- *la question à laquelle je n'ai pas pu répondre* — the question I couldn't answer
- *les projets auxquels je pense* — the projects I'm thinking about
- *les réunions auxquelles j'assiste* — the meetings I attend
- *le logiciel grâce auquel on gagne du temps* — the software thanks to which we save time

For a person, *à qui* is more common: *le collègue à qui j'ai répondu* (or *auquel*).

## de + lequel = duquel, after compound prepositions

Some prepositions are made of several words and end in *de*: *près de* (near), *à côté de* (next
to), *en face de* (opposite), *loin de* (far from), *autour de* (around), *à cause de* (because
of), and three in this lesson's word list: *au cours de* (during, in the course of), *au sein de*
(within an organisation) and *à l'aide de* (with the help of, using). These are **compound
prepositions**. Their *de* contracts with *lequel*:

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| singular | *duquel* | *de laquelle* |
| plural | *desquels* | *desquelles* |

- *le bâtiment à côté duquel je me gare* — the building I park next to
- *la réunion au cours de laquelle il a présenté le projet* — the meeting during which he presented
  the project
- *l'équipe au sein de laquelle elle travaille* — the team she works in
- *les logiciels à l'aide desquels on prépare les devis* — the programs we use to prepare quotes
- *le parc en face duquel se trouve le siège* — the park opposite which the head office stands

For people, *de qui* is also possible: *le collègue à côté de qui je suis assis*.

*Auquel, duquel* and the others are called **[[compound relative pronouns]]** (*pronoms relatifs
composés*): preposition and article fused with *quel*.

### dont or duquel?

Both contain *de*, so they are easy to confuse. The test is what the *de* belongs to:

- *de* belongs to a verb, an adjective or a noun (*parler de, être responsable de, le chef de*) →
