> Certes, les commerçants ont peur de perdre des clients, et ce n'est pas sans raison : les personnes âgées ou handicapées, notamment, doivent pouvoir accéder facilement au centre. Mais il existe des solutions, comme des navettes gratuites ou des parkings à l'entrée de la ville.
>
> En conclusion, il me semble que les avantages l'emportent sur les inconvénients. Le but n'est pas de punir les automobilistes, mais de rendre la ville à ceux qui y vivent.

Translation:

> **Should the town centre be closed to cars?**
>
> In many towns the debate comes back regularly: should cars be banned from the centre? For my part, I'm rather in favour of this measure, provided it is well prepared.
>
> First of all, a centre without cars is a nicer place to live. Noise and pollution go down, and pedestrians get space back. In my town, for example, the high street was pedestrianised five years ago: today families stroll along it and the café terraces are full.
>
> What's more, this measure encourages other ways of getting around. When you can no longer park outside the shops, you're more willing to take the bike, the bus or the tram. In fact, many people discover that they didn't really need their car for short journeys.
>
> Admittedly, shopkeepers are afraid of losing customers, and not without reason: elderly or disabled people in particular must be able to get to the centre easily. But there are solutions, such as free shuttle buses or car parks at the edge of town.
>
> In conclusion, it seems to me that the advantages outweigh the drawbacks. The aim isn't to punish drivers but to give the town back to the people who live in it.

Notes: *le commerçant* = shopkeeper; *accéder à* = to get to, to have access to; *la navette* =
shuttle; *l'emporter sur* = to outweigh, to win over. The text follows the skeleton exactly: a
position with a condition (*à condition qu'elle soit*, lesson 08), two arguments each with an
example or a supporting fact, the other side conceded and answered, and a conclusion in new
words. The writer hedges (*plutôt, il me semble que*) without sitting on the fence: hedging is
not the same as having no opinion.

## Dialogue: the four-day week

Two colleagues, Inès and Bastien, before a staff meeting.

```dialogue lang=fr-FR
# La semaine de quatre jours
Inès: Tu as lu le message de la direction ? On va débattre de la semaine de quatre jours jeudi.
= Have you read the message from management? We're going to debate the four-day week on Thursday.
Bastien: Oui. Moi, je suis plutôt pour. D'une part, on aurait plus de temps pour sa famille ; d'autre part, on serait moins fatigués, donc plus efficaces.
= Yes. I'm rather in favour. On the one hand, we'd have more time for our families; on the other, we'd be less tired, so more efficient.
Inès: Dans une certaine mesure, tu as raison. Mais on ferait les mêmes heures en quatre jours, non ? Des journées de neuf heures, ce n'est pas rien.
= To some extent you're right. But we'd do the same hours in four days, wouldn't we? Nine-hour days aren't nothing.
Bastien: Certes, ça dépend de la formule. Certaines entreprises réduisent aussi le temps de travail.
= Admittedly, it depends on the arrangement. Some companies also cut working hours.
Inès: Ce qui m'inquiète, moi, c'est le service aux clients. Ils doivent pouvoir nous joindre du lundi au vendredi.
= What worries me is customer service. Customers must be able to reach us from Monday to Friday.
Bastien: On pourrait s'organiser en deux équipes. Le service serait non seulement assuré tous les jours, mais aussi mieux organisé.
= We could organise ourselves in two teams. The service would not only be covered every day but also better organised.
Inès: Tu ne m'as pas encore convaincue, mais l'idée me plaît en partie. Il faudrait la tester pendant quelques mois.
= You haven't convinced me yet, but I partly like the idea. We'd need to try it out for a few months.
Bastien: Bref, tu es d'accord avec moi !
= In short, you agree with me!
Inès: Je n'ai pas dit ça ! Je veux peser le pour et le contre avant de prendre position.
= I didn't say that! I want to weigh up the pros and cons before taking a position.
```

Notes: *efficace* = efficient, effective; *joindre* = to reach (by phone or e-mail); *la formule*
= the arrangement. *Tu ne m'as pas convaincue*: the participle agrees with *m'* (Inès, a direct
object before *avoir*). Bastien's *Bref* is a joke: he sums up too fast.

## Pronunciation

- *Convainc* [kɔ̃vɛ̃]: nothing is heard after the nasal vowel; *convainquons* [kɔ̃vɛ̃kɔ̃].
- *En outre* [ɑ̃nutʁ]: liaison, "en-n-outre". *Notamment* [nɔtamɑ̃]: the *-mm-* is one [m].

## Common mistakes

- *Non seulement est-il cher, mais …*, copied from English: standard French normally doesn't
  invert here. Say *Non seulement il est cher, mais …* or *Il est non seulement cher, mais aussi …*.
- *D'une part* with no *d'autre part*: if you open the pair, close it.
- *~~Il convaint~~*: *il convainc*.
- Reading *d'autre part* as English "on the other hand": it usually adds a point. For a clear
  contrast, *en revanche* or *par contre*.
- Overusing *Bref*: once, at the end, is enough. In an essay, prefer *En conclusion*.
- *Je ne pense pas qu'il a raison* in writing: use *qu'il ait raison* (subjunctive).
- An argument without an example, or a conclusion that just copies the introduction.

## Key points

- An argumentative text: question and position → two or three arguments, each with an example →
  the other side conceded and answered → conclusion.
- Structure with *tout d'abord / en premier lieu / d'une part*, *de plus / en outre / par ailleurs
  / d'autre part*, *d'ailleurs*, *non seulement … mais aussi*, *enfin*, *bref / en conclusion*.
- Examples: *par exemple, notamment, comme, ainsi*.
- Hedge with *il me semble que, je dirais que, plutôt, en partie, dans une certaine mesure*.
- Concede, then answer: *Certes …, mais …*.
- Indicative after *je pense / je suis convaincu que*; subjunctive after *je ne pense pas / je ne
  suis pas convaincu que*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Writing at B1: formal letters, articles and the essay
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 gave you the skeleton of an argument. This lesson puts it on paper in the forms B1
writers need: the **[[formal letter]]**, the article or reader's letter, and the short essay. It
covers planning, **[[register]]** (how formal you are), the polite conditionnel, **[[nominalisation]]**
for titles, and a checklist for rereading. The theme is local life: a letter about a dangerous
street, an article about a reopened swimming pool, a petition.

## The B1 writing task, in general terms

In the DELF B1, the writing paper asks for one text in which you give your personal view on a
general topic. The instructions say which form to use: an essay, a letter (often to a newspaper,
a company or an official), or an article. You have 45 minutes. The official regulation gives no
word count; sample papers and preparation guides ask for at least 160 words. Always follow the
instructions on the paper you are given: the form, who you are writing to, what you must include
and the minimum length. Lesson 24 describes the whole exam.

A common way to use the 45 minutes (suggested by an older official candidate guide): about 10
minutes to read the task and plan, about 30 to write, and at least 5 to reread. Plan in rough (*au brouillon*, A2), but don't write the whole
text in rough first: you probably won't have time to copy it out.

## Planning: three parts and paragraphs

In an essay, *le plan* (A1: a town map) is the outline. The basic plan has three parts:

| part | French | what goes in it | length (about 160–200 words) |
|---|---|---|---|
| introduction | *l'introduction* | the topic or the reason you write, the question, your position | 2–3 sentences |
| main body | *le développement* | two or three arguments, one *paragraphe* each, each with an example | 3 paragraphs |
| conclusion | *la conclusion* | a short summary and your position again, in new words | 1–2 sentences |

*Rédiger* means to write a text up properly, to draft (*rédiger une lettre, un rapport*); *la
rédaction* is the writing of it, and at school a composition. *Formuler* is to put into words:
*formuler une demande, une idée*. A good paragraph starts with a connector from lesson 21 and
says one thing.

*Rédiger* keeps the *e* before *-ons* and *-ais* like *manger*: *nous rédigeons, je rédigeais*.

## The formal letter

![The layout of a French formal letter, with each part named in French in the right margin. Top left: the sender's name and address (l'expéditeur). Below it on the right: the recipient, Monsieur le Maire, Mairie de Saint-Aubin (le destinataire), then the place and date (le lieu et la date). On the left: Objet : Sécurité devant l'école (l'objet). Then the opening, Monsieur le Maire, (la formule d'appel), the body in three paragraphs (le corps), the closing formula beginning Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer (la formule de politesse), and the signature, Claire Moreau, at the bottom right (la signature).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The parts have names: *l'expéditeur* and *le destinataire* (sender and recipient, A1), *l'objet*
(the subject line, A1), *la formule d'appel* (the opening: *Madame, Monsieur,* or *Monsieur le
Maire,*), *le corps de la lettre* (the body), *la formule de politesse* (the closing formula) and
*la signature*. You met the basics at A1 and A2; here are the phrases a B1 letter
adds.

| step | phrases |
|---|---|
| say why you write | *Je vous écris afin de …* (in order to), *Je me permets de vous écrire au sujet de …*, *Suite à votre courrier du 3 mai, …* |
| ask, politely | *Je souhaiterais …, Pourriez-vous …?, Je vous serais reconnaissant(e) de bien vouloir …* |
| ask formally for something | *solliciter* (to request formally): *Je sollicite un rendez-vous. Je souhaiterais solliciter votre aide.* |
| send something with it | *Veuillez trouver ci-joint …* (Please find attached …) |
| pass something on | *Pourriez-vous transmettre ma demande au service concerné ?* |
| close | *Je vous remercie par avance de la suite que vous donnerez à ma demande. Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.* |

Notes on the new words:

- *Veuillez* is the formal imperative of *vouloir*, used with an infinitive to mean "please":
  *Veuillez patienter* (please wait), *Veuillez trouver ci-joint …*. A shorter closing formula
  uses it too: *Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations
  distinguées.*
- *Ci-joint* (attached, enclosed) agrees when it comes right after its noun: *la facture
  ci-jointe, les documents ci-joints*. At the start of a sentence (*Ci-joint la facture*) or before
  a noun without an article it doesn't change. In *Veuillez trouver ci-joint la facture*, both
  *ci-joint* and *ci-jointe* are accepted; many writers leave it unchanged.
- The closing formula: *l'expression de mes salutations distinguées* is the usual neutral choice
  and is fine for a mayor. Some writers prefer a more respectful *l'expression de mes
  respectueuses salutations* (or, to a very senior official, *de ma haute considération*). Repeat
  the opening exactly inside the formula: *Monsieur le Maire*, *Madame, Monsieur*.
- *La suite* is what comes next: the follow-up (*la suite que vous donnerez à ma demande* =
  the action you will take on my request), the rest (*la suite de l'histoire*), the next part.
- *Adresser* is to send or direct something to someone: *J'adresse cette lettre au conseil
  municipal.* *S'adresser à* is to speak to, to go to (*Adressez-vous à l'accueil*).
- *Transmettre* (to pass on, to forward) is conjugated like *mettre*: *je transmets, nous
  transmettons, ils transmettent; j'ai transmis*.

### A model letter

Claire Moreau writes to her mayor about the street outside her children's school. The body
(without the addresses, date and signature) is about 190 words.

> Objet : Sécurité devant l'école Jules-Ferry
>
> Monsieur le Maire,
>
> Je me permets de vous écrire au nom des riverains de la rue des Tilleuls, où se trouve l'école Jules-Ferry. Depuis l'ouverture de la nouvelle zone commerciale, la circulation a beaucoup augmenté dans notre rue, et les voitures roulent souvent trop vite aux heures où les enfants arrivent à l'école.
>
> Le mois dernier, un enfant a failli être renversé devant l'entrée. Heureusement, il n'a pas été blessé, mais les parents sont très inquiets. Par ailleurs, les nuisances sonores ont nettement augmenté, notamment le soir.
>
> C'est pourquoi nous souhaiterions que le conseil municipal étudie plusieurs mesures : un passage piéton surélevé, une limitation de vitesse à 30 km/h et, si possible, la présence d'un agent aux heures d'entrée et de sortie des classes. Ces améliorations ne coûteraient pas très cher et protégeraient tous les habitants du quartier.
>
> Veuillez trouver ci-joint la pétition signée par 214 riverains. Nous sommes prêts à rencontrer les élus pour en discuter.
>
> Je vous remercie par avance de la suite que vous donnerez à notre demande. Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer, Monsieur le Maire, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
>
> Claire Moreau

Translation:

> Subject: Safety outside the Jules-Ferry school
>
> Dear Mayor,
>
> I am writing to you on behalf of the residents of the rue des Tilleuls, where the Jules-Ferry school is. Since the new retail park opened, traffic in our street has increased a lot, and cars often drive too fast at the times when the children arrive at school.
>
> Last month a child was nearly knocked down outside the entrance. Fortunately he wasn't hurt, but parents are very worried. In addition, noise has clearly increased, especially in the evening.
>
> That is why we would like the town council to consider several measures: a raised pedestrian crossing, a 30 km/h speed limit and, if possible, an officer on duty when classes start and finish. These improvements would not cost very much and would protect everyone who lives in the area.
>
> Please find attached the petition signed by 214 residents. We are ready to meet the councillors to discuss it.
>
> Thank you in advance for following up our request. I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully,
>
> Claire Moreau

Notes: *le riverain* = someone who lives in a particular street or beside a road or river (*les
riverains* is what local news calls the residents); *la nuisance* = a nuisance, usually plural
(*les nuisances sonores* = noise nuisance); *a failli être renversé* = was nearly knocked down
(*faillir* + infinitive = to nearly do); *surélevé* = raised; *nettement* = clearly; *la mesure* =
a measure, a step taken (and also a measurement: *prendre les mesures d'une pièce*). The letter
uses the three-paragraph body: the problem, the facts, the request.

### Who decides in a French town

*Le conseil municipal* (town or city council) is elected by the town's voters, and it elects the
mayor (*le maire*, A2) from among its members. Its members are *les élus* (*un élu, une élue*:
elected representatives, councillors). A letter about a local problem usually goes to the mayor
or the council. *Le citoyen, la citoyenne* is a citizen, and *la citoyenneté* citizenship: *une
démarche citoyenne* is something you do as a responsible member of the community, such as
signing *une pétition* or writing to your *élus*.

## Register: formal, neutral, informal

**[[Register]]** is the level of formality you choose. A letter to an official is formal from the
first line to the last; a message to a friend is informal. Mixing them is one of the most common
problems in B1 writing.

| register | where | the same request |
|---|---|---|
| informal | a friend, family | *Tu pourrais baisser la musique ? On n'arrive pas à dormir.* |
| neutral | a neighbour you don't know well, an e-mail at work | *Est-ce que vous pourriez baisser la musique, s'il vous plaît ?* |
| formal | a letter to a council, a company, an official | *Nous vous serions reconnaissants de bien vouloir limiter le bruit après 22 heures.* |

The conditionnel is the main tool of politeness: *je voudrais, je souhaiterais, j'aimerais,
pourriez-vous, serait-il possible de …*, and in formal letters *je vous serais reconnaissant(e)
de* + infinitive (I would be grateful if you would …). In a formal letter, keep *vous*, avoid
*on* for "we" (write *nous*), and avoid informal words (*super, sympa, ça*). The honors lesson
20h1 goes further into informal and formal French.

## The article and the reader's letter

Newspapers have a *rubrique* (section, column) for local news and a *courrier des lecteurs*
(readers' letters page). An article has four parts.

![The layout of a newspaper article, with each part named in French in the right margin. A band at the top gives the section, VIE LOCALE (la rubrique). Below it, the title: Réouverture de la piscine : une amélioration très attendue (le titre). Then three lines in bold, the short introduction (l'introduction, le chapeau); the main body in two columns of text with a quotation in a box (le développement); and at the bottom a short conclusion (la conclusion).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| part | French | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| title | *le titre* | says what happened, often without a verb (below) |
| introduction | *l'introduction* (in the press *le chapeau*) | one or two sentences in bold: who, what, when |
| main body | *le développement* | the details, the people involved, their opinions |
| conclusion | *la conclusion* | what will happen next, or a final opinion |

> **Réouverture de la piscine municipale : une amélioration très attendue**
>
> *Après dix-huit mois de travaux, la piscine des Lilas rouvre ses portes samedi. Les habitants sont ravis, mais certains regrettent la hausse des tarifs.*
>
> La rénovation de la piscine, décidée par le conseil municipal il y a deux ans, a coûté plus cher que prévu. Le bâtiment avait été construit dans les années 1970 et ne respectait plus les normes. Les travaux ont permis l'installation de panneaux solaires, la création d'un bassin pour les enfants et l'agrandissement des vestiaires.
>
> Pour les nageurs, l'amélioration est nette. « L'eau est plus chaude et il y a enfin de la place », se réjouit Martine, 67 ans, qui venait nager tous les matins avant la fermeture. En revanche, l'augmentation du prix de l'entrée, qui passe de 3 à 4 euros, ne fait pas l'unanimité. Plusieurs élus de l'opposition demandent un tarif réduit pour les familles.
>
> La mairie promet de transmettre leur proposition au prochain conseil municipal.

Translation:

> **The municipal swimming pool reopens: a long-awaited improvement**
>
> *After eighteen months of building work, the Lilas swimming pool opens its doors again on Saturday. Residents are delighted, but some regret the higher prices.*
>
> The renovation of the pool, decided by the town council two years ago, cost more than planned. The building had been built in the 1970s and no longer met the standards. The work made it possible to install solar panels, create a children's pool and enlarge the changing rooms.
>
> For swimmers, the improvement is clear. "The water is warmer and at last there's room," says a delighted Martine, 67, who came to swim every morning before the closure. On the other hand, the rise in the entry price, from 3 to 4 euros, is not to everyone's liking. Several opposition councillors are asking for a reduced rate for families.
>
> The town hall promises to pass their proposal on to the next council meeting.

Notes: *les travaux* = building work; *la norme* = standard (rule); *le bassin* = pool (the water
area); *les vestiaires* = changing rooms; *se réjouir* = to be delighted; *ne pas faire
l'unanimité* = not to have everyone's support. Note *avait été construit*: a plus-que-parfait
passive (lesson 15).

A reader's letter to the *courrier des lecteurs* is shorter and more personal: it reacts to an
article or a local issue with the writer's arguments (lesson 21), in a neutral register, signed
with a name and town.

## Nominalisation: verbs turned into nouns

Look at the article again: *réouverture, rénovation, installation, création, agrandissement,
amélioration, fermeture, augmentation*. Each is a verb turned into a noun. This is
**[[nominalisation]]**, and it is everywhere in French titles and formal writing.

| verb | noun | in a title |
|---|---|---|
| *fermer* | *la fermeture* | *Fermeture de l'usine : 200 emplois menacés* |
| *arriver* | *l'arrivée* | *Arrivée des premiers touristes* |
| *améliorer* | *l'amélioration* | *Amélioration de la qualité de l'air* |
| *augmenter* | *l'augmentation* | *Augmentation du prix des loyers* |
| *construire* | *la construction* | *Construction d'un nouveau collège* |
| *interdire* | *l'interdiction* | *Interdiction des voitures dans le centre* |
| *baisser* | *la baisse* | *Baisse du chômage* |

Common endings: *-tion / -sion* (feminine), *-ment* (masculine: *l'agrandissement*), *-ure*
(feminine: *la fermeture*), *-ée* (feminine: *l'arrivée*), and the bare stem (*la baisse, la
hausse*). The verb's object follows with *de*: *on ferme l'usine → la fermeture de l'usine*. At B1,
recognise nominalisations and use them in titles; writing whole paragraphs in this style comes at
B2.

## A petition

A *pétition* is short: who is asking, what for, and why, then the signatures.

> **Pétition : pour un passage sécurisé devant l'école Jules-Ferry**
>
> Nous, parents d'élèves et riverains de la rue des Tilleuls, demandons au conseil municipal de prendre rapidement des mesures pour réduire la vitesse des voitures devant l'école. La sécurité de nos enfants doit passer avant tout.

(We, parents and residents of the rue des Tilleuls, ask the town council to take measures quickly
to reduce the speed of cars outside the school. Our children's safety must come first.)

## Before you hand it in: a checklist

![A checklist for rereading a text, as a clipboard headed Before you hand it in, with six ticked boxes: agreement (adjectives and participles); mood (subjunctive after il faut que, bien que, je ne pense pas que); tenses (passé composé, imparfait, plus-que-parfait); accents (é, è, à, ç: a / à, ou / où); punctuation (a space before : ; ! ?); register (vous all the way through).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Reread your text once for each point:

1. Agreement: adjectives with their nouns (*les mesures nécessaires*), past participles with
   *être* and with a direct object before *avoir* (*la pétition que j'ai signée*).
2. Mood: subjunctive after *il faut que, bien que, pour que, je souhaiterais que, je ne pense
   pas que*; indicative after *je pense que, parce que, même si*.
3. Tenses: events in the passé composé, background in the imparfait, earlier events in the
   plus-que-parfait; no futur or conditionnel after *si* meaning "if" (a condition).
4. Accents: *é, è, à, ç* are part of the spelling (*a / à, ou / où*).
5. Punctuation: in French as printed in France, a space comes before *: ; ! ?* and inside
   « guillemets » (French quotation marks).
6. Register and length: *vous* all the way through a formal letter; at least the number of
   words asked for.

## Common mistakes

- Starting a formal letter with *Cher Monsieur* to someone you don't know: use *Madame, Monsieur,*
  or the person's title (*Monsieur le Maire,*).
- Mixing *tu* and *vous*, or *on* and *nous*, in the same letter.
- Ending with *Cordialement* (A1) in a formal letter to an official: it is fine in e-mails at
  work, but a letter to a mayor or a council usually ends with the full formula.
- *~~Veuillez de trouver~~*: *veuillez* is followed directly by the infinitive: *Veuillez trouver*.
- One huge paragraph: give each argument its own paragraph.

## Key points

- B1 writing: one text giving your view (essay, letter or article), at least about 160 words in
  45 minutes; follow the instructions on the paper.
- Plan in three parts: *l'introduction, le développement* (one *paragraphe* per argument), *la
  conclusion*.
- Formal letter: *Objet*, *Madame, Monsieur,*, *Je me permets de …, Je souhaiterais …, Veuillez
  trouver ci-joint …*, *Dans l'attente de votre réponse*, the full closing formula.
- Keep one **[[register]]**; the conditionnel makes requests polite.
- Nominalisation (*la fermeture de l'usine*) for titles and formal writing; recognise it.
- Reread for agreement, mood, tenses, accents, punctuation and register.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Speaking at B1: discussing, negotiating, persuading
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Writing gives you time; speaking doesn't. In a real discussion you have to get a word in, stop
someone politely, check that you have understood, disagree without offending and, often, reach a
decision together. This lesson teaches the language of **[[interaction]]**: taking and keeping the
floor, interrupting, asking for clarification, **[[reformulation]]**, polite disagreement with the
conditionnel, and the steps of a negotiation, from a first proposal to a compromise. The theme is
deciding together: a weekend away with friends, life in a shared flat, a family decision.

You already have useful pieces from A2: *c'est-à-dire, autrement dit, reformuler, préciser*, the
fillers *euh, bon, en fait* (A2 24h2), and *Si on allait … ?* for suggestions. Lesson 21 gave you
the arguments; here you use them live.

## The B1 speaking test, in general terms

The DELF B1 speaking test (*production et interaction orales*) lasts about 15 minutes, in three
parts:

1. A guided interview (*entretien dirigé*): the examiner asks about you, your life, your
   interests and your plans. Not prepared.
2. An interaction (*exercice en interaction*): a role play in an everyday situation, with no
   preparation. The examiner plays a role, and you must solve a problem, convince them or
   negotiate something. This is where this lesson's phrases matter most.
3. A point of view (*expression d'un point de vue*): from a short document, you present the
   question it raises and your opinion, then discuss it with the examiner. This is the only part
   you prepare, for 10 minutes.

Lesson 24 places the speaking test in the whole exam, and the honors lesson 24h2 has model
answers for each part and advice for the day.

## Taking the floor and keeping it

*La parole* is speech, the spoken word, and in a discussion the turn to speak: *avoir la parole*
(to have the floor), *donner la parole à quelqu'un*, *prendre la parole* (to speak, to take the
floor). (A2's *les paroles*, in the plural, are the words of a song.)

| you want to | you say |
|---|---|
| come in | *Je peux ajouter quelque chose ? / Si je peux me permettre … / Moi, je voudrais dire que …* |
| keep the floor | *Attends, je n'ai pas fini. / Laissez-moi terminer, s'il vous plaît. / Juste une seconde.* |
| give the floor | *Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu en penses ? / Je vous écoute.* |

## Interrupting politely

*Interrompre* (to interrupt) and *couper la parole à quelqu'un* (to cut someone off) describe the
same thing; the second is more everyday and often a complaint: *Arrête de me couper la parole !*
To interrupt politely, apologise first and say why:

- *Pardon de vous interrompre, mais …*
- *Excuse-moi de te couper, mais c'est important.*
- *Je me permets de vous interrompre une seconde : …*

*Interrompre* is like *rompre*: *j'interromps, tu interromps, il interrompt* (with a *t*), *nous
interrompons, vous interrompez, ils interrompent; j'ai interrompu*.

## Checking that you understand

Interaction needs checking. Ask the other person to explain, then show you have understood by
saying their idea again in your own words: that is reformulation.

- Asking: *Qu'est-ce que tu veux dire par là ? Tu peux préciser ? C'est-à-dire ?*
- Reformulating: *Si je comprends bien, tu préfères … Autrement dit, pour toi, …*
- Summarising the other side: *Donc, pour toi, le plus important, c'est le prix.*
- Showing you follow: *Je vois ce que tu veux dire.* (Note *ce que*, not *qu'est-ce que*, in this
  indirect question, lesson 18.)

Summarising the other person's view before you answer is the most useful single strategy in a
discussion: it shows you listened, it gives you time to think, and the other person feels heard.

## Agreeing and disagreeing, politely

*L'accord* (agreement) and *le désaccord* (disagreement) are the nouns: *Nous sommes en désaccord
sur ce point. Ils ont trouvé un accord.* *Se mettre d'accord* is to reach agreement, to agree on
something: *On s'est mis d'accord sur la date.* (*Être d'accord avec quelqu'un*, A2, is to agree
with someone.)

To disagree without offending, soften with the conditionnel and with partial agreement:

| strength | phrases |
|---|---|
| partial agreement | *Tu n'as pas tort, mais … / Je vois ce que tu veux dire, mais … / C'est vrai en partie.* |
| polite disagreement | *Je ne serais pas tout à fait d'accord. / Je verrais plutôt les choses autrement. / Je dirais plutôt que …* |
| frank disagreement | *Franchement, je ne suis pas d'accord. / À vrai dire, je trouve ça trop cher.* |
| "you're going too far" | *Tu exagères ! / N'exagérons rien.* |

- *Franchement* (frankly, honestly) and *à vrai dire* (to tell the truth, actually) announce an
  honest opinion. *Franchement* can sound blunt; with friends it is normal.
- *Exagérer* means "to exaggerate" but also "to go too far": *Tu exagères, tu arrives toujours en
  retard !*
- *Sincère* (sincere) is the same for both genders: *Je vais être sincère avec toi.*
- *Nuancer* is to qualify an opinion, to add a nuance: *Je voudrais nuancer ce que tu dis.* *La
  nuance* is a shade, a subtle difference: *Il y a une nuance entre « franc » et « impoli ».*
- *En tout cas* (in any case, anyway) moves the discussion on: *En tout cas, il faut décider
  aujourd'hui.*

### Saying it doesn't matter

- *Ça ne me dérange pas* = it doesn't bother me, I don't mind: *Le bruit ne me dérange pas.* To
  ask: *Ça te dérange si j'ouvre la fenêtre ?* (indicative after *si*) or *Ça vous dérange que
  j'ouvre la fenêtre ?* (subjunctive after *que*, a feeling: lesson 06).
- *Ça m'est égal* = I don't mind either way, it's all the same to me. For a choice that really
  doesn't matter (the film or the concert?), it is a normal, friendly answer. But it literally
  says the thing makes no difference to you, so about something the other person cares about, or
  said flatly, it sounds indifferent, even dismissive (*Ton projet ? Ça m'est égal.*). *Les deux
  me vont* or *Ça ne me dérange pas* are warmer.
- *Déranger* also means to disturb: *Je ne vous dérange pas ?* (Am I disturbing you?)

## Negotiating and reaching a compromise

*Négocier* (to negotiate) and *la négociation* follow the same steps whether you are planning a
holiday or settling a deal at work.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The steps of a negotiation
  accDescr: A negotiation in five steps, one after the other. First a proposal: Et si on louait une maison à la mer ? Then an objection: C'est trop cher pour moi. Then a concession: D'accord, je veux bien céder sur la maison. Then a compromise: Je suis prêt à venir, à condition qu'on prenne un appartement. Finally the agreement and the close: Alors, c'est décidé : un appartement à la mer.
  A["Proposal: Et si on louait une maison à la mer ?"] --> B["Objection: C'est trop cher pour moi."]
  B --> C["Concession: D'accord, je veux bien céder sur la maison."]
  C --> D["Compromise: Je suis prêt à venir, à condition qu'on prenne un appartement."]
  D --> E["Agreement and close: Alors, c'est décidé : un appartement à la mer."]
```

| step | phrases |
|---|---|
| propose | *Et si on …? (+ imparfait) / Je propose qu'on … (+ subjunctive) / Ce que je te propose, c'est …* |
| object | *Le problème, c'est que … / Ça ne me convient pas tellement. / Je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit possible.* |
| concede | *D'accord, je veux bien céder sur … / Je peux faire une concession : …* |
| set a condition | *Je suis prêt(e) à … à condition que + subjunctive / à condition de + infinitive / En échange, …* |
| compromise | *On pourrait trouver un compromis : … / Coupons la poire en deux.* (Let's split the difference.) |
| close | *Si je résume, … / Alors, c'est décidé ? / On est d'accord ?* |

- *Céder* is to give in, to give way (*Il n'a pas voulu céder*). It changes its accent like
  *préférer*: *je cède, nous cédons, ils cèdent*; futur *je céderai* (or the 1990 spelling *je
  cèderai*).
- *Faire une concession* (to make a concession) is the noun of conceding: you give up something
  to get something. In grammar, a **[[concession]]** (lesson 20) is admitting a fact before answering
  it; the idea is the same.
- *Tenir compte de* is to take into account: *Il faut tenir compte du budget de chacun. Tu ne
  tiens pas compte de mon avis !*
- *L'échange* is an exchange, and also a conversation in which people exchange views: *un échange
  intéressant*; *en échange* = in exchange.
- *Nuancer* and *négocier* are regular, but watch the spelling: *nous nuançons* (ç before *o*),
  and *nous négocions*, imparfait *nous négociions* (two *i*: the stem *négoci-* + *-ions*).

## Dialogue: a long weekend together

Léa, Hugo and Samir want to go away together for a long weekend in May.

```dialogue lang=fr-FR
# Un week-end à trois
Léa: Alors, on décide ? Moi, je propose qu'on aille à la mer. Il fera beau en mai, et on pourrait louer une maison.
= So, shall we decide? I suggest we go to the seaside. It'll be fine in May, and we could rent a house.
Hugo: À vrai dire, la mer, ça m'est égal. Ce qui compte pour moi, c'est le prix. Une maison au bord de la mer, en mai, c'est cher.
= To tell the truth, I don't mind about the sea. What matters to me is the price. A house by the sea in May is expensive.
Samir: Pardon de te couper, Hugo, mais tu exagères un peu. Si on partage à trois, ça reste raisonnable.
= Sorry to cut in, Hugo, but you're going a bit far. If we split it three ways, it's still reasonable.
Hugo: Attends, je n'ai pas fini. Je n'ai rien contre la mer, mais il faut tenir compte du budget de chacun.
= Wait, I haven't finished. I've nothing against the sea, but we have to take everyone's budget into account.
Léa: Je vois ce que tu veux dire. Si je comprends bien, tu serais d'accord pour la mer si c'était moins cher ?
= I see what you mean. If I understand correctly, you'd be OK with the sea if it were cheaper?
Hugo: Exactement. Et si on faisait du camping ? C'est trois fois moins cher.
= Exactly. How about camping? It's three times cheaper.
Samir: Franchement, le camping en mai, je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit une bonne idée. Il peut faire froid la nuit.
= Honestly, camping in May, I'm not sure it's a good idea. It can be cold at night.
Léa: Bon, on pourrait trouver un compromis : un petit appartement au lieu d'une maison, et on fait les courses nous-mêmes au lieu d'aller au restaurant.
= Right, we could find a compromise: a small flat instead of a house, and we do our own shopping instead of eating out.
Hugo: D'accord, je veux bien céder sur la maison, à condition qu'on fasse un budget précis avant de réserver.
= OK, I'm willing to give in on the house, provided we work out a precise budget before booking.
Samir: Ça ne me dérange pas. En tout cas, il faut réserver cette semaine.
= That's fine by me. In any case, we need to book this week.
Léa: Alors, si je résume : la mer, un appartement, et Hugo s'occupe du budget. On est d'accord ?
= So, to sum up: the sea, a flat, and Hugo takes care of the budget. Are we agreed?
Hugo: On est d'accord. Vous voyez, une bonne négociation, ça marche !
= Agreed. You see, a good negotiation works!
```

Notes: Léa proposes with *je propose qu'on aille* (subjunctive after a wish, lesson 06), Hugo
suggests with *Et si on faisait …?*, Samir objects with *je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit*
(subjunctive after doubt, lesson 07), and Hugo sets a condition with *à condition qu'on fasse*
(lesson 08). Léa's two reformulations (*Si je comprends bien …, si je résume …*) keep the
discussion moving. *Tu serais d'accord … si c'était moins cher* is a si-clause of type 2
(lesson 09).

## Say it

```speak lang=fr-FR
# Phrases for a discussion
Pardon de vous interrompre, mais c'est important.
= Sorry to interrupt you, but it's important.
Si je comprends bien, tu préfères partir plus tard ?
= If I understand correctly, you'd rather leave later?
Je vois ce que tu veux dire, mais je ne serais pas tout à fait d'accord.
= I see what you mean, but I wouldn't entirely agree.
Je suis prête à céder sur la date, à condition qu'on parte ensemble.
= I'm ready to give in on the date, provided we leave together.
Ça m'est égal, les deux me vont.
= I don't mind, both suit me.
Alors, si je résume, on est d'accord ?
= So, to sum up, are we agreed?
```

## Moves in a discussion

![Four panels, each showing a person with a speech bubble. Top left: Pardon de te couper, mais …, labelled interrupting politely. Top right: Tu peux préciser ?, labelled asking for clarification. Bottom left: Tu n'as pas tort, mais …, labelled conceding a point. Bottom right: Coupons la poire en deux !, labelled proposing a compromise.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *Il interrompt* [ɛ̃tɛʁɔ̃]: the *-mpt* is silent. *Interrompu* [ɛ̃tɛʁɔ̃py].
- *Je cède* [sɛd], *nous cédons* [sedɔ̃]: *è* [ɛ] when the next syllable has a silent *-e* (*je
  cède, ils cèdent*), *é* elsewhere (*nous cédons, vous cédez*).
- *Ça m'est égal* [sa mɛ teɡal]: liaison *m'est-t-égal*.

## Common mistakes

- *~~Je vois qu'est-ce que tu veux dire~~*: in an indirect question it's *ce que*: *Je vois ce que
  tu veux dire.*
- *~~On s'est mis d'accord avec la date~~*: *se mettre d'accord sur* something, *être d'accord
  avec* someone.
- *Ça m'est égal* about something the other person cares about: it sounds as if you don't care.
  Add a reason or say *Les deux me vont*.
- *Il interromp*: the *t* is written: *il interrompt*.
- Disagreeing with only *Non* or *C'est faux*: soften (*Je ne serais pas tout à fait d'accord*) and
  give a reason.
- Never summarising: in the exam's interaction, saying the other person's view back to them
  (*Si je comprends bien …*) shows real interaction, not two monologues.

## Key points

- Take the floor (*prendre la parole, Je peux ajouter quelque chose ?*), keep it (*Je n'ai pas
  fini*), interrupt politely (*Pardon de vous interrompre, mais …*).
- Check and reformulate: *Tu peux préciser ? Si je comprends bien … Autrement dit …*
- Disagree softly with the conditionnel: *Je ne serais pas tout à fait d'accord. Tu n'as pas tort,
  mais …*
- Negotiate in steps: proposal → objection → concession → compromise → close; *à condition que* +
  subjunctive.
- *Ça ne me dérange pas* = I don't mind; *Ça m'est égal* = it's all the same to me (watch the tone).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The DELF B1 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson explains what "B1" means, describes the **[[DELF]]** B1 and how to prepare for
each part, gives you the words of exams and marking, and reviews the grammar of the course with
charts and pointers to the lessons. You don't have to take an exam, but the free official sample
papers are the best way to check that you have reached B1.

## What B1 means

The six levels A1 to C2 come from the **[[CEFR]]** (Common European Framework of Reference for
Languages), published by the Council of Europe. A1 and A2 are "basic user"; B1 and B2 are
"independent user", and B1 is the first step of it. The CEFR describes each level with
**[[can-do statements]]**: what a learner is able to do with the language, not which grammar they
know. In our own words, someone at B1 can:

- understand the main points of clear, standard speech and writing on familiar matters: work,
  school, free time;
- deal with most situations that come up while travelling where the language is spoken;
- write simple connected text on topics that are familiar or of personal interest;
- describe experiences, events, dreams, hopes and plans, and briefly give reasons and
  explanations for opinions and plans.

The step up from A2 is from short, routine exchanges to connected speech and writing: a story
with several past tenses, a chain of reasons, an argument with a conclusion. In French that
means the plus-que-parfait, the subjunctive, si-clauses and the conditionnel passé, and the
connectors of cause, consequence and concession: exactly what this course has taught.

## The DELF B1

*DELF* stands for *Diplôme d'études en langue française*: the official French diplomas of the
French Ministry of Education for levels A1 to B2, run by France Éducation international (FEI).
Each level is a separate diploma, valid for life; you can take the B1 without having taken the
A2. The adult version is the *DELF tout public*.

The exam has four parts (*épreuves*), each marked out of 25 points:

| part | time | what it involves |
|---|---|---|
| *Compréhension de l'oral* (listening) | about 25 minutes | three recordings, each heard twice: a conversation and two radio-style documents (an interview, a report), with questions |
| *Compréhension des écrits* (reading) | 45 minutes in the current format | several short informative texts to compare against a given task (a set of criteria), and two longer texts (about 300–350 words) giving information or an opinion |
| *Production écrite* (writing) | 45 minutes | one text giving your view on a general topic: an essay, a letter or an article (sample papers ask for at least 160 words) |
| *Production et interaction orales* (speaking) | about 15 minutes, after 10 minutes of preparation for the third part | a guided interview, an interaction (a role play without preparation) and a point of view from a short document |

![An overview chart of the DELF B1. A box for the written papers, about 1 hour 55 minutes in the current format (a footnote says the 2009 regulation gives 35 minutes for reading and 1 hour 45 in all), holds three parts side by side: compréhension de l'oral (listening), about 25 minutes, three recordings each heard twice, 25 points; compréhension des écrits (reading), 45 minutes, short texts and two longer texts, 25 points; production écrite (writing), 45 minutes, one text of at least about 160 words, 25 points. A separate box for the speaking test, production et interaction orales: about 15 minutes in three parts, with 10 minutes of preparation for part 3 only, 25 points. Below: total 100 points; pass with 50, and at least 5 out of 25 in every part; check the official page, as details can change.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three written parts are taken together in one sitting; the speaking test is separate, often
later the same day or on another day. To pass, you need 50 points out of 100 and at least 5
out of 25 in each part. A mark below 5 in any part is *éliminatoire*: you fail, even with a
total of 50 or more.

### Timings: check the official page

The figures above follow the 2009 regulation, updated by FEI's 2021 description of the revised
papers. (FEI's own web pages couldn't be checked for this course, so treat them as the final
word.) Three points need care, because the exam was revised and sources differ:

- Reading: the 2009 regulation gives 35 minutes. FEI's description of the revised papers says
  the reading paper became 45 minutes from March 2020, so the written parts together went from
  1 h 45 to 1 h 55. Some books and websites still give 35 minutes and 1 h 45.
- Length of the written text: the regulation gives no number. Sample papers and preparation
  guides ask for at least 160 words. The instructions on your paper decide.
- The format of the questions: since the revision, the listening and reading papers use only
  closed questions: multiple choice with three options and true/false questions that you don't
  have to justify. Older practice books still have open questions.

Always check the official pages before you register, and practise with FEI's own sample papers:

- [DELF B1 tout public: description of the exam](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-b1)
- [DELF B1 sample papers (exemples de sujets)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-b1/exemples-sujets)
- [Advice for preparing the DELF B1 (entraînement)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-b1/entrainement)
- [The official regulation of the DELF and DALF (Bulletin officiel, 2009, PDF)](https://cache.media.education.gouv.fr/file/31/55/2/DELF-DALF_reglement-epreuve_101552.pdf)

Each exam centre sets its own *sessions* (exam sittings: *la session de juin*), fees and
deadlines, so check with the centre where you register.

## The words of exams and marking

| French | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| *le barème* | marking scheme, scale of marks | *Le barème est sur 25 points.* |
| *le minimum, le maximum* | minimum, maximum | *Il faut au minimum 5 points par épreuve.* |
| *éliminatoire* | eliminatory (a mark that fails you) | *Une note inférieure à 5 est éliminatoire.* |
| *la session* | session (exam sitting) | *Je m'inscris à la session de novembre.* |
| *se préparer (à)* | to get ready, to prepare (yourself) | *Je me prépare au DELF depuis six mois.* |
| *la stratégie* | strategy | *une bonne stratégie pour l'écoute* |
| *l'astuce* (feminine) | tip, trick | *une astuce pour gagner du temps* |
| *l'essai* (masculine) | essay; attempt | *un essai de 160 mots / un premier essai* |
| *la problématique* | the central question (of a topic) | *Quelle est la problématique de ce texte ?* |
| *l'idée* (feminine) *principale / secondaire* | main / secondary idea | *les idées principales* |
| *argumenter, justifier, illustrer* | to give reasons, to justify, to illustrate | *Justifiez votre réponse. Illustrez vos arguments par des exemples.* |
| *la justification* | justification | *une réponse sans justification* |

- *Principal*: feminine *principale*, plural *principaux, principales*. *L'essai* is also an
  attempt (*au premier essai*); *essayer* (A1) is "to try".
- *La problématique* is the key question a topic raises, the thing your text has to answer: for
  "the four-day week", the *problématique* might be *Travailler moins de jours, est-ce travailler
  mieux ?* It is not "a problem" (*un problème*).
- *Argumenter* is to argue a case; to quarrel is *se disputer* (A2). *Justifier*: imparfait *nous
  justifiions*, like *étudier*.

### What examiners look at

In the writing and speaking papers, examiners mark with grids (*grilles*) of criteria. In general
terms they look at whether you did what the task asked (form, length, who you write to), how well
you present and justify your ideas, how clearly your text holds together (*la cohérence*: a
*cohérent* text has a plan and connectors), and the range and correctness of your language: *le
vocabulaire, la grammaire, la conjugaison, l'orthographe, la ponctuation*. At the oral,
pronunciation and *l'aisance* (ease, fluency) count too. So a short, correct, well-organised text
usually scores better than a long, messy one, but it must reach the minimum length.

## Strategies for each part

### Listening and reading: multiple choice with three options

- Read the questions and the three options first: they tell you what to listen or look for.
- Wrong options often repeat words from the document; the right one often says the same thing
  in other words (*Le maire a renoncé au projet* in the text, *Le projet est abandonné* in the
  option).
- Many questions ask what a speaker thinks: listen for opinion verbs, *mais, pourtant,
  cependant, en revanche*, and the conditionnel of hedging.
- For true/false questions, *vrai* only if the text really says it, not if it simply seems
  likely.
- In the exercise that compares several short texts against a set of criteria, read the criteria
  first (price, place, dates, age …), then check each text against each one.
- Preparation guides say wrong answers don't lose points, so never leave a question blank; check
  the instructions on the day.

### Writing

- Find the *problématique*: what exactly are you asked to give your view on, and to whom?
- Plan in three parts (lesson 22), with two or three arguments, each with an example (lesson 21).
- Show the B1 grammar you have: a subjunctive after *il faut que* or *je ne pense pas que*, a
  si-clause, a concession with *bien que* or *certes … mais*.
- Count your words roughly: at least the number on the paper (usually 160). Reread with the
  checklist of lesson 22.

### Speaking

- Part 1: have a few sentences ready about your life, studies or work, and plans, in several
  tenses.
- Part 2: in the role play, reach a result: negotiate, propose, concede (lesson 23).
- Part 3: use your 10 minutes to find the *problématique* of the document, choose your position
  and two arguments with examples; note key words, not full sentences.
- The honors lesson 24h2 goes through the three parts with model answers.

## Reading: practise the skill

Here is an original text at the level of the longer reading texts. Read it once for the main
idea, then answer the questions in the lesson quiz.

> **Apprendre une langue après quarante ans : trop tard ?**
>
> On entend souvent dire qu'il faut apprendre les langues étrangères quand on est enfant, et qu'après un certain âge, c'est trop tard. Pourtant, de nombreux adultes se lancent chaque année dans l'apprentissage d'une nouvelle langue, et beaucoup y réussissent très bien.
>
> Certes, les enfants ont un avantage : ils imitent facilement les sons et ils ont rarement peur de se tromper. C'est pourquoi ils ont souvent un meilleur accent. Mais les adultes ont d'autres atouts. Ils savent déjà comment fonctionne une langue, ils peuvent comparer avec leur langue maternelle, et surtout, ils savent pourquoi ils apprennent : pour leur travail, pour voyager ou pour parler avec leur famille.
>
> Marc, 52 ans, a commencé l'italien il y a trois ans, quand sa fille est partie vivre à Milan. « Au début, j'avais honte de mes fautes, raconte-t-il. Aujourd'hui, je regarde des films sans sous-titres. Ce qui m'a aidé, c'est de pratiquer un peu tous les jours plutôt que beaucoup une fois par semaine. »
>
> Bref, l'âge n'est pas un obstacle si l'on est motivé et régulier. Le vrai risque, à quarante ans comme à quinze, c'est d'abandonner trop vite.

Translation:

> **Learning a language after forty: too late?**
>
> You often hear that you have to learn foreign languages as a child, and that after a certain age it's too late. And yet many adults start learning a new language every year, and many of them do very well.
>
> Admittedly, children have an advantage: they copy sounds easily and they are rarely afraid of making mistakes. That's why they often have a better accent. But adults have other strengths. They already know how a language works, they can compare it with their mother tongue and, above all, they know why they are learning: for work, to travel or to talk with their family.
>
> Marc, 52, started Italian three years ago, when his daughter went to live in Milan. "At first I was ashamed of my mistakes," he says. "Today I watch films without subtitles. What helped me was practising a little every day rather than a lot once a week."
>
> In short, age isn't an obstacle if you are motivated and regular. The real risk, at forty as at fifteen, is giving up too soon.

Notes: *l'apprentissage* = learning; *l'atout* = strength, asset; *la langue maternelle* = mother
tongue; *les sous-titres* = subtitles; *se lancer dans* = to launch into (honors 24h2). The text
has the B1 argument shape: a common idea, *pourtant*, a concession with *certes … mais*, an
example, and a conclusion with *bref*.

## Review: the grammar of the course

### Indicative, subjunctive or infinitive?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Indicative, subjunctive or infinitive?
  accDescr: A decision chart for the verb after que or a conjunction. First question: is the subject the same in both halves? If yes, use an infinitive, as in je veux partir or pour gagner du temps. If not, second question: does the main clause express necessity, a wish, a feeling, doubt or a negative opinion, or is the conjunction one of pour que, afin que, avant que, jusqu'à ce que, sans que, à condition que, bien que? If yes, use the subjunctive, as in il faut que tu viennes or bien qu'il soit tard. If not, use the indicative, as in je pense que c'est vrai, parce que, même si, pendant que. A note: espérer que takes the indicative.
  A["A verb after que or a conjunction"] --> B{"Same subject in both halves?"}
  B -- "yes (where an infinitive exists)" --> INF["Infinitive: je veux partir, pour gagner du temps"]
  B -- no --> C{"Necessity, wish, feeling, doubt, negative opinion, or pour que, avant que, bien que, à condition que, sans que?"}
  C -- yes --> S["Subjunctive: il faut que tu viennes, bien qu'il soit tard"]
  C -- no --> I["Indicative: je pense que c'est vrai, parce que, même si; also espérer que"]
```

Lessons 05–08: the forms (*ils viennent → que je vienne*; *nous venions → que nous venions*; the
main irregulars *sois, aie, aille, fasse, puisse, sache, veuille*), necessity, will and feeling,
doubt and opinion, conjunctions. *Bien que* has no infinitive version, so it keeps the
subjunctive even with the same subject (*Bien que je sois fatigué, je continue*).

### Si-clauses

| type | *si* + | main clause | example | lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| real, likely | present | present, futur, imperative | *Si tu viens, on ira au cinéma.* | A2, 09 |
| unreal now, unlikely | imparfait | conditionnel présent | *Si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais.* | 09 |
| unreal past | plus-que-parfait | conditionnel passé | *Si j'avais su, je serais venu.* | 11 |
| mixed | plus-que-parfait | conditionnel présent | *Si j'avais pris le train, je serais déjà là.* | 11 |

Never the futur or the conditionnel after *si* = if. (After *si* = whether, any tense: *Je ne sais
pas s'il viendra*, lesson 18.)

### Tenses on a timeline

![A timeline of the tenses of the course. On the past side, from left to right: the plus-que-parfait for an earlier past, j'avais fini; the passé composé for events, je suis parti; and a wavy band under them for the imparfait, background and habits, il pleuvait. In the middle, now, the present. On the future side: the futur antérieur for something finished before another future action, j'aurai fini; then the futur simple, je partirai. Below the past side: the conditionnel passé for a past that didn't happen, j'aurais aimé.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Lessons 01–04: passé composé and imparfait in depth, the plus-que-parfait, *après avoir* +
participle and time clauses, the gérondif. Lessons 10 and 12: the conditionnel passé (*j'aurais
dû*), the futur antérieur (*quand tu auras fini*).

### Connectors

| to express | connectors | lesson |
|---|---|---|
| cause | *puisque, étant donné que, vu que, en raison de, faute de* | 19 |
| consequence | *si bien que, tellement … que, par conséquent, ainsi, d'où* | 19 |
| purpose | *pour que, afin que* + subjunctive; *pour, afin de* + infinitive | 08 |
| opposition | *alors que, tandis que, en revanche, contrairement à* | 20 |
| concession | *bien que* + subjunctive, *même si* + indicative, *cependant, toutefois, néanmoins, avoir beau, certes … mais* | 08, 20 |
| structure | *tout d'abord, de plus, en outre, par ailleurs, d'ailleurs, enfin, en conclusion* | 21 |

If you had to remember three things from this course: the subjunctive follows what is wanted,
felt or doubted, not what is known; the plus-que-parfait is the "past before the past" and feeds
type-3 si-clauses and reported speech; and a good argument has a position, reasons with examples,
a concession and a conclusion.

## Pronunciation

- *Le barème* [baʁɛm]; *éliminatoire* [eliminatwaʁ].
- *L'aisance* [lɛzɑ̃s]: the *s* between vowels is [z]. *La cohérence* [koeʁɑ̃s]: the *h* is silent
  and the two vowels are said separately.
- *Principaux* [pʁɛ̃sipo]; *l'orthographe* [lɔʁtɔɡʁaf].

## Common mistakes

- *La problématique* as "the problem": it is the question your text answers.
- *Argumenter* for "to have an argument": that is *se disputer*.
- *~~Les points principals~~*: *principaux*.
- Writing much less than the minimum because you ran out of time: plan for 10 minutes, no more.
- Learning your speaking answers by heart: examiners notice, and no role play goes exactly as you
  planned. Learn phrases, not speeches.
- Giving up on your weakest part: every part needs at least 5/25.

## What comes next

At B2 you will follow longer and more complex talks and texts, including abstract topics and
discussions in your own field; write detailed texts that weigh arguments for and against (the
honors lesson 24h1 previews the B2 essay); and use the subjonctif passé, the passé simple in
reading, and the nominal style more actively. Keep your vocabulary reviews going, read the
graded readers on the reading list, and listen to French radio and podcasts every day: at B1,
regular contact matters more than anything else.

## Key points

- B1 is the first "independent user" level: connected speech and writing on familiar topics,
  with reasons and opinions.
- The DELF B1 has four parts of 25 points: listening (about 25 min), reading (45 min in the
  current format; 35 in the 2009 regulation), writing (45 min, usually at least 160 words), speaking
  (about 15 min, 10 min of preparation for the third part). Pass: 50/100, with at least 5/25 in
  each part. Written parts together: 1 h 55 (1 h 45 in the 2009 regulation).
- The comprehension papers use multiple choice with three options and true/false questions.
- Check FEI's official pages and practise with its sample papers.
- *Le barème, éliminatoire, la session, la problématique, justifier, illustrer, l'astuce*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Félicitations : you have finished the core of French B1!

lessons.title: Honors: From B1 to B2: the argued essay
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 gave you the B1 argumentative text: a position, two or three arguments with examples,
the other side admitted, a conclusion. That is all the DELF B1 asks for. At B2, and in French
schools and universities, an essay is expected to do more: to weigh both sides properly before
deciding, and to answer the strongest objections instead of just mentioning them.

This honors lesson is a preview of B2. It shows the **[[dialectical plan]]** (*thèse, antithèse,
synthèse*), the technique of **[[refutation]]**, how to write an introduction that asks a real
question and a conclusion that opens a wider one, and it gives two original model essays of 200
to 250 words. Nothing here is needed for the B1 exam; use it if you plan to go further, or if you
want your B1 texts to stand out.

## Two kinds of plan

The B1 plan of lesson 21 is built around your position: every argument pushes the same way.
The dialectical plan is built around a question, and it gives each side its full turn before
you decide.

![Two essay plans side by side. Left, the B1 plan: introduction with your position; argument 1 with an example; argument 2 with an example; the other side, briefly, with certes … mais; conclusion. Right, the dialectical plan: introduction with the question; part 1, la thèse, the arguments for; part 2, l'antithèse, the arguments against; part 3, la synthèse, a more careful answer; conclusion, with l'ouverture, a wider question. Arrows lead from each box to the next.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| part | French | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | *la thèse* | presents one answer to the question, with its best arguments and examples |
| 2 | *l'antithèse* | presents the opposite answer, just as fairly |
| 3 | *la synthèse* | goes beyond the two: under what conditions, to what extent, in what sense each is right |

You met *la thèse* in lesson 21 as "the position you argue". In this plan it is the first answer
you test. *L'antithèse* is the counter-argument; *la synthèse* is a summing-up that resolves the
tension (in other contexts, *une synthèse* is simply a summary: *faire la synthèse d'un
rapport*).

The third part is where most essays fail. A *synthèse* is not "both sides have a point" and
it is not a copy of part 1. It answers the question more precisely than either side did: *Le
télétravail est un progrès, mais seulement s'il reste un choix.*

The dialectical plan is a tradition of French schooling (*la dissertation* at the lycée and at
university). It is not the only plan: French essays also use a thematic plan (one part per aspect
of a topic) or a problem, causes, solutions plan. Choose the one that fits the question; a
question with "yes or no" in it (*Faut-il …? Est-ce que …?*) often suits the dialectical plan.

## The introduction: three moves

A B2 introduction usually does three things in four or five sentences:

1. Brings in the topic with a fact, an observation or a common opinion: *À première vue*
   (at first sight), *le télétravail semble n'avoir que des avantages.*
2. Asks the question (the *problématique*, lesson 24): *Mais travailler chez soi, est-ce
   vraiment travailler mieux ?* You can announce it with *il s'agit de* (it's a matter of, the
   question is): *Il s'agit de savoir si …*
3. Announces the plan in one sentence: *Nous verrons d'abord …, puis …, avant de proposer …*

*Il s'agit de* is impersonal: the subject is always *il*, never a noun. You can't say *Ce livre
s'agit de …*; say *Dans ce livre, il s'agit de …* or *Ce livre parle de …*. It is also used in
everyday French: *De quoi s'agit-il ?* (What is it about?)

## Refutation: answering the other side

At B1 you concede (*Certes …, mais …*). At B2 you refute: you state the opposing argument
fairly, then show why it doesn't hold. *Réfuter* is to refute, to disprove; *la réfutation* is
the act or the passage that does it.

A refutation has three steps:

| step | phrases |
|---|---|
| state the other view | *Certains affirment que … / On pourrait objecter que … / Selon les partisans de …* |
| grant what is true in it | *Il est vrai que … / Ce raisonnement est séduisant à première vue.* |
| show where it fails | *Or …* (but, now) */ Cependant, cet argument ne tient pas, car … / Rien ne prouve que …* |

- *Or* (the same word as *l'or*, gold, but a different use) is a logical connector of formal writing: it brings in
  a fact that changes the reasoning. *On dit que les écrans isolent les jeunes. Or, la plupart
  de leurs échanges en ligne se font avec des amis qu'ils voient aussi en vrai.* It has no exact
  English equivalent: "but", "yet", "now".
- *Le raisonnement* is reasoning, a line of argument; *raisonner* is to reason: *Ce raisonnement
  est logique, mais il oublie un point essentiel. Raisonnons autrement.* Don't confuse
  *raisonner* with *résonner* (to resonate, to echo).
- *Cet argument ne tient pas* = this argument doesn't hold up.

## The conclusion and its *ouverture*

A B2 conclusion sums up the reasoning, gives a clear answer to the question, and often ends with
an ouverture: a wider question that the essay leads to but doesn't answer. *L'ouverture* is,
literally, an opening (*l'ouverture d'un magasin*: the noun of *ouvrir*, a nominalisation, lesson
22).

- Summing up: *En somme* (in short, all in all; close to *bref*, lesson 21), *En définitive* (all
  things considered, ultimately), *Au terme de cette réflexion* (at the end of this reflection).
- A formal admission: *Force est de constater que …* (one has to admit that …). It is formal and
  written, and it introduces a fact you can't deny: *Force est de constater que les choses ont
  changé.* The verb after *que* is in the indicative.
- An *ouverture* is a question, not a new argument: *Mais au-delà du travail, n'est-ce pas notre
  rapport au temps libre qui est en train de changer ?*

A good *ouverture* is related but bigger. A bad one changes the subject or adds an argument you
should have developed in the body.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a dialectical essay

The question (invented): *Le télétravail est-il un progrès ?* (Read the margin notes in brackets:
they show the plan, and are not part of the essay.)

> [Introduction] À première vue, le télétravail semble n'avoir que des avantages : moins de transports, plus de temps pour soi, une meilleure concentration. Pourtant, de nombreux salariés disent se sentir seuls. Il s'agit donc de savoir si travailler chez soi est vraiment un progrès. Nous verrons d'abord ce qu'il apporte, puis ses limites, avant de proposer une réponse plus nuancée.
>
> [Thèse] D'une part, le télétravail fait gagner du temps. Une personne qui passe une heure par jour dans les transports et qui travaille chez elle deux jours par semaine récupère ainsi deux heures par semaine. D'autre part, beaucoup de salariés se disent plus efficaces chez eux, loin du bruit des open spaces.
>
> [Antithèse] Cependant, ce mode de travail a un prix. Les échanges informels, autour d'un café par exemple, disparaissent, alors qu'ils permettent souvent de résoudre un problème en quelques minutes. De plus, la frontière entre vie privée et vie professionnelle devient floue : on consulte ses e-mails le soir, on ne « quitte » plus jamais le travail.
>
> [Synthèse] En définitive, le télétravail n'est ni un progrès ni un recul en soi. Il devient un progrès quand il reste un choix, limité à quelques jours par semaine, et quand l'entreprise organise des moments pour se retrouver.
>
> [Conclusion and ouverture] En somme, c'est la façon de le pratiquer qui compte. Mais au-delà du travail, n'est-ce pas notre rapport au temps et à l'espace qui est en train de changer ?

Translation:

> At first sight, remote work seems to have only advantages: less commuting, more time for yourself, better concentration. And yet many employees say they feel lonely. So the question is whether working from home is really progress. We will look first at what it offers, then at its limits, before suggesting a more nuanced answer.
>
> On the one hand, remote work saves time. Someone who spends an hour a day commuting and works from home two days a week gets back two hours a week. On the other, many employees say they are more efficient at home, away from the noise of open-plan offices.
>
> However, this way of working has a price. Informal exchanges, over a coffee for example, disappear, although they often make it possible to solve a problem in a few minutes. What's more, the boundary between private and working life becomes blurred: people check their e-mails in the evening and never really "leave" work.
>
> All things considered, remote work is neither progress nor a step backwards in itself. It becomes progress when it remains a choice, limited to a few days a week, and when the company organises times for people to get together.
>
> In short, it is how it is practised that counts. But beyond work, isn't it our relationship with time and space that is changing?

Notes: *le salarié* = employee (lesson 14); *l'open space* = open-plan office (an anglicism, very common in France); *flou* =
blurred; *le recul* = step backwards; *en soi* = in itself. The *synthèse* answers the question
with conditions (*quand il reste un choix …*): that is what makes it more than "both sides have a
point".

### Example 2: an essay built on refutation

The question (invented): *Les réseaux sociaux nous isolent-ils ?* This essay takes a clear
position and spends its middle part refuting the main objection.

> [Introduction] On entend souvent dire que les réseaux sociaux nous isolent : chacun regarde son écran au lieu de parler à ses voisins. Ce raisonnement est séduisant, mais est-il juste ? Nous défendrons l'idée que les réseaux ne créent pas l'isolement, même s'ils peuvent l'aggraver.
>
> [The objection, stated fairly] Certains affirment que le temps passé en ligne est du temps volé aux vraies relations. Il est vrai que l'on voit, dans les cafés ou à table, des groupes où personne ne se parle.
>
> [Refutation] Or, la plupart des échanges en ligne se font avec des personnes que l'on connaît déjà : des amis, des collègues, la famille éloignée. Pour un étudiant parti à l'étranger ou une personne âgée qui sort peu, ces échanges sont souvent un lien précieux, pas un obstacle. Rien ne prouve donc que les réseaux remplacent les rencontres ; dans bien des cas, ils les préparent.
>
> [The limit granted] Force est de constater, cependant, que certains usages posent problème : faire défiler des vidéos pendant des heures n'est pas un échange. C'est cet usage passif, plus que l'outil lui-même, qui peut isoler.
>
> [Conclusion and ouverture] En somme, les réseaux sociaux ne nous isolent pas : ils amplifient ce que nous en faisons. La vraie question est peut-être celle-ci : apprend-on aux jeunes à s'en servir ?

Translation:

> You often hear that social media isolate us: everyone looks at their screen instead of talking to the people around them. This reasoning is attractive, but is it right? We will defend the idea that social networks don't create isolation, even if they can make it worse.
>
> Some claim that time spent online is time stolen from real relationships. It is true that in cafés or at the table you see groups where nobody is talking.
>
> But most exchanges online are with people we already know: friends, colleagues, family far away. For a student who has gone abroad or an elderly person who rarely goes out, these exchanges are often a precious link, not an obstacle. So nothing proves that social networks replace meeting people; in many cases they prepare the way for it.
>
> One has to admit, however, that some uses are a problem: scrolling through videos for hours is not an exchange. It is this passive use, more than the tool itself, that can isolate people.
>
> In short, social media don't isolate us: they amplify what we do with them. The real question may be this: are young people taught how to use them?

Notes: *séduisant* = attractive, appealing; *éloigné* = distant; *faire défiler*
= to scroll; *amplifier* = to amplify. The refutation follows the three steps: the objection
(*Certains affirment que*), what is true in it (*Il est vrai que*), and why it fails (*Or …*).
Then the essay grants a limit with *force est de constater* so that its conclusion is believable.

### Example 3: from a B1 plan to a dialectical plan

Here is a B1 plan for *Faut-il fermer le centre-ville aux voitures ?* (lesson 21), and how the
same material becomes a dialectical plan.

| B1 plan | dialectical plan |
|---|---|
| Position: *plutôt pour, à condition que …* | Question: *Une ville sans voitures est-elle une ville pour tous ?* |
| Argument 1: a nicer centre | *Thèse:* yes: less noise, less pollution, space for pedestrians |
| Argument 2: other ways of getting around | (moved into the *thèse* as a second argument) |
| Other side: shopkeepers, elderly people (*certes …*) | *Antithèse:* no: access for elderly and disabled people, deliveries, shops |
| Conclusion | *Synthèse:* yes, if access is organised (shuttles, delivery times, car parks at the edge); *ouverture:* who is the city for? |

The difference: in the B1 plan the other side takes two lines; in the dialectical plan it takes a
whole part, and the conclusion is built from both.

## Common mistakes

- A *synthèse* that just repeats the *thèse*, or says "both are true". It must answer the question
  more precisely (*yes, if …; only when …*).
- An *antithèse* that is a straw man: present the other side at its strongest, or your answer
  convinces nobody.
- *~~Ce texte s'agit de …~~*: *Dans ce texte, il s'agit de …*
- An *ouverture* that changes the subject (*Et le climat ?*) or adds an argument.
- *Force est de constater* in a chat with friends: it belongs to formal writing.
- Forgetting the B1 basics in a longer plan: one idea per paragraph, an example for each argument,
  connectors between parts.

## Key points

- B2 preview: the dialectical plan *thèse → antithèse → synthèse* weighs both sides before
  answering; the B1 plan (lesson 21) is enough for the DELF B1.
- Introduction: bring in the topic (*À première vue …*), ask the question (*Il s'agit de savoir si
  …*), announce the plan.
- Refute in three steps: state the other view, grant what is true, show where it fails (*Or …,
  cet argument ne tient pas*).
- Conclude with *En somme, En définitive, Force est de constater que* + indicative, and end with an
  *ouverture*: a wider question.
- *Raisonner* (to reason) ≠ *résonner* (to resonate).
