lessons.title: Honors: L'oral du DELF B1 en pratique (the speaking test in practice)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 24 described the DELF B1 as a whole, and lesson 23 taught the language of **[[interaction]]**
and negotiation. This honors lesson goes through the speaking test part by part with original
model answers, shows how to use the 10 minutes of preparation, and deals with the two things
that worry candidates most: getting stuck, and nerves (*le trac*).

Everything here was written for this course; nothing comes from an exam paper. The official
sample papers from France Éducation international (linked in lesson 24) show real tasks and how
they are presented: use them for practice once you have worked through this lesson.

## How the test runs

![The DELF B1 speaking test, about 15 minutes in all, as three boxes linked by arrows: part 1, entretien dirigé, you talk about yourself, not prepared; part 2, exercice en interaction, a role play, not prepared; part 3, expression d'un point de vue, your view on a short document. A dashed box above part 3 says 10 minutes of preparation, for part 3 only. Below: then a discussion with the examiner about your view; check the current sample papers for details.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The test lasts about 15 minutes in all, in three parts, and only the third is prepared, for 10
minutes. An older official candidate guide gave these rough timings: part 1 about 2–3 minutes,
part 2 about 3–4 minutes, and in part 3 a presentation of about 3 minutes followed by a
discussion. It also said that you draw two documents for part 3 and choose one. Details like
these can change, so check the current sample papers and the instructions on the day.

The examiner usually uses *vous*. In the role play, the examiner may play a friend and use *tu*:
follow their lead.

## Part 1: the guided interview

The examiner asks about you: your background, your work or studies, your interests, your
plans. At B1 the examiner expects more than facts: reasons, a story from the past, a hope or a
regret. Answer each question in three or four connected sentences.

### Example 1: a model interview

```dialogue lang=fr-FR
# Entretien dirigé
Examinatrice: Bonjour. Vous pouvez vous présenter ?
= Hello. Can you introduce yourself?
Candidat: Bonjour. Je m'appelle Tomás Herrera, j'ai 29 ans et je suis ingénieur dans une entreprise de logiciels à Valence, en Espagne. J'habite avec ma compagne, qui est française : c'est un peu grâce à elle que j'ai commencé le français.
= Hello. My name is Tomás Herrera, I'm 29 and I'm an engineer at a software company in Valencia, in Spain. I live with my partner, who is French: it's partly thanks to her that I started French.
Examinatrice: Pourquoi est-ce que vous passez le DELF ?
= Why are you taking the DELF?
Candidat: Pour deux raisons. D'abord, mon entreprise travaille de plus en plus avec des clients français, et j'aimerais pouvoir gérer ces projets moi-même. Ensuite, nous pensons nous installer en France dans quelques années, et il faut que j'aie un bon niveau avant de chercher du travail là-bas.
= For two reasons. First, my company works more and more with French clients, and I'd like to be able to manage those projects myself. Then, we're thinking of moving to France in a few years, and I need to have a good level before looking for work there.
Examinatrice: Qu'est-ce qui a été le plus difficile pour vous dans l'apprentissage du français ?
= What has been the hardest thing for you in learning French?
Candidat: Au début, c'était la compréhension orale. Les Français parlent vite ! Si j'avais commencé à écouter la radio plus tôt, j'aurais sans doute progressé plus vite. Maintenant, j'écoute des podcasts tous les jours dans la voiture.
= At first it was listening. French people speak fast! If I had started listening to the radio earlier, I would probably have improved faster. Now I listen to podcasts every day in the car.
```

What makes it good at B1: reasons with *D'abord … Ensuite*; a subjunctive (*il faut que j'aie*);
a type-3 si-clause for a regret (*Si j'avais commencé …, j'aurais progressé*, lesson 11); a past
(*c'était*) and a present habit. *La compagne* = partner (in a couple); *gérer* = to manage.

## Part 2: the interaction

The role play puts you in an everyday situation with a problem to solve. You speak first or the
examiner does, depending on the task; either way, you must interact: listen, react to what
the examiner says (they will often object on purpose), propose, concede and reach a result. Use
lesson 23's steps: proposal → objection → concession → compromise → close.

### Example 2: a model interaction

The situation (invented): you share a flat with a friend, played by the examiner, who wants to
adopt a dog. You're not convinced; discuss it and come to a decision.

```dialogue lang=fr-FR
# Un chien dans l'appartement ?
Examinateur: Écoute, j'ai trouvé un chiot adorable sur le site du refuge. On pourrait l'adopter, non ?
= Listen, I found an adorable puppy on the animal shelter's website. We could adopt it, couldn't we?
Candidate: Un chien ? Attends, je ne suis pas sûre que ce soit une bonne idée. L'appartement est petit, et on travaille tous les deux toute la journée.
= A dog? Wait, I'm not sure it's a good idea. The flat is small, and we both work all day.
Examinateur: Oui, mais je peux le promener le matin et le soir. Et je rentre à midi deux fois par semaine.
= Yes, but I can walk it morning and evening. And I come home at lunchtime twice a week.
Candidate: Si je comprends bien, il resterait seul presque toute la journée les autres jours ? Ce n'est pas juste pour lui.
= If I understand correctly, it would be alone almost all day on the other days? That's not fair on it.
Examinateur: Tu exagères un peu ! Beaucoup de gens qui travaillent ont un chien.
= You're going a bit far! Lots of people who work have a dog.
Candidate: Tu n'as pas tort. Bon, je pourrais accepter, à condition qu'on trouve quelqu'un pour le promener à midi, un voisin ou un étudiant, par exemple. Et c'est toi qui paies le vétérinaire.
= You're not wrong. Right, I could accept, provided we find someone to walk it at lunchtime, a neighbour or a student, for example. And you pay for the vet.
Examinateur: D'accord pour le promeneur, mais le vétérinaire, on partage ?
= OK for the dog walker, but the vet, shall we share?
Candidate: Bon, coupons la poire en deux : on partage le vétérinaire, et toi, tu t'occupes de la nourriture. Alors, si je résume : on adopte le chiot si on trouve un promeneur avant la fin du mois. D'accord ?
= Right, let's split the difference: we share the vet, and you take care of the food. So, to sum up: we adopt the puppy if we find a dog walker before the end of the month. Agreed?
Examinateur: D'accord !
= Agreed!
```

What makes it good: the candidate objects with reasons, reformulates (*Si je comprends bien*),
concedes (*Tu n'as pas tort*), sets a condition with *à condition que* + subjunctive, proposes a
compromise and closes with a summary. *Le chiot* = puppy; *le refuge* = animal shelter (here;
lesson 04h2 has its mountain sense); *promener un chien* = to walk a dog.

## Part 3: a point of view from a document

You get a short document (in the sample papers, usually a short text) and 10 minutes to
prepare. Then you present the question it raises and your opinion, and the examiner discusses it
with you, often taking the other side.

### Using the 10 minutes

| time | what to do |
|---|---|
| 2 minutes | read the document twice: the topic, the facts, any opinion in it |
| 1 minute | write the *problématique* as a question: *Faut-il …? Est-ce que …?* |
| 4 minutes | choose your position; note two arguments, each with an example from your life or country |
| 2 minutes | note an opening sentence and a closing sentence, and two or three connectors |
| 1 minute | read your notes over and breathe |

Write key words, not sentences: if you write sentences, you will read them aloud, and
examiners want to hear you speak. *La préparation* (preparation) is for ideas and structure.

### Example 3: a model point of view

The document (an original short text):

> **Des jardins partagés au pied des immeubles**
>
> Dans de plus en plus de quartiers, des habitants transforment un terrain vide en jardin partagé. Chacun y cultive quelques légumes, on y organise des fêtes et des ateliers pour les enfants. Pour certains, ces jardins recréent du lien entre voisins ; pour d'autres, ils restent une activité réservée à quelques passionnés.

(Shared gardens at the foot of apartment blocks. In more and more neighbourhoods, residents turn
a piece of empty land into a shared garden. Everyone grows a few vegetables there, and there are
parties and workshops for children. For some, these gardens rebuild ties between neighbours; for
others, they remain an activity for a few enthusiasts.)

The candidate's notes: *jardins partagés → lien entre voisins ? / pour : rencontres, enfants,
mon quartier à Valence / limite : peu de gens, temps / conclusion : oui, si ouvert à tous*.

The presentation:

> Le document parle des jardins partagés, qui se développent dans les villes. La question, c'est de savoir si ces jardins peuvent vraiment rapprocher les voisins. Moi, je pense que oui, mais à certaines conditions.
>
> Tout d'abord, un jardin, c'est un lieu où on se rencontre naturellement. On n'a pas besoin d'un prétexte pour parler : on discute des tomates, de la pluie… Par exemple, dans mon quartier à Valence, il y a un jardin de ce type depuis deux ans, et ma voisine, qui ne connaissait personne, y a trouvé des amis.
>
> De plus, ces jardins sont bons pour les enfants. En ville, beaucoup d'enfants ne savent pas d'où viennent les légumes. Là, ils apprennent en faisant.
>
> Certes, le document a raison de dire que ce sont souvent les mêmes personnes qui y participent. Il faut du temps, et tout le monde n'aime pas jardiner. Mais je crois que c'est une question d'organisation : si le jardin est ouvert à tous et propose des fêtes, il attire d'autres gens.
>
> Bref, pour moi, les jardins partagés sont une bonne idée, à condition qu'ils restent ouverts à tout le quartier.

(The document is about shared gardens, which are spreading in towns. The question is whether these
gardens can really bring neighbours closer. I think so, but on certain conditions. First of all,
a garden is a place where people meet naturally. You don't need an excuse to talk: you chat about
the tomatoes, the rain… For example, in my neighbourhood in Valencia there has been a garden like
this for two years, and my neighbour, who didn't know anyone, has made friends there. What's more,
these gardens are good for children. In towns, many children don't know where vegetables come
from. There, they learn by doing. Admittedly, the document is right to say that it's often the
same people who take part. It takes time, and not everyone likes gardening. But I think it's a
question of organisation: if the garden is open to everyone and holds parties, it attracts other
people. In short, for me, shared gardens are a good idea, provided they stay open to the whole
neighbourhood.)

What makes it good: it names the question first, takes a position with a condition, gives two
arguments with a personal example, concedes a point from the document with *certes … mais*, and
concludes. It is spoken French (*Moi, je pense que oui; un jardin, c'est …*), which is right for
an oral: don't speak like a written essay. About 200 words: roughly two minutes at a calm pace.

After the presentation, the examiner might ask: *Mais vous ne pensez pas que les gens n'ont plus
le temps ?* That is your chance to *rebondir* (to pick up on a point, to bounce back): *Justement,
c'est pour ça que …* or *C'est vrai pour certains, mais …*.

## Keeping going when you're stuck

Everyone gets stuck at some point. What counts is what you do next.

- A word is missing: describe it (*C'est un truc qui sert à …, c'est le contraire de …*) or
  use a more general word (*l'outil, la chose, le lieu*). Don't stop to translate.
- You lose your thread: *reprendre* means to pick up again, to resume: *Je reprends : …*,
  *Pour reprendre ce que je disais, …*. *Reprendre* is conjugated like *prendre*: *je reprends,
  nous reprenons, ils reprennent; j'ai repris*.
- You need time: a short *pause* is fine; fillers help (*Alors … Comment dire …*), but not one
  per sentence.
- You didn't understand the question: ask (*Pardon, vous pouvez reformuler ?*). It is part of
  interaction, not a weakness.
- The examiner disagrees: that is the task, not a sign you are wrong. Defend your view or
  nuance it (lesson 23).
- Something unexpected comes up: *improviser* (to improvise) is a skill. You won't have
  prepared everything, and a *spontané* (spontaneous) answer with a small mistake is better than
  silence: *une réponse spontanée*.

## Managing nerves

*Le trac* is stage fright, nerves before speaking or performing; *avoir le trac* is to be
nervous: *J'ai toujours le trac avant un oral.* It is normal, and examiners know it. Some
practical habits:

- Slow down. Nerves make people speak fast. *Le débit* is your rate of speech: a calm *débit*
  is easier to follow and gives you time to think.
- Articulate. *Articuler* is to speak clearly, to pronounce every syllable: *Articulez !*
  Open your mouth and finish your words.
- Look at the examiner. *Le regard* is a look, a gaze, and also eye contact: *soutenir le
  regard* is to hold someone's gaze. Looking at your interlocutor makes it a conversation.
- Just start. *Se lancer* is to go for it, to launch into something: *Allez, je me lance !*
  The first sentence is the hardest; prepare it in the 10 minutes.
- Practise out loud before the day, with a friend, a teacher or a recording of yourself, using
  the sample papers. A timed practice in the same conditions makes the real test feel familiar.

## Common mistakes at the oral

- Reading your notes aloud in part 3.
- Answering part 1 in single sentences: give a reason or an example each time.
- Treating the role play as a monologue: react to what the examiner says.
- Giving in at the first objection, or never giving in: a role play usually ends with a
  compromise or a decision.
- Speaking too fast because of *le trac*; a slower *débit* is clearer.
- Using written connectors in speech (*en outre, en définitive*): they are not wrong, but *de
  plus, bref, en tout cas* sound more natural.
- *~~Je suis le trac~~*: *j'ai le trac*.

## Key points

- About 15 minutes, three parts; only part 3 is prepared, for 10 minutes. Check the current
  sample papers for the details.
- Part 1: connected answers with reasons, a past, a plan or a regret.
- Part 2: interact (reformulate, concede, set conditions) and reach a result.
- Part 3: name the question, take a position, two arguments with examples, a concession, a
  conclusion; prepare key words, not sentences.
- When stuck: describe, *reprendre*, pause, ask, *improviser*.
- Nerves (*avoir le trac*): slow your *débit*, *articuler*, keep eye contact (*le regard*), and
  *se lancer*.

lessons.title: Une nouvelle de Maupassant: La Parure
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 taught you to tell a story with the passé composé, the imparfait and the
plus-que-parfait. Published fiction tells its events in another tense, the **[[passé simple]]**,
which you met in French A1 (a fable) and A2 (a tale) in the *il* and *ils* forms only. Here you
follow one of the most famous French short stories, Guy de Maupassant's *La Parure* (The
Necklace), told scene by scene in simple French written for this lesson in the passé simple, then
again as you would tell it aloud. You learn to recognise the passé simple in every person and see
why the story's ending is one of the best known in French literature. You read the passé simple;
you go on writing the passé composé.

## Maupassant and the realist short story

Guy de Maupassant (1850–1893) wrote about three hundred short stories and six novels, most of them
in the 1880s. A few years before this story he had worked as a clerk at the Ministry of Education
(*le ministère de l'Instruction publique*), the ministry where Mathilde's husband works. *La
Parure* first appeared in the Paris daily *Le Gaulois* on 17 February 1884, and the next year in
his collection *Contes du jour et de la nuit* (1885).

A **[[nouvelle]]** is a short story: short enough to read at one sitting, with few characters, one
main event and an ending that often changes the meaning of everything before it (*la chute*, the
"fall", the twist). Maupassant's stories are *realist*: ordinary people, Paris streets and
flats, exact sums of money, and a narrator who judges little and lets the facts speak. Notice the
numbers in this one: 400 francs, 36,000 francs, ten years, 500 francs.

The original story, about 3,000 words long, is in the public domain: you can read it free in
*Contes du jour et de la nuit* on Project Gutenberg (eBook no. 14790). It makes a good first
"real" French text once you have finished this lesson. The French below is not Maupassant's: it is
a simplified retelling, written in the passé simple so that you can practise reading it.

![Two scenes from the story. On the left, the ball at the ministry: under a chandelier, Mathilde in a long ball gown with a diamond necklace dances with a man in a black tailcoat. On the right, the jeweller's shop at the Palais-Royal: behind the counter the jeweller shows an open black box holding a necklace, with a price card reading 36 000 F. Labels: le lustre, la robe de bal, le collier, le bijoutier, l'écrin, le prix.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The story in five scenes (passé simple)

### 1. Mathilde

> Mathilde était jolie, mais elle était née dans une famille modeste. Elle n'avait pas d'argent, et elle épousa un petit employé du ministère de l'Instruction publique. Elle rêvait de luxe, de robes et de bijoux, et sa vie simple la rendait malheureuse.

*Mathilde was pretty, but she had been born into a modest family. She had no money, and she married a minor clerk at the Ministry of Education. She dreamed of luxury, dresses and jewels, and her simple life made her unhappy.*

Background in the imparfait (*était, n'avait pas, rêvait*); one event in the passé simple:
*elle épousa* (she married), an -er verb in *-a*.

### 2. The necklace

> Un soir, son mari rentra avec une invitation à une soirée au ministère. Mathilde pleura : elle n'avait rien à mettre. Son mari lui donna les quatre cents francs qu'il avait mis de côté, et elle eut sa robe. Puis elle alla chez Mme Forestier, une amie riche, qui lui prêta un collier de diamants.

*One evening her husband came home with an invitation to a party at the ministry. Mathilde cried: she had nothing to wear. Her husband gave her the four hundred francs he had put aside, and she had her dress. Then she went to Mme Forestier, a rich friend, who lent her a diamond necklace.*

*Rentra, pleura, donna, alla, prêta*: all -er verbs (*-a*); *eut* is *avoir* (*-ut*). *Qu'il avait
mis de côté* is a plus-que-parfait: he had saved the money (for a gun) before the story begins.

### 3. The ball, and the loss

> Au bal, Mathilde fut la plus belle. Tout le monde voulut danser avec elle. Ils rentrèrent vers quatre heures du matin. Devant le miroir, elle poussa un cri : le collier n'était plus autour de son cou !

*At the ball Mathilde was the most beautiful woman there. Everyone wanted to dance with her. They went home at about four in the morning. In front of the mirror she cried out: the necklace was no longer around her neck!*

*Fut* (*être*), *voulut* (*vouloir*): the *-u-* type. *Rentrèrent* is the *ils* form of an -er
verb (*-èrent*). The event (*poussa un cri*) is passé simple; what she discovers, a state, is
imparfait (*n'était plus*).

### 4. The debt

> Ils cherchèrent le collier pendant une semaine, sans le trouver. Enfin, dans une boutique du Palais-Royal, ils virent un collier presque identique ; il coûtait trente-six mille francs. Loisel emprunta l'argent qui lui manquait. Pendant dix ans, ils vécurent dans la misère et travaillèrent sans arrêt pour rembourser leurs dettes.

*They looked for the necklace for a week without finding it. At last, in a shop at the Palais-Royal, they saw an almost identical necklace; it cost thirty-six thousand francs. Loisel borrowed the money he was short of. For ten years they lived in poverty and worked non-stop to pay off their debts.*

*Virent* (*voir*) and *vécurent* (*vivre*) have stems you just learn; *cherchèrent, emprunta,
travaillèrent* are -er verbs. In the original, Loisel has 18,000 francs from his father and
borrows the rest; Mathilde gives back the necklace and Mme Forestier doesn't open the box; the
Loisels dismiss their maid and move to an attic room.

### 5. The ending

> Un dimanche, sur les Champs-Élysées, Mathilde rencontra Mme Forestier, encore jeune et belle. Elle lui raconta tout. Son amie fut très émue et lui prit les mains : le collier qu'elle lui avait prêté était faux. Il ne valait pas plus de cinq cents francs.

*One Sunday, on the Champs-Élysées, Mathilde met Mme Forestier, still young and beautiful. She told her everything. Her friend was deeply moved and took her hands: the necklace she had lent her was fake. It was worth no more than five hundred francs.*

The story stops there. Ten years of *misère* were paid for a fake: that is *la chute*. Notice that
in Maupassant's dialogue, as in this course, the characters speak in the passé composé (*tu as
acheté …*): the passé simple belongs to the narration.

## The story in B1 French

> Mathilde Loisel était jolie, mais elle n'était pas riche : son mari était un petit employé du ministère. Elle rêvait de luxe, de belles robes et de bijoux. Un soir, son mari est rentré avec une invitation à un bal au ministère. Au lieu d'être contente, elle a pleuré : elle n'avait rien à mettre. Son mari lui a donné les quatre cents francs qu'il avait mis de côté pour s'acheter un fusil, et elle a eu sa robe. Mais il lui fallait aussi une parure, alors elle est allée voir Mme Forestier, une amie riche, qui lui a prêté un collier de diamants.
>
> Au bal, Mathilde a eu un grand succès. Mais de retour chez elle, vers quatre heures du matin, elle s'est aperçue que le collier avait disparu. Ils l'ont cherché partout pendant une semaine, en vain. Ils ont fini par acheter un collier presque identique dans une boutique du Palais-Royal, pour trente-six mille francs. Loisel avait les dix-huit mille francs qu'il avait reçus de son père ; il a emprunté le reste.
>
> Pendant dix ans, ils ont vécu dans la misère pour rembourser leurs dettes. Un dimanche, sur les Champs-Élysées, Mathilde a revu Mme Forestier, encore jeune et belle, et lui a tout raconté. Son amie a été très émue : son collier était faux et ne valait pas plus de cinq cents francs.

This is how you would tell it: imparfait for the background (*était, rêvait, n'avait rien*),
passé composé for the events, plus-que-parfait for what came before (*qu'il avait mis de côté,
avait disparu, qu'il avait reçus de son père*: the participle agrees with *que* = the francs).
*Elle s'est aperçue* agrees, because *s'apercevoir* is a pronominal verb whose *se* is not an
object.

## Reading the passé simple

In written narration the passé simple carries the events, and the imparfait still gives the
background. In speech, and in the characters' own words, French uses the passé composé: in the retelling above, the
narration says *rencontra, raconta*, but if Mme Forestier spoke, she would say *Tu as acheté un
autre collier ?* (Some modern novels are narrated in the passé composé, Albert Camus's
*L'Étranger* (1942) famously, but most fiction and history books still use the passé simple.)

There are three sets of endings, plus *venir* and *tenir*:

| | -er verbs: *parler* | -i- type: *finir* (and *partir, prendre, dire, faire, mettre, voir*) | -u- type: *vouloir* (and *être, avoir, pouvoir, savoir, connaître, lire*) | *venir* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| je | parlai | finis | voulus | vins |
| tu | parlas | finis | voulus | vins |
| il / elle / on | parla | finit | voulut | vint |
| nous | parlâmes | finîmes | voulûmes | vînmes |
| vous | parlâtes | finîtes | voulûtes | vîntes |
| ils / elles | parlèrent | finirent | voulurent | vinrent |

- -er verbs (and *aller*: *j'allai, ils allèrent*) all follow *parler*. *-ger* verbs keep
  their *e* before *a* (*je mangeai, nous mangeâmes*), and *-cer* verbs take *ç* before *a* (*il
  commença*, but *ils commencèrent*).
- The -i- and -u- verbs add the endings to a stem you often know from the participle:
  *pris → il prit, mis → il mit, dit → il dit, lu → il lut, voulu → il voulut, connu → elle
  connut, paru → il parut, pu → il put, su → il sut*. Some stems you just learn: *être → je fus,
  il fut, nous fûmes, ils furent; avoir → j'eus, il eut, ils eurent; faire → il fit; voir → il
  vit; naître → il naquit; mourir → il mourut*.
- Only the *nous* and *vous* forms carry a circumflex (*-âmes, -îmes, -ûmes; -âtes, -îtes,
  -ûtes*); the *il* form of an -er verb never does (*il parla*).

The *je* and *nous* forms turn up in first-person novels and memoirs (*Nous partîmes le
lendemain*). Watch the look-alikes. *Il finit, il dit, je finis* are also present forms, and *je parlai*
(passé simple) differs from *je parlais* (imparfait) by one letter. In a past story, between other
passé simple forms, they are passé simple.

### Example 1: Who, and which verb?

Give the person and the infinitive.

1. *nous allâmes*: *nous*, -âmes = an -er verb: *aller* (we went).
2. *vous fûtes*: *vous*, the *fu-* stem of *être* (you were).
3. *je vins*: *je*, the special stem of *venir* (I came).
4. *ils prirent*: *ils*, -irent, *pris → pri-*: *prendre* (they took).
5. *tu eus*: *tu*, the *eu-* stem of *avoir* (you had).

### Example 2: From the story to spoken French

Retell each sentence in the passé composé.

1. *Elle découvrit un collier de diamants.* *Découvrir* is like *ouvrir*: participle
   *découvert*, with *avoir*: *Elle a découvert un collier de diamants.*
2. *Ils allèrent chez tous les bijoutiers.* *Aller* takes *être*, plural: *Ils sont allés chez
   tous les bijoutiers.*
3. *Mme Forestier lui prêta son collier.* *Lui* is an indirect object, so no agreement: *Mme
   Forestier lui a prêté son collier.*
4. *Ils vécurent dans la misère.* *Vivre → vécu*, with *avoir*: *Ils ont vécu dans la misère.*
5. *Son amie lui prit les mains.* *Prendre → pris*: *Son amie lui a pris les mains.*

## Two literary forms to recognise

The **[[imperfect subjunctive]]** is the subjunctive that classic literature uses after a verb in the
past, where today's French uses the subjonctif présent (lesson 05): *Il fallait qu'elle partît*
= today *Il fallait qu'elle parte*. Take the *tu* form of the passé simple, drop the *-s* and add
*-sse, -sses, -t* (with a circumflex on the vowel before it), *-ssions, -ssiez, -ssent*: *tu parlas → qu'il parlât; tu finis → qu'il finît;
tu fus → qu'il fût; tu eus → qu'il eût; tu vins → qu'il vînt*. You will meet the *il* form with its
circumflex most often (*qu'il fût*). Don't write it: it sounds old-fashioned or comic in speech.

Its pluperfect (the imperfect subjunctive of *avoir* or *être* + participle) also turns up in
nineteenth-century prose, including Maupassant's. Two made-up sentences in that style:

- *Elle eût aimé briller* = *elle aurait aimé briller* (she would have liked to shine). Here it
  replaces the conditionnel passé (lesson 10), a literary use you'll study properly at B2.
- *Il parlait comme s'il eût tout vu* = *comme s'il avait tout vu* (as if he had seen
  everything).

## Why the ending works

Reread the story knowing the end. Mathilde's *orgueil* (pride) and *vanité* make her borrow the
necklace; her honesty and pride make her replace it rather than confess. The ten years of work
change her, and the narrator even admires her courage. Then one sentence shows that the
sacrifice was for nothing, and the story stops without comment. During the hard years, Mathilde
sometimes thinks back to the ball and wonders what her life would have been without the loss.
In your own French: *Quelle vie aurait-elle eue si elle n'avait pas perdu le collier ?* (What life
would she have had if she hadn't lost the necklace?) That is a type-3 si-clause (lesson 11).

## Common mistakes

- Writing the passé simple in a message or a DELF text. Read it; write the passé composé.
- Taking *il finit* or *il dit* in a past story for the present tense.
- Reading *il parla* as an imparfait: the imparfait is *il parlait*. *Parla* is one finished
  event.
- Reading *qu'il fût* as *qu'il fut*: without the circumflex, *fut* is the passé simple (he
  was); with it, *fût* is the imperfect subjunctive.

## Key points

- *La Parure*: Maupassant (1850–1893), *Le Gaulois*, 17 February 1884; then *Contes du jour et de
  la nuit* (1885). A realist **[[nouvelle]]** with a twist ending (*la chute*): the necklace was fake.
- The passé simple: *-ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent*; *-is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent*;
  *-us, -us, -ut, -ûmes, -ûtes, -urent*; *vins, vint, vinrent*. Recognise it; write the passé
  composé.
- Narration in the passé simple + imparfait; dialogue in the passé composé.
- The imperfect subjunctive (*qu'il fût, qu'il eût, qu'il parlât*) and its pluperfect (*il eût
  désiré*) are literary: recognise them only.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Le français dans le monde
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French A1's honors lesson on *la francophonie* showed where French is spoken, how to say *au
Québec* and *en Côte d'Ivoire*, and the Belgian and Swiss *septante* and *nonante*. This lesson
goes further, at B1: how many people speak French and where, what it means for a language to be
*official*, how French lives alongside other languages, and a handful of everyday words that
differ from region to region. The course teaches the French of France; this lesson is about
understanding the others, not ranking them.

## How many speakers, and where

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) publishes a report on French in the
world every four years. Its 2026 report counts about 396 million French speakers (*les
locuteurs*) in 2025, which makes French the fourth most spoken language in the world, after
English, Mandarin Chinese and Spanish. Nearly 65 % of them live in Africa. The figure depends on
the method: with the counting method of its earlier reports, the OIF gets about 348 million. Any
such number depends on how well someone must speak to count as a speaker, so treat it as an
estimate.

The OIF itself is an organisation of states and governments, not only of countries where French
is the main language. In November 2026 it has 90 members: 53 full members, 5 associate members and
32 observers. Some members are governments within a country (Québec, the Fédération
Wallonie-Bruxelles, New Brunswick). Membership changes: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger announced in
March 2025 that they were leaving, and a summit in Cambodia in mid-November 2026 may admit new
members, so check francophonie.org for today's figure. The *Journée internationale de la
Francophonie* is on 20 March.

```map
base: world
title: Where French is an official language (simplified)
view: -35, -110 to 62, 60
region: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg | Europe
region: Canada, Haiti | The Americas
region: Senegal, Guinea, Ivory Coast, Togo, Benin, Cameroon, Chad, Central African Republic, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Republic of the Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Djibouti, Madagascar | Africa
region: Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger | French now a working language, not official
caption: Simplified. French is also official in Monaco, the Seychelles, the Comoros and Vanuatu (too small to show), and in New Brunswick as well as Québec; in Canada as a whole it is official with English. France's overseas departments and territories are French-speaking too. In Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Lebanon French is not official but is widely used.
```

The picture below shows the same thing as a still map, with six places to remember.

![A simplified map of the Americas, Europe and Africa. Countries where French is an official language are blue: Canada, Haiti, France, Belgium, Switzerland and many countries of West and Central Africa, and Madagascar. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger are yellow: French is now a working language there. An inset enlarges France and its neighbours. Labels: le Québec (a point in eastern Canada), Haïti, le Sénégal, la Côte d'Ivoire, la Belgique and la Suisse.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## What "official" means

A *langue officielle* is the language (or one of the languages) that the law says the state
uses: in parliament, the courts, schools and public services. It isn't the same as the language
people speak at home. In 2026 France's foreign ministry, citing the OIF report, counted French as an official language
in 32 states and governments.

- Québec: French is the only official language of the province; in Canada as a whole, French
  and English are both official, a form of *bilinguisme* (bilingualism) at federal level.
- Belgium: three official languages, French, Dutch and German. French is spoken mainly in
  Wallonia and Brussels.
- Switzerland: four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. French is spoken
  in the west, *la Suisse romande* (Geneva, Lausanne, Neuchâtel).
- West and Central Africa: in Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of
  the Congo and many other countries, French is official alongside many national languages
  (Wolof in Senegal, for example), and many speakers use two or three languages every day. In
  2023 Mali's new constitution made its national languages official and French a working language;
  Burkina Faso changed its constitution in December 2023, and Niger's charter of March 2025 also
  makes French a working language. French remains widely used in schools and administration there.

## Varieties, dialects, creoles

Every language that is spoken over a large area has **[[varieties]]**: forms of the same language
that differ in pronunciation, vocabulary and some grammar, but whose speakers understand one
another. Québec French, Belgian French, Swiss French, the French of Abidjan or Dakar and the
French of Paris are all varieties of French, each correct where it is used. A word or expression
used in one region only is a **[[regionalism]]** (*un régionalisme*): *septante* is a regionalism of
Belgium and Switzerland.

Linguists use other words too, and the line between them is not always sharp:

- *une variante* is one form among several: *le souper* is the Belgian, Swiss and Québec variant
  for the evening meal.
- *un dialecte* is a regional form of a language, often spoken more than written and sometimes
  hard for outsiders to follow (the Swiss German dialects, for example).
- *un créole* is a language born where speakers of different languages had to communicate, often
  under colonisation and slavery: most of its words come from one language (French, for the
  creoles of Haiti, Guadeloupe, Martinique and Réunion), but it has its own grammar and is a
  language in its own right, not "broken French". Haitian Creole is an official language of Haiti
  with French.

This *diversité* (diversity) is normal: English is the same, with British, American, Indian
and Australian varieties.

## Accents

All French speakers have an accent; there is no accent-free French. In general terms:

- In Québec, *t* and *d* before *i* and *u* sound close to "ts" and "dz" (*tu, dire*), and some
  vowels are longer or more open than in France.
- In the south of France many speakers pronounce the final *e* (*une petite bière* has more
  syllables than in Paris).
- In Belgium, Switzerland and Africa accents differ too, often shaped by the other languages
  spoken around them (Dutch, German, Wolof, Lingala and many more).

These are tendencies, not rules: accents vary from town to town, by age and by person. Listening
to radio from several countries (RFI, Radio-Canada, RTBF, RTS) is the best training.

## Words that change across borders

| Word | Where | Meaning | In France |
|---|---|---|---|
| *le dépanneur* | Québec | convenience store, corner shop | *l'épicerie, la supérette* |
| *magasiner* | Québec | to go shopping | *faire les magasins, faire du shopping* |
| *le chum* | Québec (informal) | friend, mate; boyfriend | *le pote, le copain* |
| *le kot* | Belgium | student room | *la chambre d'étudiant* |
| *la drache* | Belgium (also northern France) | downpour | *l'averse, il pleut à verse* |
| *le natel* | Switzerland | mobile phone | *le portable* |

- *Le dépanneur* is the recommended Québec term: the OQLF, Québec's language
  office, notes that English in Québec has borrowed it too. In France *un dépanneur* is a
  breakdown mechanic.
- *Magasiner* is a regular -er verb (*je magasine, on a magasiné*). Québec prefers it to the
  anglicism *faire du shopping*, which is common in France.
- *Le chum* comes from English and is pronounced roughly "tchomme". In the sense "boyfriend", the
  feminine partner is *ma blonde* (my girlfriend), whatever her hair colour. It is informal, and
  the OQLF advises against it in careful writing.
- *Le kot* (from a Dutch word for a shed or a cramped little room) is a student room, often in a shared house: *Je
  cherche un kot à Louvain-la-Neuve.*
- *La drache* is a heavy downpour: *On a pris une drache en rentrant.* Dictionaries label it regional (Belgium, northern France);
  it's an everyday spoken word.
- *Le natel* began as the name of the Swiss PTT's mobile network (NATEL, from German *Nationales
  Autotelefonnetz*, national car-phone network) and became the everyday word for a mobile phone in
  French-speaking Switzerland. In Belgium many people say *le GSM*.

Recognise these words; in your own French, use the France column unless you live in the region.
Using a regionalism from somewhere else can sound odd, the way an American saying "lorry" would.

### Example 1: Reading a message from Montréal

> Salut ! Mon chum et moi, on a magasiné toute la journée au centre-ville. Au retour, on s'est arrêtés au dépanneur pour acheter du lait. Ce soir, on soupe chez mes parents !

Read it as someone from France would:

1. *Mon chum* = *mon copain* (here probably her boyfriend: the context decides).
2. *On a magasiné* = *on a fait les magasins*. Passé composé of a regular -er verb.
3. *Le dépanneur* = the corner shop (*l'épicerie du coin*), not a mechanic.
4. *On soupe* = *on dîne* (A1: *le souper* is the evening meal in Québec).
5. *On s'est arrêtés*: when *on* means *nous* (two people), the participle may agree with it in
   writing; *on s'est arrêté* is also accepted.

### Example 2: Belgium or Switzerland?

Sort each sentence by region, and say it in France's French.

1. *J'ai oublié mon natel dans le train.* → Switzerland. *J'ai oublié mon portable dans le train.*
2. *Mon kot est à dix minutes de l'université.* → Belgium. *Ma chambre d'étudiant est à dix
   minutes de l'université.*
3. *Quelle drache ! Je suis trempé.* → Belgium. *Quelle averse ! Je suis trempé.*
4. *On a fait septante kilomètres.* → Belgium or Switzerland (both say *septante*). *On a fait
   soixante-dix kilomètres.*

## Reading: one year, three Frenchs

> Quand j'ai décidé d'étudier en français, je pensais qu'il n'existait qu'un seul français, celui des manuels. J'ai passé un semestre à Liège, où j'habitais dans un kot que je partageais avec deux étudiants flamands : chez nous, on parlait français, néerlandais et anglais, parfois dans la même phrase. Ensuite, j'ai fait un stage à Lausanne, où mes collègues m'envoyaient des messages sur mon natel dès sept heures du matin. Enfin, je suis parti à Montréal, où j'ai découvert les dépanneurs ouverts tard le soir et le plaisir de magasiner le samedi.
>
> Au début, je comprenais mal certains accents, et il fallait souvent que je fasse répéter les gens. Mais personne ne s'est moqué de moi, et j'ai compris une chose dont je n'avais jamais entendu parler en classe : chaque région a ses mots, et aucune n'a « le vrai français ». Aujourd'hui, ce que j'aime le plus dans cette langue, c'est justement sa diversité.

*When I decided to study in French, I thought there was only one French, the textbooks'. I spent a semester in Liège, where I lived in a student room that I shared with two Flemish students: at home we spoke French, Dutch and English, sometimes in the same sentence. Then I did an internship in Lausanne, where my colleagues sent messages to my mobile from seven in the morning. Finally I went to Montréal, where I discovered corner shops open late and the pleasure of going shopping on Saturdays. At first I understood some accents badly, and I often had to make people repeat themselves. But nobody made fun of me, and I understood something I had never heard about in class: every region has its words, and none has "the real French". Today what I like most about the language is precisely its diversity.*

Course grammar in the text: *où* and *que* (A2), *dont* with *entendre parler de* (lesson 13),
*ce que … c'est* (lesson 13), *il fallait que je fasse* (subjunctive, lesson 05), *faire répéter*
(lesson 16).

## Common mistakes

- Calling Québec, Belgian or African French "wrong" or "not real French". They are varieties with
  their own norms; the course simply teaches France's.
- Thinking *un créole* is a dialect of French. Creoles are languages of their own.
- Mixing up *la langue officielle* (what the law says) with the language most people speak at
  home.
- Using *un dépanneur* in France for a shop: there it means a breakdown mechanic.
- Quoting an exact number of French speakers as a fact: it is an estimate, and it depends on the
  method.

## Key points

- About 396 million French speakers in 2025 (OIF, 2026 report), nearly 65 % in Africa; French is
  the fourth most spoken language in the world.
- The OIF has 90 states and governments (November 2026); Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger announced
  their withdrawal in March 2025.
- French is official in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Monaco, Canada (with English;
  alone in Québec), Haiti, many African countries and Vanuatu, usually alongside other languages.
- **[[Varieties]]** and **[[regionalisms]]** are normal: *le dépanneur, magasiner, le chum* (Québec), *le
  kot, la drache* (Belgium), *le natel* (Switzerland). Recognise them; use France's words yourself.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Du latin au français
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have now met about 1,900 French words, and many looked familiar: *la destination, la
coïncidence, l'obstacle, la diversité*. This lesson explains why. It tells the history of French
in short, from the Latin of Roman Gaul to the spelling changes of 1990, shows where French words
come from and how words travel between French and English, and ends with how dictionaries and
institutions record change. The history texts use the passive (lesson 15) and the
plus-que-parfait (lesson 02), as history books do.

## From Latin to Old French

After Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul in the first century BC, the people of Gaul slowly gave
up their Celtic language, *le gaulois*, for *le latin* spoken by soldiers, traders and officials
(not the written Latin of Cicero). Over the centuries this spoken Latin changed so much that, by
the 9th century, people in the north of Gaul no longer understood written Latin: a new language
had been born.

The first text to show it is the *Serments de Strasbourg* (the Strasbourg Oaths) of 842. Two
grandsons of Charlemagne, Louis the German and Charles the Bald, swore an alliance (*un serment*
is an oath) in front of their armies. So that each army would understand, Louis swore in the
Romance language of Charles's soldiers and Charles in the Germanic language of Louis's. The
historian Nithard copied both oaths into his Latin chronicle. The Romance one begins *Pro Deo amur
…* (for the love of God): it is not French yet, and not Latin any more.

The language of the next centuries is called **[[Old French]]** (*l'ancien français*), spoken and
written roughly from the 9th to the 14th century. It still had two cases (one for the subject, one for other uses), unlike modern French, and many
regional forms. In the north people said *oïl* for "yes" (today *oui*) and in the south *oc*:
hence the *langue d'oïl* and the *langue d'oc* (Occitan), two families of Romance dialects. The
French of Paris and the royal court, one *langue d'oïl* among others, slowly became the standard.

### What the Gauls and the Franks left

Gaulish left only a small number of words, many of them about the countryside: *le chêne* (oak),
*le mouton* (sheep), *la ruche* (beehive), *l'alouette* (lark), *la boue* (mud). The Franks, a
Germanic people who ruled Gaul from the 5th century and gave France its name, left more: *la
guerre* (war), *le jardin* (garden), *bleu, blanc, gris*, and the "aspirated" *h* of words such as
*la honte* (shame) and *haïr* (to hate), which blocks elision (*la honte*, not *l'honte*).

```mermaid

  accDescr: Most French words come from spoken Latin, passed down and changed over the centuries. A small number come from Gaulish, the Celtic language spoken before the Romans, and more from Frankish, the Germanic language of the Franks. Later, French borrowed learned words from written Latin and Greek, and loanwords from other languages such as Italian, Arabic and English.

  G["Gaulois : chêne, ruche, mouton"] --> F
  K["Francique : guerre, jardin, bleu"] --> F
  L["Latin et grec écrits : fragile, hôpital, téléphone"] --> F
  E["Emprunts : italien, arabe, anglais…"] --> F
```

## Two routes from Latin

Many Latin words entered French twice. The first time, they were passed down by speakers for
centuries and worn smooth; the second time, scholars borrowed them again from written Latin, much
closer to the original. That gives pairs called doublets:

| Latin | Passed down (popular) | Borrowed later (learned) | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *hospitalem* | *l'hôtel* | *l'hôpital* | hotel, hospital |
| *fragilem* | *frêle* (slight, frail) | *fragile* | frail, fragile |
| *potionem* | *le poison* | *la potion* | poison, potion |

The circumflex often marks a lost *s*: *l'hôpital* (hospital), *la forêt* (forest), *la fête*
(feast), *la bête* (beast). The English words keep the *s* because English borrowed them before
French dropped it. That's a quick way to guess an English cognate: put the *s* back.

## French into English, and back

After the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, French was for about three centuries the language
of the English court, law and nobility. English took thousands of words from it (*des emprunts*, loanwords), which is why so
many French words look familiar to you: *le gouvernement, la justice, le parlement, la
destination*. In the classic example, English farmers kept their Germanic words for the animals (cow, pig, sheep), while
the meat served at French-speaking tables got French names (beef from *bœuf*, pork from *porc*,
mutton from *mouton*).

Words also travel back. Dictionaries of *étymologie* (the history of words) trace *le tennis* to *tenez !* (said by the
server in the old French game of *jeu de paume*), *le budget* to Old French *bougette* (a small
bag) and *le tunnel* to *la tonnelle* (an arbour): French words that came home through English.

Today the traffic is mostly the other way. An anglicism (*un anglicisme*) is a word or
expression borrowed from English: *le week-end, le parking, le marketing, le mail*. France and
Québec both create French alternatives (*le courriel* for e-mail, *la fin de semaine* in Québec),
with different success. Whether anglicisms are a threat or a normal part of a living language is
debated in France; dictionaries record the words that are used, whichever side you take.

## Laws, the Académie and spelling

Some dates mark how French became the language of the state:

- 1539: the *ordonnance de Villers-Cotterêts*, signed by King François Ier, required legal and
  administrative documents to be written in French rather than Latin. (An *ordonnance* here is a
  royal decree, not a doctor's prescription.) In 2023 the château of Villers-Cotterêts became the
  *Cité internationale de la langue française*, a museum and cultural centre.
- 1635: the *Académie française* was founded by Cardinal Richelieu. Its forty members, known as
  *les Immortels*, work on its dictionary (*le dictionnaire de l'Académie*), whose first edition appeared in 1694.
- From the Revolution and especially after free, compulsory primary school in the 1880s, French
  replaced regional languages and *les patois* (the local dialects of the countryside) in daily
  life. Breton, Occitan, Alsatian, Basque and Corsican are still spoken, by far fewer people.

The **[[1990 rectified spellings]]** (*les rectifications de l'orthographe de 1990*) were proposed by
the Conseil supérieur de la langue française and published that December, with the Académie's
approval. They were a set of recommendations, not a compulsory *réforme*: the old and new spellings are both correct, and French school programmes refer to
the new ones. The main changes:

- no circumflex on *i* and *u*: *paraître → paraitre, le coût → le cout*, except where it tells two
  words apart (*sûr, mûr, dû* keep theirs) and in verb endings (*nous fûmes, qu'il fût*);
- hyphens between all the words of a number: *vingt-et-un, deux-cents*;
- a few odd spellings regularised: *l'oignon → l'ognon, l'événement → l'évènement*.

This course gives the traditional spelling first and accepts the 1990 one.

## New words and new forms

A *néologisme* is a new word: *le télétravail, le covoiturage*. Each year the editors of *Le Petit
Robert* and *Le Petit Larousse* add new words and senses that have become
common, including regionalisms and words from French-speaking Africa: a dictionary describes how
the language is used, it doesn't decide it.

Job titles show change at work. For centuries many had only a masculine form (*le professeur, le
ministre, l'auteur*), even for a woman. Québec began recommending feminine forms in the late
1970s, France issued government guidance in 1986 and 1998, and in 2019 the Académie française
accepted the *féminisation* of job titles: *la professeure, la ministre, l'autrice* or
*l'auteure, la cheffe*. These forms are now standard in France (this course uses them:
*la chercheuse, la sculptrice*).

*L'écriture inclusive*, which writes both genders in one word (*les étudiant·e·s*), is a separate
and more disputed question: some organisations use it, while the Académie française and a 2017
French government circular for official texts reject it. Here, as with anglicisms, this lesson
describes; you will form your own view.

![A timeline of the French language, not to scale. 842: the Strasbourg Oaths. 1539: the ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts. 1635: the founding of the Académie française. 1694: the Académie's first dictionary. 1990: the rectified spellings.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: Tracing a word

Where does *la fête* come from, and what English word matches it?

1. The circumflex on *ê* often marks a lost *s*: put it back: *feste*.
2. English *feast* kept the *s*: it was borrowed from Old French before the *s* fell silent and
   disappeared from the spelling.
3. So *la fête* and *feast* are the same Latin word (*festa*). The same trick gives *la côte*
   (coast), *la tempête* (tempest), *l'île* (isle).

### Example 2: Old or new spelling?

Which spelling is traditional, which is 1990, and is either wrong?

1. *Il connait la réponse.* 1990 spelling (traditional *connaît*): both correct.
2. *J'ai acheté deux-cents grammes.* 1990 hyphens (traditional *deux cents*): both correct.
3. *Le cout de la vie augmente.* 1990 (traditional *le coût*): both correct.
4. *C'est bien sur.* Wrong: *sûr* (certain) keeps its circumflex in both systems, because *sur*
   (on) is another word.

### Example 3: A sentence about history, in the passive

*Richelieu a fondé l'Académie française en 1635.* In the passive (lesson 15): *L'Académie
française a été fondée par Richelieu en 1635.* The participle agrees with the new subject,
*l'Académie* (feminine): *fondée*. In a history book written in the passé simple you would read
*fut fondée*.

## Common mistakes

- Calling the 1990 spellings mistakes: *paraitre* and *ognon* are correct, and so are *paraître*
  and *oignon*.
- Dropping the circumflex from *sûr, mûr, dû*: they keep it to stay distinct from *sur, mur, du*.
- Thinking French "comes from" Gaulish: it comes from Latin, with a few Gaulish and more Frankish
  words.
- Reading *l'ordonnance de Villers-Cotterêts* as a prescription: here *l'ordonnance* is a royal
  decree.
- Writing *l'honte* or *l'haricot*: an aspirated *h* blocks elision (*la honte, le haricot*).

## Key points

- Spoken Latin became French; **[[Old French]]** runs from about the 9th to the 14th century; the
  Strasbourg Oaths (842) are its first written trace.
- A few words come from Gaulish (*le chêne, la ruche*) and more from Frankish (*la guerre, le
  jardin, bleu*); learned words were later borrowed again from Latin (*hôtel / hôpital*).
- 1539 Villers-Cotterêts (French for official documents), 1635 Académie française, 1694 its first
  dictionary, 1990 **[[rectified spelling]]** (optional; both spellings correct).
- Feminine job titles are standard (*la professeure, l'autrice*); anglicisms and inclusive writing
  are debated: dictionaries record usage.

lessons.title: Inventé en France: du Minitel au TGV
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the course's last lesson, and a capstone: a short dossier of original texts about French
inventions and engineering, from Braille's alphabet to the high-speed train, followed by a writing
task that uses everything you have learned. Read each text twice: once for the facts, once for the
grammar. The texts are full of the **[[passive voice]]** (lesson 15), relative pronouns (lessons 13
and 14), the plus-que-parfait (lesson 02) and **[[nominalisation]]** (lesson 22), the noun style of
headlines and articles (*la mise en service, le lancement, la fermeture*).

![A timeline of six French inventions and records, not to scale, each with a small picture. 1829: Louis Braille's alphabet, a cell of six raised dots. 1885: Pasteur's rabies vaccine, a syringe. 1979: the first Ariane rocket. 1981: the first TGV service, a high-speed train. 1982: the Minitel, a small terminal with a screen and keyboard. 2007: the rail speed record, a speedometer at 574.8 km/h.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Document 1: Lire avec les doigts

> Louis Braille est né en 1809 à Coupvray, près de Paris. À trois ans, il s'est blessé à l'œil dans l'atelier de son père, et il est devenu aveugle peu à peu. Élève, puis professeur à l'Institution royale des jeunes aveugles de Paris, il a perfectionné un système de points en relief qu'un officier, Charles Barbier, avait imaginé pour lire la nuit. En 1829, il a publié une méthode dans laquelle chaque lettre est représentée par une combinaison de six points au plus. Ce système, qui est aujourd'hui utilisé dans le monde entier, porte son nom : le braille.

*Avait imaginé* is a plus-que-parfait: Barbier's idea came before Braille's work. *Dans laquelle*
(lesson 14) refers to *une méthode*; *est représentée* and *est utilisé* are passives. Six dots,
each raised or flat, give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 patterns, so 63 usable signs once the empty
cell is left out.

## Document 2: Le premier vaccin contre la rage

> Le 6 juillet 1885, une mère alsacienne arrive à Paris avec son fils, Joseph Meister, âgé de neuf ans, qui a été mordu par un chien enragé. La rage tue presque toujours une fois que les symptômes sont apparus. Louis Pasteur, qui n'est pas médecin mais chimiste, travaille depuis plusieurs années sur un vaccin qu'il a testé sur des chiens, mais jamais sur un être humain. Bien qu'il hésite, il accepte de traiter l'enfant, que des médecins vaccinent pendant dix jours. Joseph survit. Le succès est immense, et l'Institut Pasteur, financé par des dons venus du monde entier, ouvre ses portes en 1888.

The text uses the **[[historic present]]** (*arrive, travaille, accepte*), as French biographies often do (lesson 04h1).
*Bien qu'il hésite* takes the subjunctive (lesson 08); *financé par des dons* is a passive
participle with its agent.

## Document 3: Kourou, 24 décembre 1979

> Pour que l'Europe ne dépende plus des États-Unis pour envoyer ses satellites dans l'espace, les pays européens avaient décidé, au début des années 1970, de construire leur propre lanceur. Le programme, dont la France était le principal acteur, a abouti le 24 décembre 1979 : ce jour-là, la première fusée Ariane a décollé de Kourou, en Guyane. Depuis, plusieurs générations d'Ariane ont mis en orbite des centaines de satellites de télécommunications, de météo et de recherche. L'industrie spatiale et l'aéronautique, très présentes autour de Toulouse, font partie des grandes réussites industrielles françaises.

*Pour que … ne dépende plus* (subjunctive, lesson 08); *avaient décidé* (before 1979); *dont la
France était le principal acteur* = of which France was the main player (lesson 13). *Un
lanceur* is the rocket that carries a satellite into orbit; *décoller* = to take off.

## Document 4: Le train à grande vitesse

> Le 27 septembre 1981, le premier TGV commercial a relié Paris à Lyon. Ses ingénieurs avaient testé plusieurs prototypes, dont un à turbine à gaz, avant de choisir l'électricité. La grande vitesse ferroviaire a transformé la géographie du pays : en rapprochant les villes, elle a changé la façon de vivre et de travailler de millions de personnes. Le 3 avril 2007, une rame d'essai a atteint 574,8 km/h sur la ligne à grande vitesse de l'Est, un record du monde de vitesse pour un train sur rails qui n'a pas été battu depuis.

*En rapprochant les villes* is a gérondif (lesson 04) whose subject is the sentence's subject, *la
grande vitesse*. *Une rame* is a trainset. French writes 574,8 with a comma where English writes
574.8.

## Document 5: Le Minitel, un internet avant Internet

> Lancé en 1982, le Minitel était un petit terminal équipé d'un écran et d'un clavier, que les abonnés au téléphone pouvaient recevoir gratuitement. Grâce à lui, on pouvait consulter l'annuaire, acheter un billet de train ou lire les nouvelles, des années avant l'arrivée d'Internet dans les foyers. Le service a été fermé le 30 juin 2012. Si le Minitel n'avait pas été aussi réussi, la France se serait-elle tournée plus tôt vers Internet ? La question est encore discutée.

*Le service a été fermé* (passive, passé composé); *si … n'avait pas été …, … se serait-elle
tournée* is a type-3 si-clause (lesson 11), with the inversion of a written question. The verb
for all of this is *innover* (to innovate): *une innovation* can succeed too well.

## Nominalisation: from sentence to headline

Articles and headlines often turn a verb into a noun. The sentence's subject becomes a *de*
phrase:

| Sentence | Nominalised (headline, note, title) |
|---|---|
| *Le premier TGV est mis en service en 1981.* | *La mise en service du premier TGV (1981)* |
| *Ariane est lancée pour la première fois.* | *Le premier lancement d'Ariane* |
| *Le Minitel ferme en 2012.* | *La fermeture du Minitel* |
| *Pasteur découvre un vaccin.* | *La découverte d'un vaccin par Pasteur* |
| *Les villes se rapprochent.* | *Le rapprochement des villes* |

Lesson 22 teaches it for recognition and for titles; use it in your title and perhaps one
sentence, not all through a text.

### Example 1: Turning facts into a passive sentence

Fact: *Des ingénieurs français ont conçu le TGV.* In the passive (lesson 15): the object becomes
the subject, *être* takes the tense of the active verb (passé composé: *a été*), and the participle
agrees with the new subject: *Le TGV a été conçu par des ingénieurs français.* With *la rame*
instead: *La rame a été conçue …*. With a feminine plural: *Les fusées ont été construites en
Europe.*

### Example 2: Joining two facts with a relative

Facts: *Braille a publié une méthode en 1829. Dans cette méthode, chaque lettre est une
combinaison de points.* The second sentence repeats *méthode* after the preposition *dans*, so use
*lequel* (lesson 14), feminine: *Braille a publié en 1829 une méthode dans laquelle chaque lettre
est une combinaison de points.* With *de* you would use *dont*: *le programme dont la France était
le principal acteur*.

## A patent, a prototype, an innovation

Three words that are easy to mix up:

- *un brevet* (a patent) protects an invention: for a period (usually twenty years), only its
  owner may make or sell it. *Déposer un brevet* = to file a patent.
- *un prototype* is the first working model, built for tests (*les prototypes du TGV*).
- *une innovation* is a new idea, product or method that is actually used; *innover* is to bring
  one in.

## Your task: an article on an invention

Write a 200–250 word article for a general-interest magazine about an invention you know (French
or not). Give it a title, a short introduction, two or three paragraphs and a conclusion that
opens a question.

### Model article

> **Le Minitel : la France connectée avant l'heure**
>
> Qui se souvient du Minitel ? Ce petit terminal beige a pourtant fait entrer des millions de Français dans l'ère numérique, bien avant Internet.
>
> Lancé en 1982, il a été distribué gratuitement aux abonnés au téléphone. L'idée était simple : remplacer l'annuaire en papier, qui coûtait cher à imprimer, par un annuaire électronique. Mais très vite, des milliers de services ont été créés : on pouvait réserver un billet de train, consulter son compte en banque ou discuter avec des inconnus. Les services les plus connus commençaient par le numéro 3615. En quelques années, le Minitel était devenu un objet de la vie quotidienne.
>
> Ce succès a pourtant eu un prix. Comme le réseau fonctionnait bien et rapportait beaucoup, certains pensent que la France a mis plus de temps que ses voisins à adopter Internet. D'autres répondent que le Minitel avait habitué les Français aux services en ligne, ce qui les a aidés ensuite. Les deux points de vue se défendent.
>
> Le service a été fermé le 30 juin 2012, après trente ans d'existence. Aujourd'hui, le Minitel est exposé dans les musées, mais il pose une question toujours actuelle : une innovation peut-elle réussir trop bien ?

That is about 205 words. Notice the parts: a title with a colon, a question to open, facts with
dates in the passive, a paragraph with two views (*certains pensent que … d'autres répondent
que …*), and a conclusion that asks a wider question. (In an exam you would leave out the bold;
it marks the title here.)

### Checklist: the whole course in ten lines

1. Past tenses: imparfait for background, passé composé for events, plus-que-parfait for what
   came before (lessons 01–03).
2. Agreement with *être*, and with a direct object placed before *avoir* (01, 02, 15).
3. Gérondif: same subject as the main verb (04).
4. Subjunctive after *il faut que, pour que, bien que, avant que*, wishes, feelings and doubt
   (05–08); indicative after *espérer que* and an affirmative *penser que*.
5. Si-clauses: for "if", *si* + present / imparfait / plus-que-parfait, not the conditionnel
   (09–11).
6. Relatives: *qui, que, où, dont, lequel* after a preposition (13, 14).
7. Passive with the tense on *être* and an agreeing participle (15).
8. Connectors for cause, consequence and contrast: *car, donc, pourtant, cependant* (19–21).
9. One register throughout: no *bosser* in a magazine article (20h1, 22).
10. Accents, apostrophes and numbers: *574,8 km/h, le 27 septembre 1981* (lowercase months).

## Common mistakes

- *Le Minitel a été fermé en 30 juin 2012*: before a full date, use *le*: *le 30 juin 2012*.
- *La rame a été conçu*: in the passive the participle agrees with the subject: *conçue*.
- *Une méthode dans quelle …*: after a preposition, use *laquelle*: *dans laquelle*.
- Writing *spatiale* for a masculine noun: *un programme spatial, l'industrie spatiale, des
  programmes spatiaux*.
- Overusing nominalisation: *La réalisation de la mise en place …* is heavy. One noun phrase in a
  title, verbs in the text.

## Key points

- Braille's system (1829); Pasteur's rabies vaccine (6 July 1885); the first Ariane launch (24
  December 1979, Kourou); the first TGV service (27 September 1981, Paris–Lyon); the Minitel
  (1982–2012); the rail speed record of 574.8 km/h (3 April 2007).
- History texts use the passive, *dont / lequel*, the plus-que-parfait and the historic present;
  headlines use nominalisation.
- *Spatial, spatiale, spatiaux; ferroviaire* (one form for both genders).
- An article: title, opening question, facts, two views, a conclusion that opens a wider question.

questions.stem: Where and when did Maupassant's La Parure first appear?
choices: In the daily Le Gaulois, on 17 February 1884
In his collection Contes du jour et de la nuit, in 1880
In the daily Le Figaro, on 18 January 1885
In a book of Perrault's tales, in 1697
questions.explanation: La Parure was first published in the Paris daily Le Gaulois on 17 February 1884, and collected the next year in Contes du jour et de la nuit (1885, not 1880). 18 January is the date of the ball in the story, and 1697 is Perrault's tales.

questions.stem: Why does Mathilde Loisel borrow a necklace from Mme Forestier?
choices: She wants to sell it to pay her debts.
She wants to copy it at a jeweller's.
Her husband asks her to have it valued.
She has no jewels to wear to the ball at the ministry.
questions.explanation: After her husband gives her 400 francs for a dress, Mathilde still has no jewels for the evening at the ministry, so she asks her rich friend from convent school to lend her some. The debts come later, after she loses the necklace.

questions.stem: In the retelling "Au bal, Mathilde fut la plus belle. Tout le monde voulut danser avec elle", what tense are "fut" and "voulut"?
questions.explanation: Fut (être) and voulut (vouloir) are passé simple, the -u- type: events in a written narrative. Spoken, you'd say "elle a été la plus belle, tout le monde a voulu danser avec elle". The imparfait would be était, voulait.

questions.stem: Match each passé simple form to its passé composé.
questions.explanation: Allâmes: -er verb, nous form (aller, with être). Fûtes: the fu- stem of être. Vins: venir (with être). Prirent: prendre (pris → pri-). Connut: connaître (connu → connu-). Prier would be ils prièrent, concevoir elle conçut.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of these two scenes from La Parure.

image.alt: Two scenes with no labels. On the left, a ball: a chandelier, a woman in a long gown with a necklace dancing with a man in a black tailcoat. On the right, a jeweller's shop: a man with glasses behind a counter, an open black box holding a necklace, and a small card with a price. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 the chandelier (le lustre), 2 the necklace (le collier) at Mathilde's neck, 3 her ball gown (la robe de bal), 4 the jeweller behind his counter, 5 the jewel box (l'écrin), 6 the price card: 36,000 francs. La glace (the mirror) and le fusil (the gun her husband wanted) are not in the picture.

questions.stem: Which of these are passé simple forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Partîmes (-îmes), eurent (avoir, -urent) and fîtes (faire, -îtes) are passé simple. Il parlait is the imparfait (the passé simple is il parla), and elle a pris the passé composé.

questions.stem: Retell "Elle perdit le collier de son amie" in the passé composé: Elle ___ le collier de son amie.
questions.explanation: Perdit is the passé simple of perdre (-it). In the passé composé: avoir + perdu, and no agreement, because the direct object (le collier) comes after the verb: elle a perdu le collier.

questions.stem: In "Elle poussa un cri : le collier n'était plus autour de son cou", why is "n'était plus" in the imparfait?
choices: It is one event that moves the story on.
It is a habit that lasted for years.
It is the passé simple of être.
It describes the state she discovers at that moment.
questions.explanation: The imparfait describes a state: the necklace was no longer there. The event, her cry, is passé simple (poussa). The passé simple of être is fut, which would make the absence a sudden event.

questions.stem: In a nineteenth-century novel you read "Elle eût aimé briller." What does it mean?
choices: She would have liked to shine.
questions.explanation: Eût aimé is a literary form (the pluperfect of the imperfect subjunctive) used here for the conditionnel passé: today, "elle aurait aimé briller". Mathilde, who dreams of being admired, is exactly that kind of character.

questions.stem: Put the events of La Parure in order.
choices: Loisel brings home an invitation to a ball at the ministry.
Mathilde borrows a diamond necklace from Mme Forestier.
At home after the ball, she sees that the necklace is gone.
They buy a similar necklace at the Palais-Royal for 36,000 francs.
For ten years they live in poverty to repay the debt.
Mme Forestier tells her that the necklace was fake.
questions.explanation: The invitation, the borrowed necklace, the loss discovered in front of the mirror, the replacement bought with borrowed money, ten years of misère, and the twist on the Champs-Élysées.

questions.stem: What is the twist ending (la chute) of La Parure?
choices: Mme Forestier had stolen the necklace herself.
Loisel had found the necklace but kept it secret.
The lost necklace was fake, worth five hundred francs at most.
The jeweller had sold them a fake necklace.
questions.explanation: Mme Forestier tells her that the necklace she lent her was fake, worth five hundred francs at most. Ten years of poverty paid for a necklace of paste. The story stops there, without comment.

questions.stem: In a classic novel you read "Il fallait qu'il fût prêt." What is "fût", and how would you say this today?
choices: The passé simple of être: "Il fallait qu'il fut prêt."
The imperfect subjunctive of être: "Il fallait qu'il soit prêt."
The futur of être: "Il fallait qu'il sera prêt."
The imparfait of être: "Il fallait qu'il était prêt."
questions.explanation: With its circumflex, fût is the imperfect subjunctive of être, used in literature after a main verb in the past. Today's French uses the subjonctif présent: qu'il soit prêt. Without the circumflex, fut is the passé simple, which can't follow il faut que.

questions.stem: Retell the moment in spoken French. Build: "She realised that the necklace had disappeared."
questions.explanation: Elle s'est aperçue que le collier avait disparu. S'apercevoir is a pronominal verb whose se isn't an object, so the participle agrees with elle (aperçue). Disparaître takes avoir: avait disparu, a plus-que-parfait for what had happened before she noticed.

questions.stem: A story says "Son amie lui prit les mains", but when the friend speaks, she says "Tu as acheté un autre collier ?". Why the two tenses?
choices: Characters speak in the passé composé; the narration uses the passé simple.
The passé composé is for women, the passé simple for men.
Maupassant changes tense when the scene moves to the Champs-Élysées.
The passé simple is used only with lui and leur.
questions.explanation: The passé simple is a written, narrative tense; even in Maupassant's stories, the characters' own words use the passé composé, as people do today. That is why you read the passé simple but write and speak the passé composé.

questions.stem: According to the OIF's 2026 report, about how many people spoke French in 2025?
questions.explanation: The OIF's 2026 report counts about 396 million French speakers in 2025 (about 348 million with the method of its earlier reports), which makes French the fourth most spoken language in the world. Such figures are estimates: they depend on how well someone must speak to count.

questions.stem: On which continent do nearly 65 % of French speakers live?
questions.explanation: Nearly two thirds of French speakers live in Africa (OIF, 2026), and the share is growing. Most of the rest live in Europe (France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg) and the Americas.

questions.stem: A friend in Montréal says: "Je descends au dépanneur." Where is she going?
questions.explanation: In Québec, le dépanneur is a convenience store with long opening hours: the term recommended by the OQLF. In France un dépanneur is a breakdown mechanic, and the shop would be une épicerie or une supérette.

questions.stem: Match each word to the place where it is used.
questions.explanation: Le kot (a student room) and la drache (a downpour) are Belgian; le natel (a mobile phone) is Swiss; magasiner (to go shopping) and le chum (a friend or boyfriend) are from Québec. In France: une chambre d'étudiant, une averse, un portable, faire les magasins, un copain.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this simplified map of where French is an official language.

image.alt: A simplified map of the Americas, Europe and Africa with countries where French is official shaded blue and Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger shaded yellow, and an inset of France and its neighbours. Six places are numbered: a point in eastern Canada, a point in the Caribbean, two points on the coast of West Africa, and two points in the inset.

questions.explanation: 1 Québec in eastern Canada, 2 Haiti in the Caribbean, 3 Senegal at the western tip of Africa, 4 Côte d'Ivoire further along the coast, 5 Belgium north of France, 6 Switzerland east of France. Cameroon and Madagascar are French-speaking too but not numbered.

questions.stem: Which of these are national languages of Switzerland? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Dutch is an official language of Belgium (with French and German); English is not a national language of Switzerland.

questions.stem: Which description of Haitian Creole is right?
choices: A dialect of French spoken mainly in Paris
A language of its own, with most of its words from French and its own grammar
An old form of French no longer spoken
questions.explanation: A creole is a language born where speakers of different languages had to communicate; most words of the French-based creoles come from French, but the grammar is their own. Haitian Creole is an official language of Haiti, with French. It isn't "broken French".

questions.stem: A Belgian student writes: "Je cherche un kot." Say it in France's French: Je cherche une chambre d'___.
questions.explanation: Le kot is Belgian for a student room: une chambre d'étudiant (also written une chambre d'étudiants). In Québec and France the Belgian word isn't used.

questions.stem: What did Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger announce in March 2025?
choices: That French would become their only official language
That they were leaving the OIF
That they would host the next Francophonie summit
That they were joining the OIF as observers
questions.explanation: The three Sahel states announced their withdrawal from the OIF on 17 and 18 March 2025. Mali (2023) and Burkina Faso (December 2023) had already made French a working language rather than an official one; Niger's transition charter of March 2025 did the same.

questions.stem: Which of these is a regionalism?
choices: "soixante-dix" for 70, the form taught in this course
"le livre", the normal word for a book
"septante" for 70, used in Belgium and Switzerland
"le français", the name of the language
questions.explanation: A regionalism is a word or expression used in one region only: septante belongs to Belgium and Switzerland. Soixante-dix is the form of France, Québec and most of the French-speaking world, and le livre and le français are common to all varieties.

questions.stem: In the reading text, what does the writer conclude after a year in Liège, Lausanne and Montréal?
choices: That the French of Paris is the only real French
That every region has its own words and none has "the real French"
That regional words should be avoided by everyone
That accents are impossible to understand
questions.explanation: "Chaque région a ses mots, et aucune n'a « le vrai français »." At first some accents were hard, but nobody laughed at him, and what he likes most is the language's diversity.

questions.stem: Build the writer's last sentence: "What I like most is its diversity."
questions.explanation: Ce que j'aime le plus, c'est sa diversité. Ce que is the object of j'aime (ce qui would be a subject); c'est picks it up. Diversité is feminine, so sa.

questions.stem: Which statement matches the lesson?
choices: Québec and Belgian French are mistakes that learners should correct.
African varieties of French are dialects, not French.
Each variety is correct where it is used; this course simply teaches France's.
questions.explanation: Varieties of French differ in accent, words and some grammar, and each has its own norms. The course teaches the French of France so that you have one consistent model, and teaches you to understand the others.

questions.stem: A Québec friend writes: "On a magasiné tout l'après-midi." How would most people in France say it?
choices: On a fait les magasins tout l'après-midi.
On a rangé le magasin tout l'après-midi.
On a travaillé au magasin tout l'après-midi.
On a fermé les magasins tout l'après-midi.
questions.explanation: Magasiner is Québec's verb for going shopping (and for shopping around). In France people say faire les magasins, or faire du shopping, an anglicism that Québec avoids.

questions.stem: Why are the Strasbourg Oaths of 842 important in the history of French?
choices: They made French the official language of France.
They are the first written trace of the Romance language that became French.
They were the first French dictionary.
questions.explanation: In 842 Louis the German swore an oath in the Romance language of his brother Charles's soldiers, and the historian Nithard copied it into his Latin chronicle: no longer Latin, not yet French. Official documents in French came with Villers-Cotterêts (1539); the Académie dates from 1635.

questions.stem: Put these events in the history of French in order.
choices: The ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts is signed.
questions.explanation: The Roman conquest (1st century BC), the Franks (from the 5th century), the Oaths (842), Villers-Cotterêts (1539), the Académie (1635), the rectified spellings (1990).

questions.stem: Name the event at each numbered date on this timeline of French.

image.alt: A timeline, not to scale, with five dates and no event names: 842, 1539, 1635, 1694 and 1990. Each date is numbered.

questions.explanation: 842 the Strasbourg Oaths, 1539 the ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts, 1635 the founding of the Académie française, 1694 its first dictionary, 1990 the rectified spellings. The Norman Conquest was in 1066 and the Revolution began in 1789.

questions.stem: L'hôtel and l'hôpital both come from Latin hospitalem. Why are they so different?
choices: One is French and the other is English.
L'hôtel was passed down by speakers for centuries; l'hôpital was borrowed again later from written Latin.
L'hôtel is a 1990 spelling of l'hôpital.
questions.explanation: That's a doublet: the popular word, worn smooth by centuries of speech (hôtel), and the learned word, taken again from written Latin (hôpital). Frêle / fragile and poison / potion are other pairs.
