questions.stem: The circumflex in "la forêt" marks a lost letter. Which English word is its cognate?
questions.explanation: The circumflex often marks an s that was dropped: forêt (once forest), fête (feast), hôpital (hospital), île (isle). English borrowed these words before the s disappeared.

questions.stem: Which spellings are correct (traditional or 1990)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Paraitre, ognon and évènement are 1990 spellings, oignon the traditional one: all correct. Sûr (certain) keeps its circumflex in both systems, so "c'est bien sur" is wrong: sur means "on".

questions.stem: What did the ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts (1539) require?
choices: That legal and administrative documents be written in French rather than Latin
That every child learn to read
That the Académie française publish a dictionary
That regional languages be banned in the home
questions.explanation: François Ier's ordinance made French the language of legal and administrative documents instead of Latin. Free compulsory schooling came in the 1880s, the Académie in 1635. (Here l'ordonnance is a royal decree, not a prescription.)

questions.stem: Match each word to where it comes from.
questions.explanation: La ruche (beehive) is one of the few Gaulish words; la guerre and le jardin come from Frankish, the Germanic language of the Franks; le week-end is a modern anglicism.

questions.stem: Put into the passive: "Richelieu a fondé l'Académie française en 1635." L'Académie française ___ par Richelieu en 1635.
questions.explanation: The passive keeps the tense on être (a été, passé composé) and the participle agrees with the new subject, l'Académie (feminine): a été fondée. A history book in the passé simple would write fut fondée.

questions.stem: Which of these is an anglicism?
questions.explanation: Le parking (a car park) is borrowed from English. Le courriel and la fin de semaine are French alternatives to e-mail and week-end, and le dépanneur is a Québec word built from French dépanner.

questions.stem: Which statement about feminine job titles is right?
choices: They have been compulsory in France since 1635.
The Académie française still rejects them all.
The Académie française accepted the feminisation of job titles in 2019.
questions.explanation: Québec began recommending feminine forms in the late 1970s, France issued guidance in 1986 and 1998, and the Académie française accepted the feminisation of job titles in 2019 (la professeure, l'autrice, la cheffe).

questions.stem: Which noun begins with an aspirated h, so that le or la is not shortened to l'?
questions.explanation: The aspirated h of words such as honte and haïr (a Frankish legacy in many words) blocks elision: la honte, not l'honte. Hôtel, homme and heure come from Latin and have a mute h: l'hôtel, l'homme, l'heure.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, what does a dictionary such as Le Petit Robert do with new words?
choices: It decides which words French speakers may use.
It adds only words approved by the government.
It records words that have become common in use.
questions.explanation: Dictionaries describe usage: each year Le Petit Robert and Le Petit Larousse add new words and senses that people actually use, including regionalisms. They don't decide the language.

questions.stem: Le tennis, le budget and le tunnel came into French from English. What do dictionaries say about where English got them?
choices: English invented them in the 20th century
questions.explanation: Etymological dictionaries trace them to French words (tenez !, bougette, tonnelle) that English borrowed and changed, and that came back into French in their English form.

questions.stem: When and between which cities did the first commercial TGV service run?
questions.explanation: The first commercial TGV linked Paris and Lyon on 27 September 1981. 3 April 2007 is the 574.8 km/h speed record; 24 December 1979 is the first Ariane launch.

questions.stem: In Louis Braille's system, published in 1829, what is each letter?
choices: A combination of up to six raised dots
A raised outline of the printed letter
A pattern of long and short sounds
questions.explanation: Each sign is a combination of up to six raised dots in a cell of two columns of three: 64 patterns, 63 once the empty cell is left out. Braille built on Charles Barbier's "night writing".

questions.stem: Name the invention or record at each numbered picture.

image.alt: A timeline, not to scale, with six small pictures and their dates but no names: 1829 a cell of six dots, 1885 a syringe, 1979 a rocket, 1981 a high-speed train, 1982 a small terminal with a screen showing 3615, 2007 a speedometer reading 574,8 km/h. Each picture is numbered.

questions.explanation: 1829 Braille's alphabet, 1885 Pasteur's rabies vaccine, 1979 the first Ariane rocket, 1981 the first TGV, 1982 the Minitel, 2007 the rail speed record (574.8 km/h).

questions.stem: Complete the passive with construire: "Les fusées ont été ___ en Europe."
questions.explanation: In the passive the participle agrees with the subject: les fusées is feminine plural, so construites. The tense is on être (ont été, passé composé).

questions.stem: Braille a publié une méthode ___ chaque lettre est une combinaison de points.
questions.explanation: The meaning is "in which", so you need a preposition + lequel, feminine to match méthode: dans laquelle (lesson 14). Dont replaces de + noun, que a direct object; "dans quelle" is a question word, not a relative.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its noun (nominalisation).
questions.explanation: Headlines turn verbs into nouns: la fermeture du Minitel, le premier lancement d'Ariane, la mise en service du TGV, la découverte d'un vaccin, le rapprochement des villes. La fermure and le lançage are not the nouns used for these verbs.

questions.stem: Les deux pays ont lancé plusieurs programmes ___.
questions.explanation: Spatial follows the -al → -aux pattern in the masculine plural: des programmes spatiaux. The feminine is spatiale(s): l'industrie spatiale. Spatials is not used.

questions.stem: Who was the first person treated with Pasteur's rabies vaccine, in July 1885?
choices: Joseph Meister, a nine-year-old boy from Alsace
questions.explanation: On 6 July 1885 Joseph Meister, aged nine, bitten by a rabid dog, was brought to Pasteur, who agreed to have him treated although the vaccine had never been tried on a human. He survived.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct French? Select all that apply.
choices: La rame a été conçue pour rouler très vite.
Le Minitel a été fermé le 30 juin 2012.
C'est une méthode dans quelle chaque lettre a six points.
La France a lancé plusieurs programmes spatials.
En rapprochant les villes, la grande vitesse a changé la vie de millions de personnes.
questions.explanation: Conçue agrees with la rame; le 30 juin 2012 needs le before the full date; the gérondif en rapprochant has the same subject as the sentence (la grande vitesse). After a preposition the relative is laquelle (dans laquelle), and the plural of spatial is spatiaux.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the model article on the Minitel in order.
choices: An opening question: "Qui se souvient du Minitel ?"
The facts, with dates, in the passive
Two points of view: "certains pensent que … d'autres répondent que …"
A conclusion that asks a wider question
questions.explanation: Title, an introduction that opens with a question, the facts, a paragraph weighing two views, and a conclusion that opens a wider question ("une innovation peut-elle réussir trop bien ?").

questions.stem: What is "un brevet" in "L'ingénieure a déposé un brevet"?
questions.explanation: Un brevet is a patent: déposer un brevet = to file a patent, which protects the invention (usually for twenty years). A prototype is the first working model; le brevet is also the name of an exam taken at about 15.

questions.stem: "Si le Minitel n'avait pas été aussi réussi, la France se serait-elle tournée plus tôt vers Internet ?" What kind of si-clause is this?
choices: si + present, futur: a likely future
si + imparfait, conditionnel présent: an imagined present
si + plus-que-parfait, conditionnel passé: an unreal past
si + passé composé, present: a fact
questions.explanation: N'avait pas été (plus-que-parfait) + se serait tournée (conditionnel passé): a type-3 si-clause about a past that didn't happen (lesson 11). The inversion se serait-elle makes it a written question.

questions.stem: On 3 April 2007 a French test train reached 574.8 km/h. How does a French article write the number?
questions.explanation: French uses a comma as the decimal sign: 574,8 km/h (said "cinq cent soixante-quatorze virgule huit"). A space, not a comma, separates thousands: 36 000 francs.

questions.stem: Build the passive sentence: "The TGV was designed by French engineers."
questions.explanation: Le TGV a été conçu par des ingénieurs français: être in the passé composé (a été), the participle agreeing with le TGV (masculine singular: conçu), and the agent with par.

questions.stem: Choose the right form: "Hier, nous ___ pendant six heures sans nous arrêter." (marcher)
questions.explanation: One walk on one day, with a stated length (pendant six heures), is presented as a finished block: passé composé, "nous avons marché". The imparfait "marchions" would describe a habit or the background, not one day's walk. Marcher takes avoir, so "étions marchés" is wrong; "marcherions" is the conditionnel.

questions.stem: What does "J'ai su la vérité le soir même" mean?
choices: I already knew the truth that evening.
I could tell the truth that evening.
I wanted the truth that same evening.
I found out the truth that same evening.
questions.explanation: In the passé composé, savoir describes the moment knowledge begins: "j'ai su" = I found out. "I knew" (a state) would be "je savais". "Le soir même" = that same evening.

questions.stem: Choose the best translation: "I managed to call the emergency services."
questions.explanation: "J'ai pu" (passé composé of pouvoir) = I managed to, I was able to and did. "Je pouvais" only says the possibility existed; "je voulais" = I wanted; "j'ai dû" = I had to.

questions.stem: "J'ai voulu appeler, mais il n'y avait pas de réseau." What does "j'ai voulu" mean here?
questions.explanation: In the passé composé, vouloir + infinitive usually means you acted on the wish: you tried (and here it failed, because there was no signal). A lasting wish would be "je voulais"; "I had to" is "j'ai dû"; "I was supposed to" is "je devais".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I met Inès in Spain" (for the first time)?
questions.explanation: "J'ai connu" (passé composé) = I got to know, I met for the first time. "Je connaissais Inès" describes a state: I knew her already. "Connaissé" is not a French participle (connaître → connu), and "connue" would agree with an object that comes after avoir, which never happens.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ce matin, Léa ___ la poubelle." (sortir = to take out)
questions.explanation: With a direct object (la poubelle), sortir takes avoir: "Léa a sorti la poubelle". The object comes after the verb, so there is no agreement ("a sortie" is wrong). "Est sortie" means "went out" and can't take an object.

questions.stem: Complete: "La tente ? Nous l'___ dans la grotte."
questions.explanation: Monter la tente (to put up the tent) has a direct object, so it takes avoir. The object pronoun l' (= la tente, feminine) comes before the verb, so the participle agrees: "nous l'avons montée". "Sommes montés" means "we went up".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Elle s'est rendue compte de son erreur.
Elle s'a rendu compte de son erreur.
Elle s'est rendu compte de son erreur.
Elle s'est rendue comptes de son erreur.
questions.explanation: Se rendre compte takes être (like all pronominal verbs) but the participle doesn't agree: "elle s'est rendu compte". Se is not the direct object here. "S'a" is impossible: pronominal verbs take être.

questions.stem: Which marker fits best? "___, nous avons tout vendu et nous sommes partis faire le tour du monde."
questions.explanation: "Un beau jour" (one fine day) introduces a single event that changes the story, so it fits the passé composé. "Chaque été, d'habitude, autrefois" introduce habits, which would need the imparfait, and you only sell everything once.

questions.stem: What does "sur le coup" mean in "Sur le coup, je n'ai rien dit, mais après j'étais furieux"?
questions.explanation: "Sur le coup" = at the time, in the moment, before you thought about it. It is often followed by a later contrast (mais après …). "By chance" is "par hasard"; "in the end" is "finalement".

questions.stem: Which sentence tells that a storm happened (an event in the story)?
choices: Il y a eu un orage terrible.
questions.explanation: "Il y a eu" (passé composé of il y a) presents the storm as something that happened. "Il y avait du vent, il faisait froid, il pleuvait" are all imparfait: the background.

questions.stem: In the reading, Sam writes "Nous étions perdus" rather than "Nous nous sommes perdus". What is the difference?
choices: The first describes their state (lost); the second tells the moment it happened (we got lost).
The first is informal; the second is formal.
The first is the plus-que-parfait; the second is the imparfait.
There is no difference in meaning or tense.
questions.explanation: "Nous étions perdus" is être in the imparfait + perdus as an adjective: a state, the situation at that moment. "Nous nous sommes perdus" is the passé composé of se perdre: the event of getting lost. Both are correct; they tell the story from a different angle.

questions.stem: In the reading "Perdus dans les Pyrénées", why did Sam and Inès get lost?
choices: A shepherd gave them the wrong directions.
They had left the path, and their compass stopped working.
They took the wrong bus to Pau.
They lost their map in a cave.
questions.explanation: They left the path (nous avons voulu quitter le sentier) to reach a summit, black clouds came, and Sam realised the compass wasn't working (je me suis rendu compte qu'elle ne marchait plus). The shepherd only appears at the end, giving them a lift.

questions.stem: Which word means "the route you plan to follow"?
questions.explanation: "L'itinéraire" (masculine) is the planned route. "La destination" is where you're going; "le sentier" is a footpath; "le sommet" is the summit.

questions.stem: Write the passé composé of "apercevoir": "Au loin, nous ___ les lumières du village."
questions.explanation: Apercevoir takes avoir, and its participle is aperçu, with ç before u: "nous avons aperçu". The direct object (les lumières) comes after the verb, so there is no agreement. — In the distance, we caught sight of the village lights.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "At first, we weren't scared."
questions.explanation: "Sur le coup, nous n'avons pas eu peur." The marker opens the sentence (capital S, comma); ne … pas goes around the auxiliary avons, and the participle eu comes after pas. Avoir peur in the passé composé tells the reaction at that moment.

questions.stem: Match each verb form to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Imparfait = a state: je savais (I knew), je devais (I was supposed to). Passé composé = an event: j'ai su (I found out), j'ai pu (I managed to), j'ai voulu (I tried to). "I met" would be "j'ai connu".

questions.stem: Which sentences use the auxiliary correctly? Select all that apply.
choices: J'ai sorti les vélos du garage.
Elle a monté la tente près du lac.
Ils ont rentré tard de la randonnée.
Nous avons descendu les sacs jusqu'à la voiture.
questions.explanation: Sortir, monter, descendre take avoir when they have a direct object: les vélos, la tente, les sacs. "Rentrer tard" has no object (it means to come home), so it takes être: "Ils sont rentrés tard".

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this walking map.

image.alt: A map of a mountain walk with a lake, a dashed path, a cave in a rock band, a small tent and a snowy summit, each with a numbered marker.

questions.explanation: The summit (le sommet) is the snowy peak; the dashed path is le sentier; the dark opening in the rock is la grotte; the small triangle is la tente; the blue water is le lac. A compass (la boussole) appears in the corner but isn't numbered, and there is no desert.

questions.stem: Complete so that the sentence means you missed the beginning: "Quand je suis arrivé, le film ___."
questions.explanation: The plus-que-parfait "avait commencé" puts the start of the film before your arrival: you missed the beginning. "A commencé" means it started when you arrived (you saw it all). "Commencera" and "commence" don't fit a past story.

questions.stem: Complete with the plus-que-parfait of "partir": "Quand tu as appelé, elle ___ déjà ___."
questions.explanation: Partir takes être, so the plus-que-parfait is the imparfait of être + parti, agreeing with elle: "elle était déjà partie". Déjà goes between the auxiliary and the participle. "Avait parti" uses the wrong auxiliary; "était parti" forgets the agreement; "a partie" is neither the right auxiliary nor the right tense.

questions.stem: Complete with the plus-que-parfait: "Les clés ? Je les ___ dans le tiroir." (cacher)
questions.explanation: Cacher takes avoir. The direct object pronoun les (= les clés, feminine plural) comes before the verb, so the participle agrees: "je les avais cachées". "Cachés" is masculine; "étais" is the wrong auxiliary.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Je n'avais vu pas le panneau.
Je ne pas avais vu le panneau.
Je n'avais pas vu le panneau.
J'avais ne pas vu le panneau.
questions.explanation: As in the passé composé, ne … pas goes around the auxiliary: "Je n'avais pas vu le panneau." — I hadn't seen the sign. The participle comes after pas.

questions.stem: Why is the plus-que-parfait used in "Il était furieux : on lui avait menti"?
choices: The lie happened after he became furious.
The lie came before his anger and explains it.
It makes the sentence more polite.
questions.explanation: The story describes a past situation (il était furieux) and then goes back to an earlier action that explains it: someone had lied to him. That earlier past is the plus-que-parfait.

questions.stem: Which sentence means that he had already left before I got there?
choices: Quand je suis arrivé, il était parti.
Quand je suis arrivé, il est parti.
Quand je suis arrivé, il partira.
questions.explanation: "Il était parti" (plus-que-parfait) places his leaving before my arrival. "Il est parti" means he left when (or just after) I arrived. "Quand j'arrivais, il est parti" means he left while I was on my way. "Il partira" is the futur.

questions.stem: Translate: "She realised she had forgotten her passport."
choices: Elle s'est rendue compte qu'elle avait oublié son passeport.
Elle s'est rendu compte qu'elle oubliait son passeport.
Elle se rendait compte qu'elle oublie son passeport.
Elle s'est rendu compte qu'elle avait oublié son passeport.
questions.explanation: Forgetting came before realising, so it's in the plus-que-parfait: "qu'elle avait oublié". Se rendre compte doesn't agree ("rendu", not "rendue"). "Oubliait" means "was forgetting", and "oublie" is the present.

questions.stem: Translate: "I had been waiting for an hour when the bus came."
choices: J'avais attendu depuis une heure quand le bus est arrivé.
J'attendais depuis une heure quand le bus est arrivé.
J'ai attendu depuis une heure quand le bus arrivait.
J'attends depuis une heure quand le bus est arrivé.
questions.explanation: For something that was still going on at that past moment, French uses the imparfait + depuis: "J'attendais depuis une heure" (had been waiting). The plus-que-parfait with depuis is a copy of English "had been"; "J'ai attendu … quand le bus arrivait" swaps the roles of the two tenses.

questions.stem: "Elle est partie le 12 mai. La veille, elle avait fait ses valises." When did she pack?
questions.explanation: "La veille" is the day before the moment in the story: the day before 12 May, so 11 May. The day after would be "le lendemain".

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: "Quand je suis revenu, mon vélo ___."
questions.explanation: Disparaître takes avoir in the plus-que-parfait (and the passé composé): "mon vélo avait disparu". Its participle is disparu. "Était disparue" uses être and is feminine, while vélo is masculine; "disparé" is not a word.

questions.stem: In "Le cambriolage qui n'en était pas un", who had shut the cat in the bathroom?
questions.explanation: Hugo admits: "Il avait aussi enfermé le chat pour l'empêcher de sortir… et il l'avait oublié." M. Benali never came, and there was no burglar.

questions.stem: In the same story, why had M. Benali lied?
choices: He had stolen the computer and wanted to hide it.
He had mixed up the dates, never came, and was ashamed.
Hugo had asked him to say nothing.
questions.explanation: "Il avait confondu les dates … Il n'était jamais venu, et il avait menti parce qu'il avait honte." He was innocent of the burglary, but not of the lie.

questions.stem: Write the plus-que-parfait of "mentir": "Il m'___ sur son âge."
questions.explanation: Mentir takes avoir and its participle is menti: "Il m'avait menti sur son âge." — He had lied to me about his age. (M' is an indirect object, mentir à quelqu'un, so nothing agrees.)

questions.stem: Write the plus-que-parfait of "sortir" (the speakers are a mixed group): "Quand le cambrioleur est entré, nous ___."
questions.explanation: Sortir without an object takes être; with nous for a mixed group the participle takes -s: "nous étions sortis". (A group of women would write "nous étions sorties".)

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I hadn't seen him."
questions.explanation: "Je ne l'avais pas vu." Ne and the object pronoun l' come before the auxiliary, pas comes after it, and the participle comes last.

questions.stem: Put the events of "Le cambriolage qui n'en était pas un" in the order in which they really happened.
choices: Claire leaves a key with M. Benali.
Hugo borrows the computer and shuts the cat in.
Claire comes home and calls the police.
Hugo admits everything on the phone.
questions.explanation: The story starts on Sunday evening (Claire comes home) and jumps back with the plus-que-parfait: the day before she left (la veille de son départ) she had left a key with the neighbour; on Saturday, while she was away, Hugo had come by. Hugo's confession comes on Monday morning.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its plus-que-parfait with "il".
questions.explanation: Same auxiliary as in the passé composé: venir and pronominal verbs take être (il était venu, il s'était levé); prendre and voir take avoir (il avait pris, il avait vu).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Quand nous sommes arrivés, ils étaient partis.
Elle n'avait jamais vu la mer.
questions.explanation: The first three are correct plus-que-parfaits (être for partir and se tromper, with agreement; avoir for voir). Pronominal verbs take être: "Je m'étais levé(e) très tôt", not "m'avais".

questions.stem: Name the tense that goes with each numbered part of this timeline: "Il pleuvait. Je suis arrivé à 20 h. Le film avait commencé à 19 h 45."

image.alt: A timeline towards "now" with a point at 19 h 45, a later point at 20 h with a dashed arrow back to the first marked "earlier", and a long wavy band under the line. Each has a numbered marker.

questions.explanation: The earliest point, 19 h 45, is the film that had started: plus-que-parfait (avait commencé). The event at 20 h is the passé composé (je suis arrivé). The wavy band running under everything is the background in the imparfait (il pleuvait).

questions.stem: Complete: "Après ___ ses études, elle a trouvé du travail." (finir)
questions.explanation: After après, French uses the past infinitive: avoir or être + participle. Finir takes avoir: "après avoir fini". The plain infinitive "après finir" is not used in writing; "être finie" uses the wrong auxiliary.

questions.stem: Complete: "Après ___ à Paris, Lucie a cherché un appartement." (arriver)
questions.explanation: Arriver takes être, and with être the participle agrees with the subject of the sentence, Lucie: "après être arrivée". "Avoir arrivé" uses the wrong auxiliary; "être arrivé" forgets the agreement.

questions.stem: Complete: "Après ___, nous avons pris le petit déjeuner." (se lever)
questions.explanation: Pronominal verbs take être, and the reflexive pronoun matches the subject (nous): "après nous être levés". "S'être levés" would only fit a subject like ils; "avoir" is the wrong auxiliary.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Après avoir fini le dîner, le téléphone a sonné.
Après que nous avons fini le dîner, le téléphone a sonné.
Après finir le dîner, le téléphone a sonné.
Après que avoir fini le dîner, le téléphone a sonné.
questions.explanation: Après + past infinitive needs the same subject in both parts, and here the subjects differ (we finished, the phone rang). So you need a clause: "Après que nous avons fini le dîner, …" (indicative). The first choice says the phone finished dinner; "que" can't be followed by an infinitive.

questions.stem: Complete this habit in the past: "Dès qu'il ___ son travail, il sortait se promener."
questions.explanation: The main verb (sortait) is an imparfait of habit. The time clause describes something finished each time before he went out, so the plus-que-parfait fits: "Dès qu'il avait fini son travail, il sortait." The futur and futur antérieur belong to the future; "finit" is a present.

questions.stem: What does "au moment où" mean in "Au moment où il allait abandonner, il a trouvé l'erreur"?
questions.explanation: "Au moment où" points to one precise moment: just as he was about to give up. "As long as" is "tant que", "every time" is "chaque fois que", "ever since" is "depuis que".

questions.stem: What does this sentence mean? "Tant qu'elle n'avait pas de laboratoire, elle travaillait dans sa cuisine."
choices: Once she had a laboratory, she worked in her kitchen.
Every time she had no laboratory, she cooked.
As long as she had no laboratory, she worked in her kitchen.
Although she had no laboratory, she worked in a kitchen.
questions.explanation: "Tant que" = as long as: two situations that lasted together, both in the imparfait. "Once" would be "une fois que"; "although" is a different structure (lesson 08).

questions.stem: In careful written French, which form follows "après que"?
questions.explanation: Après que presents the action as done, so the traditional rule gives it the indicative: "après qu'il est parti". "Après qu'il soit parti" (subjunctive) is very common, especially in speech, but careful writing and this course use the indicative. "Parte" is a present subjunctive and "partir" an infinitive.

questions.stem: A story set in 1958: "Elle a présenté son invention le 3 mai. ___, tous les journaux en parlaient."
questions.explanation: In a story, the day after a past moment is "le lendemain" (here 4 May 1958). "Demain, hier, aujourd'hui" count from today, so they don't fit a story about 1958.

questions.stem: In a story set in 1958, how do you say "the year before" (1957)?
questions.explanation: Seen from a past year, the year before is "l'année précédente". "L'année dernière" means last year counted from today; "l'année suivante" is the year after; "l'année prochaine" is next year from today.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il est arrivé à Lyon le 10 ; sa sœur était arrivée deux jours ___, le 8."
questions.explanation: The 8th is two days before the 10th: "deux jours plus tôt" (two days earlier). "Plus tard" would be the 12th. "Il y a" and "dans" count from today, and they go before the number.

questions.stem: Complete: "Marie Curie était ___ génie."
questions.explanation: "Le génie" is always masculine, even for a woman: "C'est un génie. Marie Curie était un génie."

questions.stem: In the reading about Lucie Garnier, what happened in 1957?
choices: She presented her filter in Paris.
questions.explanation: "Elle a connu des dizaines d'échecs et, en 1957, elle a presque abandonné." She presented the filter on 3 May 1958, founded her company the following year (1959), and passed her bac in 1939.

questions.stem: Write the past infinitive of "partir" (the subject is a woman): "Après ___ de Lyon, elle s'est installée à Paris."
questions.explanation: Partir takes être, and the participle agrees with the subject (elle): "Après être partie de Lyon, elle s'est installée à Paris." — After leaving Lyon, she settled in Paris.

questions.stem: Fill in the time word: "Il a passé l'examen le 3 juin et il a eu les résultats le 4 juin, c'est-à-dire le ___."
questions.explanation: The day after a moment in a story is "le lendemain". From today, you would say "demain".

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "As soon as she received the results, she called her team."
questions.explanation: "Dès qu'elle a reçu les résultats, elle a appelé son équipe." The time clause comes first, closed by a comma; both verbs are in the passé composé because it happened once.

questions.stem: Match each conjunction to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Dès que = as soon as; tant que = as long as; chaque fois que = every time, whenever; au moment où = (just) when, just as; une fois que = once. "Although" (bien que) and "until" (jusqu'à ce que) take the subjunctive and come in lesson 08.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Après avoir mangé, nous sommes partis.
Après être arrivés, ils ont dîné.
Après avoir arrivé, elle a téléphoné.
Une fois qu'on était arrivés, on allait se baigner.
questions.explanation: "Après avoir mangé" and "après être arrivés" use the right auxiliaries. "Une fois qu'on était arrivés, on allait se baigner" is a habit (plus-que-parfait + imparfait). Arriver takes être: "après être arrivée", not "avoir arrivé".

questions.stem: The starred day is the day of the story. Name each numbered day.

image.alt: Five day boxes in a row along a line; the middle box is highlighted with a star. Each box has a numbered marker.

questions.explanation: Seen from the day of the story (ce jour-là): the day before is la veille, the day after is le lendemain, and two days away are deux jours plus tôt and deux jours plus tard. "Hier" and "demain" count from today, not from the story.

questions.stem: What is the present participle of "faire"?
questions.explanation: Nous faisons → fais- → "faisant". It comes from the nous present, not from the infinitive (fairant) or the participle fait (faitant).

questions.stem: What is the present participle of "savoir"?
questions.explanation: Savoir is one of the three exceptions: "sachant" (with étant and ayant). "Savant" exists, but it's an adjective or noun (learned; a scholar).

questions.stem: Complete with a gérondif: "Ne téléphone pas ___." (conduire)
questions.explanation: The gérondif is en + the present participle: nous conduisons → conduisant → "en conduisant". En is not followed by an infinitive; without en, "conduisant" is a present participle, not a gérondif.

questions.stem: "En partant à six heures, tu éviteras les bouchons." What does the gérondif express here?
questions.explanation: With a future main verb, the gérondif often means "if": Si tu pars à six heures, tu éviteras les bouchons.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: En traversant la rue, une voiture m'a renversé.
Pendant que je traversais la rue, une voiture m'a renversé.
En arrivant à Paris, il pleuvait.
Traversant la rue, une voiture m'a renversé.
questions.explanation: The gérondif (and the participle) belongs to the subject of the main verb. In the first and last sentences that subject is "une voiture", so the car would be crossing; in the third, "il" (the weather) would be arriving. With two different subjects, use a clause: "Pendant que je traversais la rue, …"

questions.stem: "Il roulait vite tout en sachant que c'était dangereux." What does "tout en sachant" mean here?
questions.explanation: Tout en + participle says two things go together, often with a contrast: he drove fast even though he knew it was dangerous.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: "Voici des conseils ___ tous les conducteurs."
questions.explanation: With a direct object after it (tous les conducteurs), the -ant form describes an action: it's the present participle (= qui intéressent), which never agrees. Without the object it would be the verbal adjective, which agrees: "des conseils intéressants". "Intéressantes" is feminine; "intéressent" is a conjugated verb and would need qui.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling: "C'était une journée très ___."
questions.explanation: After très, this is the verbal adjective (a quality), spelled fatigant without u, and it agrees with journée: "fatigante". "Fatiguant" is the present participle (en se fatiguant).

questions.stem: Translate: "I like driving at night."
questions.explanation: After a verb like aimer, French uses the infinitive: "J'aime conduire la nuit." English -ing is not a gérondif here. Aimer takes no de before an infinitive.

questions.stem: "Les passagers voyageant à l'arrière doivent aussi attacher leur ceinture." Here "voyageant" means…
choices: en voyageant (while travelling, at the same time as fastening)
questions.explanation: Without en, the present participle often replaces qui + verb in written French: les passagers voyageant à l'arrière = les passagers qui voyagent à l'arrière.

questions.stem: In France, which word names the place where you leave your car (a car park)?
questions.explanation: "Le parking" is the place (a false friend: not the act). The act of parking is "le stationnement" (Stationnement interdit = No parking). A rond-point is a roundabout and un bouchon a traffic jam.

questions.stem: According to Nadia's advice, what is the speed limit on a French motorway when it rains?
questions.explanation: "Sur l'autoroute, c'est 130 km/h par temps sec et 110 km/h quand il pleut." 80 km/h is the usual limit on two-way roads outside towns.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'ai rayé la voiture ___." (se garer; rayer = to scratch)
questions.explanation: A pronominal verb keeps its pronoun in the gérondif, matching the subject (je): "en me garant". "En se garant" would fit il or elle; "en garant" drops the pronoun; en needs the -ant form, not the infinitive.

questions.stem: Write the gérondif of "prendre": "On voit de beaux paysages ___ le train."
questions.explanation: Nous prenons → pren- → prenant, so the gérondif is "en prenant". — You see beautiful scenery by taking the train.

questions.stem: Write the present participle of "être": "___ fatiguée, elle s'est arrêtée sur une aire d'autoroute."
questions.explanation: Être is an exception: "étant". "Étant fatiguée, elle s'est arrêtée …" — Being tired, she stopped at a motorway rest area. The participle gives the cause (written style).

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "He was talking on the phone while driving."
questions.explanation: "Il parlait au téléphone tout en conduisant." Tout en goes straight before the participle, at the end of the sentence.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Le piéton = pedestrian; le virage = bend in the road; le bouchon = traffic jam (also a cork); l'amende (feminine) = fine; freiner = to brake. "To overtake" is doubler and "roundabout" le rond-point.

questions.stem: In which sentences is the gérondif used correctly? Select all that apply.
choices: En arrivant au rond-point, prenez la deuxième sortie.
Elle s'est blessée en tombant de vélo.
En arrivant à la gare, le train était déjà parti.
En roulant moins vite, on consomme moins d'essence.
questions.explanation: In the correct sentences, the person who arrives, falls or drives is the subject of the main verb (vous, elle, on). In "En arrivant à la gare, le train était déjà parti", the subject is le train, so the train would be arriving: say "Quand je suis arrivé à la gare, le train était déjà parti."

questions.stem: Name the numbered things in this street plan.

image.alt: A street plan seen from above: a roundabout, a pedestrian at a zebra crossing, a cyclist on a cycle path, a speed camera on a post, a sharp bend and a line of cars nose to tail, each with a numbered marker.

questions.explanation: The circle in the middle is le rond-point; the person at the zebra crossing is le piéton; the bike on the green lane is le cycliste; the box on a post is le radar; the sharp curve is le virage; the cars stuck nose to tail are le bouchon. The car park in the corner isn't numbered.

questions.stem: When and where was Marie Curie born?
questions.explanation: Maria Skłodowska was born on 7 November 1867 in Warsaw, then part of the Russian Empire. She moved to Paris at the end of 1891; 4 July is the date of her death in 1934.

questions.stem: Who shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics?
choices: Marie Curie and her daughter Irène
Marie and Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel
Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, without Marie
questions.explanation: The 1903 prize went half to Henri Becquerel and half jointly to Pierre and Marie Curie. It was the first Nobel Prize awarded to a woman. Marie won the 1911 Chemistry prize alone.

questions.stem: Why is "avait découverts" in the plus-que-parfait in "les rayons de l'uranium, qu'Henri Becquerel avait découverts en 1896"?
choices: It describes a habit of Becquerel's.
Becquerel's discovery came before the moment of the story (Marie choosing her subject).
questions.explanation: The story is at the moment Marie chooses her thesis subject; Becquerel's discovery came earlier, so it goes back one step: plus-que-parfait.

questions.stem: In the same phrase, why does "découverts" end in -s?
choices: It's plural because of the date 1896.
It agrees with que (= les rayons), a direct object placed before avoir.
questions.explanation: With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it. Que stands for "les rayons" (masculine plural), so "découverts".

questions.stem: Rewrite in the historic present: "En 1895, elle a épousé Pierre Curie."
choices: En 1895, elle avait épousé Pierre Curie.
questions.explanation: In the historic present, the events (passé composé) become present: "elle épouse". The imparfait and plus-que-parfait would keep it in the past; the futur is for later events seen from the story's moment.

questions.stem: In a historic-present biography: "En 1903, elle reçoit le prix Nobel de physique ; elle en ___ un second en 1911." Which form is typical?
questions.explanation: When a biography is told in the historic present, a later event is often told in the futur: "elle en recevra un second en 1911" (she was later to receive a second one). The conditionnel "recevrait" belongs to a past narration; "avait reçu" would place it before 1903.

questions.stem: Which passage mixes the past narration and the historic present without reason?
choices: En 1891, elle part pour Paris et elle s'inscrit à la Sorbonne.
En 1891, elle est partie pour Paris et elle s'est inscrite à la Sorbonne.
En 1891, elle part pour Paris et elle a obtenu sa licence en 1893.
En 1891, elle part pour Paris ; deux ans plus tard, elle obtient sa licence.
questions.explanation: The third passage starts in the historic present (part) and switches to the passé composé (a obtenu) for a later event. Keep one system: "elle part … elle obtient" or "elle est partie … elle a obtenu".

questions.stem: Complete: "Après la mort de Pierre, Marie est restée ___ à trente-huit ans."
questions.explanation: A widow is "une veuve"; as an adjective after rester or être, "elle est veuve". "Veuf" is the masculine (a widower).

questions.stem: What was polonium named after?
questions.explanation: "Le polonium, ainsi nommé en hommage à la Pologne": the Curies named it after Poland, which at the time was divided between three empires.

questions.stem: Past narration: "Quand Marie a reçu son second prix Nobel en 1911, Pierre ___ mort depuis cinq ans." Write the auxiliary.
questions.explanation: Pierre's death (1906) came before 1911, so it is in the plus-que-parfait, and mourir takes être: "Pierre était mort depuis cinq ans" (had been dead for five years).

questions.stem: Put these events of Marie Curie's life in order.
choices: She arrives in Paris and enrols at the Sorbonne.
She marries Pierre Curie in Sceaux.
The Curies announce polonium and radium.
She shares the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Pierre dies in a street accident.
She receives the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
questions.explanation: 1891 Paris; 1895 marriage (26 July); 1898 polonium (July) and radium (December); 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics; 19 April 1906 Pierre's death; 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: A widower is "le veuf"; a chemist's shop is "la pharmacie" (un chimiste is a scientist). Rendre hommage à quelqu'un = to pay tribute to someone.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, which statements about Marie Curie are true? Select all that apply.
choices: She was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize.
She received the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone.
Her remains were moved to the Panthéon in 1995.
questions.explanation: She was the first woman Nobel laureate (1903), won the Chemistry prize alone in 1911, and on 20 April 1995 her ashes and Pierre's were moved to the Panthéon. She was born in Warsaw.

questions.stem: What does "Ayant préparé nos sacs la veille au soir, nous étions prêts en dix minutes" mean?
choices: While packing our bags the evening before, we were ready in ten minutes.
Having packed our bags the evening before, we were ready in ten minutes.
Before packing our bags, we were ready in ten minutes.
Without packing our bags, we were ready in ten minutes.
questions.explanation: Ayant + participle (the perfect participle) = having done: the packing was finished before the main action, and it explains why they were ready so fast.

questions.stem: Complete with the perfect participle of "arriver": "___ tard, nous avons dormi au refuge." (a mixed group)
questions.explanation: Arriver takes être, so its perfect participle is étant + arrivé, agreeing with nous (a mixed group): "Étant arrivés". Ayant is for avoir verbs.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a dangling participle (a participle that doesn't fit the subject)?
choices: Arrivés au sommet, nous avons mangé.
Ayant marché dix heures, nous étions épuisés.
Le soleil couché, nous avons allumé une lampe.
Arrivés au sommet, le brouillard est tombé.
questions.explanation: "Arrivés au sommet" has no subject of its own, so it belongs to the subject of the main verb, le brouillard: the fog would have arrived at the summit. "Le soleil couché" is fine: it has its own subject (le soleil).

questions.stem: "Le brouillard s'étant levé, nous sommes repartis." What had lifted?
questions.explanation: This participle clause has its own subject, le brouillard: "the fog having lifted". It is a formal written construction.

questions.stem: In "Arrivés au col, nous avons découvert un panorama extraordinaire", what does "arrivés" agree with?
questions.explanation: A past participle on its own at the start of the sentence belongs to the subject of the main verb, nous, and agrees with it as with être (arrivés; arrivées for a group of women).

questions.stem: Which word means "dusk"?
questions.explanation: "Le crépuscule" is dusk (the walkers see the village lights au crépuscule). "L'aube" is dawn, "la brume" mist and "l'horizon" the horizon.

questions.stem: Why did the walkers stop near a big rock?
choices: A thick fog came up and they didn't want to get lost.
It was dusk and they wanted to sleep.
The warden had told them to wait there.
questions.explanation: "Brusquement, un brouillard épais est monté de la vallée … Ne voulant pas nous perdre, nous nous sommes arrêtés près d'un gros rocher."

questions.stem: In everyday conversation, which is the most natural way to say "Étant arrivés tard, nous avons dormi au refuge"?
choices: Ayant arrivé tard, on a dormi au refuge.
Comme on est arrivés tard, on a dormi au refuge.
Arrivant tard, on dormait au refuge.
Étant arrivés tard, on dort au refuge.
questions.explanation: The perfect participle sounds written. In speech, French uses a clause: "Comme on est arrivés tard, …" (or "On est arrivés tard, alors …"). "Ayant arrivé" uses the wrong auxiliary.

questions.stem: Write the perfect participle of "marcher": "___ plus de dix heures, nous avons dormi comme des bébés."
questions.explanation: Marcher takes avoir, so its perfect participle is "ayant marché": having walked more than ten hours, we slept like babies.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Once we had gone round the glacier, there were still three hours of walking."
questions.explanation: "Une fois le glacier contourné, il a fallu encore trois heures de marche." Une fois + noun + participle is a participle clause with its own subject (le glacier).

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: "Dusk" is le crépuscule and "fog" le brouillard. Le col also means a collar; le refuge is a hut where walkers can sleep, often with a warden.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Étant partis à l'aube, nous sommes arrivés avant midi.
Arrivée au refuge, elle s'est reposée.
Ayant arrivé au col, nous avons mangé.
La nuit tombée, nous avons allumé une lampe.
questions.explanation: "Étant partis" and "Arrivée" use être verbs correctly and agree with the subject; "La nuit tombée" is a participle clause with its own subject (la nuit, so tombée). Arriver takes être: "Étant arrivés au col", not "ayant arrivé".

questions.stem: Complete: "Il faut que tu ___ samedi." (venir)
questions.explanation: Il faut que + subjunctive. Venir has two stems: the ils present "viennent" gives vienn- for je, tu, il, ils: que tu viennes. "Viens" is the indicative present; "venes" uses the nous stem in the wrong person; "viendras" is the futur.

questions.stem: Which is "que nous ___" for prendre?
questions.explanation: Nous and vous look like the imparfait: nous prenions → que nous prenions. "Prennions" wrongly uses the ils stem (prenn-) for nous; "prenons" is the present; "prendions" is built on the infinitive.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il est important que vous ___ à l'heure." (être)
questions.explanation: Être is irregular: que je sois, que tu sois, qu'il soit, que nous soyons, que vous soyez, qu'ils soient. Its nous and vous forms have no i: "soyiez" doesn't exist. "Êtes" is the present and "serez" the futur.

questions.stem: In which pair do the indicative present and the subjunctive sound different?
questions.explanation: For regular -er verbs the je, tu, il and ils forms are identical in both moods. For finir the subjunctive adds -iss- + -e: "je finis" [fini] but "que je finisse" [finis].

questions.stem: Complete: "Il faut que j'___ à la banque avant midi." (aller)
questions.explanation: Aller is irregular: que j'aille, que tu ailles, qu'il aille, qu'ils aillent (but que nous allions, que vous alliez). "Vais" is the indicative; "alle" doesn't exist; "allions" is the nous form.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly spelled sentence: "We need to study this file."
choices: Il faut que nous étudions ce dossier.
Il faut que nous étudiions ce dossier.
Il faut que nous étudiyons ce dossier.
Il faut que nous étudiyions ce dossier.
questions.explanation: The nous subjunctive is the nous imparfait: nous étudiions (stem étudi- + -ions), with a double i. "Étudions" is the present; the forms with y don't exist (y only appears in verbs like voir: voyions).

questions.stem: What does "Il ne faut pas que tu viennes." mean?
choices: You can come if you want.
questions.explanation: Il ne faut pas que = must not. "You don't have to come" is "Il n'est pas nécessaire que tu viennes" or "Tu n'es pas obligé de venir".

questions.stem: Which sentence states a general rule, not an instruction to one particular person?
choices: Il faut que tu réserves à l'avance.
Il faut que vous réserviez à l'avance.
Il faut que je réserve à l'avance.
questions.explanation: For a general rule (anyone, people in general), use il faut + infinitive. With que + subjunctive you name the person: tu, vous, je.

questions.stem: Your friend asks who will bring the drinks. You answer "Je m'en charge." What do you mean?
questions.explanation: Se charger de = to take care of, to take on (a task). En replaces "des boissons": Je m'en charge = I'll take care of it.

questions.stem: Read: "Pour la fête de samedi, il suffit que chacun apporte une boisson. La salle est réservée et le traiteur s'occupe du repas. Il faut juste que quelqu'un vienne à 17 heures pour décorer." What do the guests need to bring?
questions.explanation: "Il suffit que chacun apporte une boisson" = all that's needed is for everyone to bring a drink. The caterer (le traiteur) takes care of the meal, and only one person is needed at 5 pm to decorate.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il vaut mieux que vous ___ le budget avant de choisir." (faire)
questions.explanation: Faire has one irregular stem, fass-, in every person: que vous fassiez. "Faites" is the present, "ferez" the futur, and "fassez" has the wrong ending (-iez in the subjunctive).

questions.stem: "Samedi à 15 heures, ça te convient ?" Which answer accepts?
questions.explanation: Ça me convient = that suits me. The subject is ça, so the verb is "convient" (3rd person), and the pronoun me refers to you. "Ça te convient" would be repeating the question.

questions.stem: Write the subjunctive of finir: "Il faut que je ___ le dossier avant vendredi."
questions.explanation: Ils finissent → finiss- + -e: que je finisse.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "We have to choose the caterer."
questions.explanation: Il faut que nous choisissions le traiteur. Choisir: nous choisissions (imparfait form), so que nous choisissions.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its "que je" form.
questions.explanation: The irregular subjunctives: que je sois, que j'aie, que je sache, que je veuille, que je puisse. "Voie" is the regular subjunctive of voir (ils voient → que je voie).

questions.stem: Which sentences use the subjunctive correctly? Select all that apply.
choices: Il faut que tu prennes ton manteau.
Il est essentiel qu'on soit à l'heure.
Il faut que nous allons au marché.
questions.explanation: Prennes, soit and appelles are subjunctives (appelles looks like the present, as with most -er verbs). "Que nous allons" is the indicative: the subjunctive is "que nous allions".

questions.stem: Give the "que je / j'" form of each numbered verb on the wheel.

image.alt: A wheel with seven segments around the centre "que je / j' …": être, with its form sois shown as an example, then avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir and vouloir, each with a numbered blank.

questions.explanation: avoir → que j'aie; aller → que j'aille; faire → que je fasse; pouvoir → que je puisse; savoir → que je sache; vouloir → que je veuille. "Voie" belongs to voir, and "faille" to il faut (qu'il faille).

questions.stem: Name each numbered item on the wedding checklist.

image.alt: A wedding checklist on a clipboard with six numbered icons and no words: a building with a door, a chef's hat over a covered dish, a wallet with coins, a calendar page with the 30th circled, balloons and a garland, a dress and a suit on hangers.

questions.explanation: 1 the hall (la salle), 2 the caterer (le traiteur), 3 the budget (le budget), 4 the deadline (la date limite), 5 the decorations (la décoration), 6 what to wear (la tenue). La priorité and la contrainte are abstract words with no picture.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mes parents veulent que je ___ des études." (faire)
questions.explanation: Vouloir que + a new subject → subjunctive: que je fasse. "Fais" is the indicative; "ferai" the futur; the infinitive is only possible with the same subject (Je veux faire des études).

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Je veux que je parte demain.
questions.explanation: One person both wants and leaves, so French uses the infinitive, with no de after vouloir: Je veux partir. Que + subjunctive is only for a different subject (Je veux que tu partes).

questions.stem: Complete: "J'espère que tu ___ samedi."
questions.explanation: Espérer que takes the indicative in the affirmative, very often the futur: J'espère que tu viendras. (Souhaiter que would take the subjunctive: Je souhaite que tu viennes.)

questions.stem: Complete: "Je suis content ___ voir."
questions.explanation: Same subject (I'm happy, I see you) → infinitive. After an adjective of feeling, the infinitive needs de: Je suis content de te voir.

questions.stem: What does "J'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve." mean?
choices: I'm not afraid of the rain.
I was afraid it would rain.
questions.explanation: The ne after avoir peur que is a ne explétif: it is not negative. A real negative needs pas: J'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve pas = I'm afraid it won't rain.

questions.stem: Choose the everyday way to say "My parents don't let me go out in the evening."
choices: Mes parents m'interdisent que je sorte le soir.
Mes parents m'interdisent de sortir le soir.
Mes parents interdisent moi sortir le soir.
Mes parents m'interdisent à sortir le soir.
questions.explanation: Interdire à quelqu'un de + infinitive: m'interdisent de sortir. You can't combine the indirect object me with que + subjunctive, and interdire takes de, not à.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mes parents m'autorisent ___ rentrer à minuit."
questions.explanation: Autoriser quelqu'un à + infinitive: they allow me to come home at midnight. Compare permettre à quelqu'un de, interdire à quelqu'un de.

questions.stem: "J'ai réussi mon examen ! J'avais tellement peur de rater…" How does the speaker feel now?
questions.explanation: After a fear that turned out wrong, you feel relieved: soulagé. Gêné = embarrassed, vexé = offended, sévère = strict.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ma grand-mère tient ___ ce que nous venions à Noël."
questions.explanation: Tenir à = to be keen on; before a clause it becomes tenir à ce que + subjunctive: elle tient à ce que nous venions.

questions.stem: Complete: "C'est dommage que ta sœur ne ___ pas venir."
questions.explanation: C'est dommage que expresses a feeling → subjunctive. Pouvoir is irregular: que je puisse, qu'elle puisse.

questions.stem: Read: "Mon fils a quinze ans. Je refuse qu'il passe ses soirées sur son téléphone, mais je ne suis pas trop sévère : je l'autorise à jouer une heure le week-end." What does the parent allow?
choices: One hour of games at the weekend
One hour of games every evening
questions.explanation: "Je l'autorise à jouer une heure le week-end" = I let him play for an hour at the weekend. The parent refuses evenings on the phone.

questions.stem: What is "le fossé entre les générations"?
questions.explanation: Le fossé is literally a ditch; between groups of people it means a gap: le fossé entre les générations = the generation gap.

questions.stem: Write the subjunctive of savoir: "Je suis surprise que tu ___ déjà la nouvelle."
questions.explanation: Savoir is irregular: que je sache, que tu saches, qu'il sache. Être surpris que → subjunctive.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I'd like you to tidy your room."
questions.explanation: Je voudrais que tu ranges ta chambre. A new subject (tu) after vouloir needs que + subjunctive; for -er verbs the tu subjunctive looks like the present.

questions.stem: Match each adjective with its meaning.
questions.explanation: Déçu = disappointed; soulagé = relieved; gêné = embarrassed; ému = moved; vexé = offended. Furious is furieux.

questions.stem: Which sentences need a subjunctive in the blank? Select all that apply.
choices: Ma mère est fière que je ___ (réussir).
questions.explanation: Souhaiter que (a wish) and être fier que (a feeling) take the subjunctive: que tu réussisses, que je réussisse. Espérer que and savoir que take the indicative: que tu réussiras, que tu réussis.

questions.stem: How does each person feel? Name each numbered face.

image.alt: Five numbered cartoon faces without words: 1 eyebrows raised in the middle, mouth turned down, a burst balloon below; 2 eyes closed, a smile, a puff of breath and a drop of sweat; 3 pink cheeks, eyes looking sideways, a wavy mouth and a drop of sweat; 4 red face, frown, clenched teeth, steam rising; 5 a tear, a small smile and a red heart.

questions.explanation: 1 disappointed (déçu: the burst balloon), 2 relieved (soulagé: a sigh of relief), 3 embarrassed (gêné: blushing), 4 furious (furieux: steam), 5 moved (ému: a tear and a heart). No face shows surprise (étonné) or strictness (sévère).

questions.stem: Complete: "Je doute que cette information ___ vraie."
questions.explanation: Douter que → subjunctive: que cette information soit vraie. "Soient" is plural, but the subject (cette information) is singular.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je pense que ce site ___ fiable."
questions.explanation: An affirmative opinion (je pense que) presents the clause as true for the speaker: indicative. Only the negative (je ne pense pas que) takes the subjunctive.

questions.stem: Complete in standard written French: "Je ne crois pas que l'IA ___ tout faire."
questions.explanation: A negative opinion takes the subjunctive in standard French: je ne crois pas que + subjunctive. Pouvoir: que je puisse, qu'elle puisse. "Peut" is heard in relaxed speech, not in careful writing; the infinitive "pouvoir" needs no que.

questions.stem: Which expression is followed by the indicative?
questions.explanation: Something probable is still treated as a fact: il est probable que + indicative. Possible, il se peut que and peu probable all take the subjunctive.

questions.stem: What does "Il viendra sans doute." mean?
choices: He may come, but I doubt it.
questions.explanation: Sans doute means "probably". "Without any doubt" is sans aucun doute.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il me semble que tu ___ raison."
questions.explanation: Il me semble que gives a personal opinion, like je pense que: indicative. (Il semble que, with no person, usually takes the subjunctive.)

questions.stem: "Il paraît que le nouveau robot parle dix langues." What is the speaker doing?
choices: Describing a robot she has seen herself
questions.explanation: Il paraît que = apparently, people say that: it reports hearsay, with the indicative. It doesn't say whether the speaker believes it.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il est évident que l'IA ___ des limites."
questions.explanation: Il est évident que expresses certainty → indicative: l'IA a des limites. "Ait" would be the subjunctive, used after il est possible que or je doute que.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct in standard written French?
choices: Je ne pense pas qu'il ait raison.
Je ne pense pas qu'il a raison.
Je ne pense pas qu'il aie raison.
Je ne pense pas qu'il avoir raison.
questions.explanation: Negative opinion → subjunctive: qu'il ait (with t; aie is the je form). "Qu'il a raison" is heard in relaxed speech but not used in careful writing.

questions.stem: What does "Ce site n'est pas fiable." mean?
questions.explanation: Fiable = reliable, trustworthy (from se fier à, to trust). Real = réel; free = gratuit.

questions.stem: Read: "Sur Internet, il paraît qu'une IA a trouvé un remède contre le rhume. Les experts doutent que ce soit vrai : aucune étude scientifique ne le prouve, et la source est un site inconnu." Why do the experts doubt it?
choices: The AI made a mistake in its calculations.
No study proves it and the source is unknown.
The experts haven't seen the news.
questions.explanation: "Aucune étude scientifique ne le prouve" = no scientific study proves it; "la source est un site inconnu" = the source is an unknown website.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il se peut qu'il ___ demain." (pleuvoir)
questions.explanation: Il se peut que always takes the subjunctive. The subjunctive of il pleut is qu'il pleuve.

questions.stem: Write the subjunctive of être: "Je ne suis pas sûr que ce robot ___ dangereux."
questions.explanation: Ne pas être sûr que expresses doubt → subjunctive: qu'il soit.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I don't think it's true."
questions.explanation: Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai. Ne … pas surrounds pense; the negative opinion takes the subjunctive (ce soit).

questions.stem: Which mood follows each expression?
questions.explanation: Probable, il me semble que and il paraît que present things as facts or opinions: indicative. Possible and doubt: subjunctive. None of them is followed by an infinitive.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Il est possible que le robot soit en panne.
Je suis sûre qu'il ait raison.
Il semble que la machine soit en panne.
questions.explanation: Il est possible que and il semble que (usually) take the subjunctive (soit); peut-être que takes the indicative (viendra). "Je suis sûre que" expresses certainty, so it needs the indicative: qu'il a raison.

questions.stem: Put each expression in its place on the certainty scale, from surest (1) to least sure (4).

image.alt: A scale from "plus sûr" on the left to "moins sûr" on the right with four numbered empty zones. The first two zones are over a green band "+ indicative", the last two over a purple band "+ subjunctive".

questions.explanation: Certain → probable (both + indicative) → possible → doubtful (both + subjunctive). Il faut que is about necessity, not certainty.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je donne des vêtements pour que les enfants ___ chaud." (avoir)
questions.explanation: Pour que (purpose) + subjunctive: qu'ils aient. "Ont" is the indicative; "avoir" would need the same subject (pour avoir chaud).

questions.stem: Complete: "Rentrons avant qu'il ___ nuit." (faire)
questions.explanation: Avant que + subjunctive: qu'il fasse nuit (before it gets dark). Faire is irregular: que je fasse, qu'il fasse.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je travaille pour ___ ma vie."
questions.explanation: The same person works and earns, so French uses pour + infinitive: pour gagner ma vie. Que + subjunctive is for a new subject (pour que mes enfants fassent des études).

questions.stem: Which conjunction is followed by the indicative?
questions.explanation: Parce que gives a real cause, a fact: indicative. Bien que, pourvu que and sans que take the subjunctive.

questions.stem: What does "Pourvu qu'il fasse beau samedi !" mean?
choices: Let's hope it's nice on Saturday!
It will definitely be nice on Saturday!
Luckily, it was nice on Saturday!
Even if it's nice on Saturday!
questions.explanation: Alone at the start of a sentence, pourvu que + subjunctive expresses a wish or a worry: let's hope (that).

questions.stem: Complete: "Bien qu'elle ___ fatiguée, elle aide à la collecte."
questions.explanation: Bien que + subjunctive, even when the fact is real: bien qu'elle soit fatiguée. "Sois" is the je / tu form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Même s'il ___ froid, la collecte aura lieu."
questions.explanation: Même si follows the rule of si: present indicative here, never the subjunctive, and no futur or conditionnel after si.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence: "I eat before I leave."
choices: Je mange avant que je parte.
questions.explanation: One subject (I eat, I leave) → avant de + infinitive. Avant que + subjunctive is for a new subject: Je mange avant que tu partes.

questions.stem: What does "quoique" (one word) mean?
questions.explanation: Quoique = bien que = although, + subjunctive. Quoi que in two words means "whatever"; unless is à moins que; because is parce que.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous resterons ___ tout soit rangé."
questions.explanation: Before a clause, "until" is jusqu'à ce que + subjunctive (soit). Jusqu'à is only used before a noun; pendant que and dès que would need the indicative (est).

questions.stem: Read: "Collecte de jouets samedi. Les dons sont acceptés à condition que les jouets soient en bon état. Les bénévoles seront là de 9 h à 17 h, à moins qu'il pleuve : dans ce cas, la collecte aura lieu dans la salle des fêtes." What happens if it rains?
choices: The collection moves to the village hall.
questions.explanation: "À moins qu'il pleuve : dans ce cas, la collecte aura lieu dans la salle des fêtes" = unless it rains: in that case the collection will take place in the village hall.

questions.stem: What is "le sans-abri"?
questions.explanation: Un abri is a shelter, so un sans-abri is someone without shelter: a homeless person (plural les sans-abri).

questions.stem: Write the conjunction (two words) that means "so that": "Je parle lentement ___ tout le monde comprenne."
questions.explanation: Pour que (everyday) or afin que (formal) + subjunctive: pour que tout le monde comprenne.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Although he's tired, he's helping."
questions.explanation: Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il aide. Bien que + subjunctive (soit) opens the sentence; the main clause follows the comma.

questions.stem: What follows each word?
questions.explanation: Pour que and à moins que + subjunctive; parce que and même si + indicative; afin de + infinitive (same subject).

questions.stem: Which conjunctions take the subjunctive? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Avant que, sans que and à condition que take the subjunctive. Alors que, dès que and pendant que introduce facts and take the indicative.

questions.stem: Name each numbered part of the scene.

image.alt: A stand outside a supermarket with four numbers: 1 a banner reading "Main dans la main" with a heart; 2 crates of tins, pasta and rice on a table; 3 a woman in a yellow vest holding out a leaflet; 4 a shopping bag of food that a man is holding out to her.

questions.explanation: 1 the banner gives the name of the charity (l'association); 2 the food collected (la collecte); 3 the volunteer in her vest (la bénévole); 4 what the man gives (le don).

questions.stem: Complete: "Je suis content que tu ___ hier." (venir)
questions.explanation: Hier puts the coming before the feeling → subjonctif passé. Venir takes être: que tu sois venu(e). "Es venu" is the passé composé (indicative).

questions.stem: Choose the auxiliary: "Je doute qu'il ___ compris."
questions.explanation: Comprendre takes avoir in the passé composé (il a compris), so its subjonctif passé is qu'il ait compris. "A" is indicative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Bien qu'elle ___ arrivée en retard, elle a tout fini."
questions.explanation: Arriver takes être (elle est arrivée), and bien que needs the subjunctive: bien qu'elle soit arrivée.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'm sorry you were ill (last week)"?
choices: Je suis désolé que tu sois malade.
Je suis désolé que tu as été malade.
Je suis désolé que tu étais malade.
Je suis désolé que tu aies été malade.
questions.explanation: The illness is over before the feeling → subjonctif passé: que tu aies été. "Que tu sois malade" means you are ill now; the other two use the indicative after a feeling.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je suis heureux que ta sœur soit ___." (arriver)
questions.explanation: With être the participle agrees with the subject, as in the passé composé: ta sœur (feminine singular) → arrivée.

questions.stem: Which sentence fits a message of sympathy after a death?
choices: Toutes mes félicitations à la famille.
Je te présente mes sincères condoléances.
Je suis content que tu aies réussi.
questions.explanation: Les condoléances (plural only) = condolences. Félicitations, bravo and être content que are for happy news.

questions.stem: What is "un faire-part"?
choices: a card announcing a birth, wedding or death
questions.explanation: Un faire-part (plural les faire-part) announces a family event: un faire-part de naissance, de mariage, de décès. A funeral is les obsèques.

questions.stem: What does "Je compatis à ta peine." mean?
choices: I'm sorry for the trouble I caused you.
I feel for you in your sorrow.
questions.explanation: Compatir à = to sympathise with; la peine = sorrow here. (La peine can also be "trouble, effort", or a sentence in court, but not in a sympathy message.)

questions.stem: Read: "Chère Lucie, j'ai appris avec beaucoup de peine le décès de ta grand-mère. Je suis désolée de ne pas avoir pu venir aux obsèques, mais je pense fort à toi." What does the writer regret?
choices: Not having been able to go to the funeral
questions.explanation: "Je suis désolée de ne pas avoir pu venir aux obsèques" = I'm sorry I couldn't come to the funeral (les obsèques).

questions.stem: Write the subjonctif passé of finir (two words): "Je suis fier que tu ___ ___ tes études."
questions.explanation: Finir takes avoir: tu as fini → que tu aies fini. No agreement with avoir here (the object comes after).

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I doubt he understood."
questions.explanation: Je doute qu'il ait compris: douter que + subjunctive; the understanding is already over, so the subjonctif passé.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the kind of message it comes from.
left: Nous avons la joie de vous annoncer la naissance de Léo.
Nous avons la tristesse de vous faire part du décès de notre mère.
Toutes mes félicitations pour votre mariage !
Je te présente mes sincères condoléances.
questions.explanation: La joie … la naissance: a birth announcement; la tristesse … le décès: a death notice (faire-part de décès); félicitations: congratulations; condoléances: sympathy.

questions.stem: Which sentences use the subjonctif passé correctly? Select all that apply.
choices: Je suis content que tu sois venu.
Il faut que tu aies fini avant midi.
Je suis triste que tu as perdu.
Bien qu'il a plu, nous sommes sortis.
questions.explanation: Sois venu, ait fini and aies fini are subjunctive auxiliaries + participles. "Que tu as perdu" and "bien qu'il a plu" use the indicative auxiliary: que tu aies perdu, bien qu'il ait plu.

questions.stem: Write the formal noun for "death" used in announcements: "Nous avons la tristesse de vous faire part du ___ de notre père."
questions.explanation: Le décès is the formal word (la mort is everyday). Du = de + le: du décès.

questions.stem: How do you say "Nobody move!"?
questions.explanation: The jussive: que + subjunctive for a third person. Personne takes ne without pas: Que personne ne bouge !

questions.stem: What does "Quoi que tu fasses, …" mean?
questions.explanation: Quoi que (two words) + subjunctive = whatever. Although is quoique (one word); whoever is qui que.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ la raison, je ne peux pas accepter."
questions.explanation: Quel agrees with the noun after soit: la raison is feminine singular → quelle que soit. "Quelque soit" is a common misspelling.

questions.stem: Which is the right spelling for "Although it's cold, we're going out"?
choices: Quoi qu'il fasse froid, nous sortons.
Quoique il fasse froid, nous sortons.
Quoi qu'il fait froid, nous sortons.
questions.explanation: "Although" is quoique (one word; you can replace it with bien que), elided before il: quoiqu'il, + subjunctive (fasse).

questions.stem: Complete: "Où que tu ___, écris-moi."
questions.explanation: Où que (wherever) + subjunctive. Aller: que j'aille, que tu ailles.

questions.stem: Someone says "Soit !" on its own. What do they mean?
questions.explanation: Soit ! alone accepts something, sometimes reluctantly. Soit … soit is "either … or".

questions.stem: Which form is the usual one before a plural noun: "___ les vacances !"?
questions.explanation: Vive, treated as a fixed interjection, is the usual form before a plural noun. Vivent is also accepted by some grammars, but much less common; vivez and vivons are not used.

questions.stem: What does "Il veut gagner coûte que coûte." mean?
choices: He wants to win as cheaply as possible.
He wants to win, but not at any price.
He wants to win the money.
He wants to win at all costs.
questions.explanation: Coûte que coûte = whatever it costs, at all costs.

questions.stem: In the tournament speech, "quoi qu'il arrive sur le terrain, on respecte l'arbitre". What must everyone do?
choices: Stay on the court until the end
questions.explanation: Quoi qu'il arrive = whatever happens; on respecte l'arbitre = we respect the referee.

questions.stem: Write the missing form of quel: "___ que soient tes idées, je t'écoute."
questions.explanation: Tes idées is feminine plural: quelles que soient tes idées. Soit is plural too: soient.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "May the best one win!"
questions.explanation: Que le meilleur gagne ! The jussive: que + subject + subjunctive (gagne).

questions.stem: Match each French phrase to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Sauve qui peut ! = every man for himself; Ainsi soit-il = amen; qui que ce soit = anyone at all; où que = wherever. Although is quoique.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Où que tu vas, je te suivrai.
questions.explanation: Quelle que soit l'heure agrees with l'heure (feminine). Qu'il vienne demain ! is a jussive. "Whatever you do" needs quoi que in two words (quoi que tu fasses), and où que needs the subjunctive (où que tu ailles).

questions.stem: Turn the order into a jussive: "Tell Paul to wait!" → "Que Paul ___ !" (attendre)
questions.explanation: Ils attendent → attend- + -e: que Paul attende.

questions.stem: Complete: "Si j'avais plus de temps, j'___ le piano."
questions.explanation: Si + imparfait (avais) → conditionnel présent: j'apprendrais (future stem apprendr- + -ais). "Apprendrai" is the futur, which goes with si + present; "apprenne" is a subjunctive and "apprendre" an infinitive.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Si j'avais une voiture, j'irai au travail en voiture.
Si j'avais une voiture, j'irais au travail en voiture.
Si j'aurais une voiture, j'irais au travail en voiture.
Si j'avais une voiture, j'aille au travail en voiture.
questions.explanation: Type 2: si + imparfait (avais), then the conditionnel (irais). "Si j'aurais" puts a conditionnel after si; "j'irai" is a futur, which doesn't match an imparfait; "j'aille" is a subjunctive.

questions.stem: Complete: "Si tu ___ (être) à ma place, qu'est-ce que tu ferais ?"
questions.explanation: The main clause is conditionnel (ferais), so the si clause takes the imparfait: si tu étais. Never "serais" or "seras" after si = if, and never a subjunctive ("sois").

questions.stem: Léa had a good interview and thinks she will probably get the job in Montreal. Which sentence is correct and fits?
choices: Si on me prenne, je partirai en septembre.
Si on me prend, je partirai en septembre.
Si on me prendrait, je partirai en septembre.
Si on me prenait, je partirai en septembre.
questions.explanation: A real possibility: type 1, si + present (prend), then the futur (partirai). The other three are wrong: a subjunctive after si, a conditionnel after si, and imparfait + futur, which don't match.

questions.topic: Même si, sinon, au cas où
questions.stem: Complete: "Même s'il ___ demain, on fera la randonnée."
questions.explanation: Même si works like si: present (pleut) with a futur in the main clause. No futur (pleuvra) or conditionnel (pleuvrait) after it, and no subjunctive (pleuve): même si always takes the indicative.

questions.topic: Même si, sinon, au cas où
questions.stem: In standard French, complete: "Prends ton manteau au cas où il ___ froid ce soir."
questions.explanation: Au cas où takes the conditionnel: au cas où il ferait froid. (You may hear "au cas où il fait froid" in casual speech, but the standard form is the conditionnel.) It is the opposite of si, which never takes the conditionnel.

questions.topic: Même si, sinon, au cas où
questions.stem: What does "sinon" mean in "Réserve maintenant, sinon il n'y aura plus de places."?
questions.explanation: Sinon = otherwise, or else: book now; if you don't, there won't be any seats left. "Even if" is même si, "in case" is au cas où, "as long as" is tant que.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "standard of living" (how much you can afford)?
questions.explanation: Le niveau de vie is the standard of living. La qualité de vie is how good life feels, le mode de vie how you live (lifestyle), and le coût de la vie what it costs to live.

questions.stem: Read: "Si je n'avais pas d'enfants, je m'expatrierais au Canada. Mais mes enfants sont à l'école ici, alors je reste." What is true?
choices: She has already moved to Canada.
She will move as soon as her children leave school.
She has children and is staying.
She has no children and is moving to Canada.
questions.explanation: Si + imparfait describes the present as it isn't: "if I didn't have children" means she does have them. "Je reste" confirms she is staying. Nothing is said about moving later.

questions.stem: In which sentence is a conditionnel after "si" correct?
choices: Si je serais à la campagne, je serais heureux.
Si tu voudrais, on pourrait partir.
Je me demande si je serais heureux à la campagne.
Même si je serais riche, je travaillerais.
questions.explanation: In "Je me demande si je serais heureux à la campagne", si means "whether" (an indirect question after je me demande), so any tense is possible. After si or même si meaning "if", the conditionnel is never used: si j'étais, même si j'étais, si tu voulais.

questions.stem: What does "S'il faisait beau, on mangeait dans le jardin." describe?
choices: a past habit: whenever it was nice
a regret about one day in the past
questions.explanation: Both halves are in the imparfait (faisait, mangeait), so nothing is imagined: si means "whenever", and the sentence describes what used to happen. An unreal situation now would have a conditionnel: on mangerait.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "Le télétravail, ça te tente ?" What is she asking?
choices: Are you afraid of working from home?
Have you ever worked from home?
Do you fancy working from home?
questions.explanation: Tenter also means "to tempt": ça te tente ? = does it tempt you, do you fancy it? It isn't about having tried it (that would be essayer) or about fear.

questions.stem: What does "Tu risques de t'ennuyer à la campagne." mean?
choices: You might get bored in the country.
You'll never be bored in the country.
You're taking a big risk by moving to the country.
You risk boring people in the country.
questions.explanation: Risquer de + infinitive often means "might, be likely to" for something unwelcome. S'ennuyer is to be bored (not to bore someone else).

questions.stem: Type the verb in the conditionnel présent: "Si nous habitions à la campagne, nous ___ (avoir) un grand jardin."
questions.explanation: Si + imparfait (habitions) → conditionnel présent: the future stem of avoir, aur-, + -ions → nous aurions.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "If I were you, I would accept this offer."
questions.explanation: Si + imparfait first, then a comma, then the conditionnel: "Si j'étais toi, j'accepterais cette offre." Note toi, not tu, after j'étais.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to what it expresses.
left: Si tu viens, on ira au cinéma.
Si j'étais riche, je ne travaillerais plus.
Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
S'il faisait beau, on mangeait dehors.
questions.explanation: Present + futur: real (type 1). Imparfait + conditionnel présent: unreal now (type 2). Plus-que-parfait + conditionnel passé: unreal past (type 3). Imparfait + imparfait: what used to happen whenever it was nice.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct standard French? Select all that apply.
choices: Si j'avais le choix, je vivrais au bord de la mer.
